items.title: Sets
explanation: What is a Set?

A set is an unordered collection of unique elements in Python. The most important characteristics of a set are that it does not allow duplicate values and it supports mathematical set operations such as union, intersection, and difference.
numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40} print(numbers)
Definition: A set is a collection of unique elements used when duplicate values are not required and fast membership checking or set operations are useful.
Important Characteristics of Sets

• Sets contain only unique elements.
  • Sets are unordered collections.
  • Sets are mutable.
  • Sets do not support indexing.
  • Sets support fast membership testing using in.
  • Sets can contain values of different hashable data types.
LIST → Ordered + Mutable + Duplicates allowed TUPLE → Ordered + Immutable + Duplicates allowed SET → Unordered + Mutable + Unique values
Creating a Set
Sets are usually created using curly braces {}.
numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40} names = {"Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"} print(numbers) print(names)
Duplicate Values Are Automatically Removed
If duplicate values are added to a set, Python keeps only one copy of each value.
numbers = {10, 20, 20, 30, 30, 30} print(numbers)
The result contains only 10, 20, and 30.
Memory Rule: Set = Unique values. If you put duplicates into a set, duplicates are automatically removed.
Empty Set
Be careful when creating an empty set. {} creates an empty dictionary, not an empty set.
empty_set = set() print(empty_set) print(type(empty_set))
empty = {} print(type(empty)) # dict
Important: Use set() to create an empty set. Use {} for an empty dictionary.
Creating a Set from Another Collection
The set() function can convert an iterable such as a list or tuple into a set.
numbers = [10, 20, 20, 30, 30, 40] unique_numbers = set(numbers) print(unique_numbers)
This is one of the most useful ways to remove duplicate values from a collection.
Sets Do Not Support Indexing
Because sets are unordered, you cannot access elements using indexes.
numbers = {10, 20, 30} # print(numbers[0]) # TypeError
Unlike lists and tuples, a set does not provide positional access.
Looping Through a Set
You can iterate through a set using a for loop.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM", "SSD"} for part in parts: print(part)
Do not rely on the iteration order of a set for application logic.
Checking Membership
The in operator is one of the main reasons sets are useful. It checks whether a value exists in the set.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM", "SSD"} print("RAM" in parts) print("GPU" in parts) print("GPU" not in parts)
Data Engineering Connection: Sets are very useful when you need to quickly check whether an ID, part number, store code, or other value belongs to a known collection of unique values.
Adding Elements with add()
Use add() to add one element to a set.
numbers = {10, 20, 30} numbers.add(40) print(numbers)
If the value already exists, adding it again does not create a duplicate.
numbers = {10, 20, 30} numbers.add(20) print(numbers)
Adding Multiple Elements with update()
Use update() to add multiple elements from another iterable.
numbers = {10, 20, 30} numbers.update([40, 50, 60]) print(numbers)
You can also update a set using another set or tuple.
numbers = {10, 20} numbers.update((30, 40)) print(numbers)
Removing Elements with remove()
The remove() method removes a specific element.
numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40} numbers.remove(30) print(numbers)
If the value does not exist, remove() raises a KeyError.
Removing Elements with discard()
discard() also removes an element, but it does not raise an error if the element does not exist.
numbers = {10, 20, 30} numbers.discard(20) numbers.discard(100) print(numbers)
Remember: remove() raises an error when the value is missing. discard() safely does nothing when the value is missing.
Removing an Arbitrary Element with pop()
The pop() method removes and returns an arbitrary element from a set.
numbers = {10, 20, 30} value = numbers.pop() print(value) print(numbers)
Because sets are unordered, you should not assume which element pop() will remove.
Removing All Elements with clear()
numbers = {10, 20, 30} numbers.clear() print(numbers)
clear() removes every element from the set.
Set Union
Union combines all unique elements from two sets. It can be written using | or the union() method.
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {3, 4, 5} result = a | b print(result)
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {3, 4, 5} result = a.union(b) print(result)
Set Intersection
Intersection returns only the elements that exist in both sets. It can be written using & or intersection().
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {3, 4, 5} result = a & b print(result)
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {3, 4, 5} result = a.intersection(b) print(result)
A = {1, 2, 3} B = {3, 4, 5} A ∩ B = {3}
Set Difference
Difference returns elements that are present in the first set but not in the second set.
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {3, 4, 5} print(a - b) print(b - a)
A - B = {1, 2} B - A = {4, 5}
The order matters when using difference.
Symmetric Difference
Symmetric difference returns elements that are in either set, but not in both.
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {3, 4, 5} result = a ^ b print(result)
Subset
A set is a subset of another set when every element of the first set is also present in the second set.
small = {1, 2} big = {1, 2, 3, 4} print(small.issubset(big))
You can also use the <= operator.
print(small <= big)
Superset
A set is a superset when it contains all elements of another set.
small = {1, 2} big = {1, 2, 3, 4} print(big.issuperset(small))
You can also use the >= operator.
Disjoint Sets
Two sets are disjoint when they have no elements in common.
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {4, 5, 6} print(a.isdisjoint(b))
Meaning: If the intersection of two sets is empty, the sets are disjoint.
Set Size
Use len() to find the number of unique elements in a set.
numbers = {10, 20, 20, 30, 30} print(len(numbers))
The result is based on unique values, because duplicates are automatically removed.
Sets and Data Engineering
Sets are particularly useful in Data Engineering for comparing unique IDs, detecting differences between datasets, checking membership, and removing duplicate values.
source_ids = {101, 102, 103, 104} target_ids = {101, 102, 104, 105} missing_ids = source_ids - target_ids new_ids = target_ids - source_ids print("Missing:", missing_ids) print("New:", new_ids)
This kind of comparison can help identify records that exist in one dataset but not another.
Removing Duplicate Data
A common practical use is converting a list containing duplicate values into a set to obtain unique values.
part_numbers = [ "2YNZK4", "2YNZK4", "96ABC1", "96ABC1", "78XYZ9" ] unique_parts = set(part_numbers) print(unique_parts)
This is useful during basic data cleaning when the requirement is simply to identify unique values.
Comparing Two Data Sources
Suppose one system contains store codes and another system contains store codes. Sets make it easy to compare them.
system_a = {"BM11", "BM12", "BM13"} system_b = {"BM11", "BM13", "BM14"} print("Only in A:", system_a - system_b) print("Only in B:", system_b - system_a) print("Common:", system_a & system_b)

Data Engineering Connection: Set difference and intersection are useful for reconciliation tasks, such as checking missing IDs, new records, common keys, or differences between source and target systems.
Hashable Values in Sets
Set elements must be hashable. Common immutable values such as integers, strings, and tuples containing hashable values can be stored in a set.
valid = {10, "Python", (1, 2)} print(valid)
A list cannot be directly stored as a set element because lists are mutable and therefore unhashable.
# invalid # data = {[1, 2], [3, 4]} # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
Important: A set can contain immutable hashable objects, but mutable objects such as lists and dictionaries cannot be set elements.
Set vs List vs Tuple

FeatureListTupleSet
OrderedYesYesNo
MutableYesNoYes
DuplicatesAllowedAllowedNo
IndexingYesYesNo
Membership checkingSupportedSupportedVery useful
Set operationsNoNoYes
Common Mistakes
# Mistake 1: Expecting indexing numbers = {10, 20, 30} # print(numbers[0])
# Mistake 2: Assuming the order is fixed numbers = {10, 20, 30} for number in numbers: print(number)
Do not write code that depends on a particular set iteration order.
# Mistake 3: Creating an empty set incorrectly empty = {} print(type(empty)) # dict # Correct empty = set() print(type(empty)) # set
# Mistake 4: Trying to store a list inside a set # data = {[1, 2], [3, 4]} # TypeError
Quick Memory Rule
SET ↓ Unique values ↓ No indexing ↓ Fast membership checking ↓ Union / Intersection / Difference
Remember: Use a set when you mainly care about unique values, membership checking, or comparing collections rather than maintaining a specific order.
Summary

• Sets store unique values.
  • Sets are unordered collections.
  • Sets are mutable.
  • Sets do not support indexing.
  • Use set() to create an empty set.
  • Use add() for one element and update() for multiple elements.
  • remove() raises an error when the value is missing, while discard() does not.
  • Use in for membership checking.
  • Union combines unique values.
  • Intersection finds common values.
  • Difference finds values present in one set but not another.
  • Symmetric difference finds values that are in either set but not both.
  • Sets are highly useful for unique IDs and dataset reconciliation in Data Engineering.
practice: Step 1: Create a set containing five numbers and print it.
numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50} print(numbers)
Step 2: Create a set containing duplicate values and verify that duplicates are removed.
numbers = {10, 20, 20, 30, 30, 40} print(numbers)
Step 3: Create an empty set and verify its type.
data = set() print(type(data))
Step 4: Add one value using add() and multiple values using update().
numbers = {10, 20} numbers.add(30) numbers.update([40, 50]) print(numbers)
Step 5: Practice remove(), discard(), and clear().
numbers = {10, 20, 30, 40} numbers.remove(20) numbers.discard(100) print(numbers) numbers.clear() print(numbers)
Step 6: Create two sets and practice union, intersection, and difference.
a = {1, 2, 3, 4} b = {3, 4, 5, 6} print(a | b) print(a & b) print(a - b) print(b - a)
Step 7: Check whether one set is a subset of another.
small = {1, 2} big = {1, 2, 3, 4} print(small.issubset(big)) print(big.issuperset(small))
Step 8: Remove duplicate part numbers from a list using a set.
parts = ["A100", "A100", "B200", "C300", "B200", "C300"] unique_parts = set(parts) print(unique_parts)
Step 9: Compare two sets of IDs and find records missing from each source.

source_ids = {101, 102, 103, 104} target_ids = {101, 102, 104, 105} print("Missing from target:", source_ids - target_ids) print("Only in target:", target_ids - source_ids) print("Common IDs:", source_ids & target_ids)
Step 10: Create two sets of store codes and perform a reconciliation check.

system_a = {"BM11", "BM12", "BM13", "BM14"} system_b = {"BM11", "BM13", "BM14", "BM15"} print("Common:", system_a & system_b) print("Only in A:", system_a - system_b) print("Only in B:", system_b - system_a)
Practice Goal: Be able to use sets for unique-value handling, membership checking, duplicate removal, and comparing datasets or collections.

qna.q: Q1. What is a set in Python?
qna.a: A set is an unordered collection of unique elements.

qna.q: Q2. Does a set allow duplicate values?
qna.a: No. Duplicate values are automatically removed.

qna.q: Q3. Are sets ordered?
qna.a: No. You should not rely on a set having a particular order.

qna.q: Q4. Are sets mutable?
qna.a: Yes. You can add and remove elements from a set.

qna.q: Q5. Can you use indexing with a set?
qna.a: No. Sets do not support positional indexing.

qna.q: Q6. How do you create an empty set?
qna.a: Use set(). The expression {} creates an empty dictionary.

qna.q: Q7. How do you add one element to a set?
qna.a: Use the add() method.

qna.q: Q8. How do you add multiple elements to a set?
qna.a: Use the update() method with an iterable.

qna.q: Q9. What is the difference between remove() and discard()?
qna.a: remove() raises a KeyError when the value does not exist, while discard() does nothing.

qna.q: Q10. What does pop() do on a set?
qna.a: It removes and returns an arbitrary element from the set.

qna.q: Q11. How do you check whether a value exists in a set?
qna.a: Use the in operator, such as value in my_set.

qna.q: Q12. What is set union?
qna.a: Union combines the unique elements from two or more sets.

qna.q: Q13. What is set intersection?
qna.a: Intersection returns elements that are common to both sets.

qna.q: Q14. What is set difference?
qna.a: Difference returns elements that exist in the first set but not in the second set.

qna.q: Q15. What is symmetric difference?
qna.a: It returns elements that belong to either set but not to both.

qna.q: Q16. What is a subset?
qna.a: A set is a subset of another set when every element in the first set is also present in the second set.

qna.q: Q17. What does isdisjoint() check?
qna.a: It checks whether two sets have no elements in common.

qna.q: Q18. Why are sets useful for removing duplicates?
qna.a: Because a set automatically keeps only unique values.

qna.q: Q19. Why are sets useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: They are useful for unique-value handling, membership checks, and comparing IDs or values between datasets.

qna.q: Q20. Give a Data Engineering example of set difference.
qna.a: If source_ids and target_ids are sets, source_ids - target_ids can identify IDs present in the source but missing from the target.

items.title: Dictionaries
explanation: What is a Dictionary?
A dictionary is a mutable collection of data stored as key-value pairs. Each key is used to identify and access its corresponding value.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "Data Engineering" } print(employee)
Definition: A dictionary stores data in the form key: value, allowing you to access values using meaningful keys instead of numeric indexes.
Dictionary Structure
Dictionary ↓ Key → Value "id" → 101 "name" → "John" "salary" → 50000
For example, in "name": "John", name is the key and John is the value.
Creating a Dictionary
Dictionaries are commonly created using curly braces {}.
student = { "name": "Alice", "age": 21, "course": "Python" } print(student)
A dictionary can contain values of different data types.
data = { "id": 101, "name": "Laptop", "price": 54999.50, "available": True } print(data)
Empty Dictionary
An empty dictionary can be created using {} or dict().
data1 = {} data2 = dict() print(data1) print(data2)
Dictionary Keys
Dictionary keys must be unique and hashable. Common key types include strings, integers, and tuples containing hashable values.
data = { "name": "John", 101: "Employee ID", (1, 2): "Coordinate" } print(data)
Keys cannot normally be mutable objects such as lists or dictionaries.
# Invalid # data = {[1, 2]: "value"} # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'
Dictionary Keys Must Be Unique
If the same key is written more than once, the later value replaces the earlier value.
data = { "name": "John", "name": "David" } print(data)
The dictionary contains only one name key, with the final value.
Remember: Dictionary keys are unique. Values can be duplicated.
Accessing Dictionary Values
Unlike lists and tuples, dictionaries are accessed using keys rather than numeric indexes.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } print(employee["id"]) print(employee["name"]) print(employee["department"])
Accessing a Missing Key
Using square brackets with a key that does not exist raises a KeyError.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } # print(employee["salary"]) # KeyError: 'salary'
Using get()
The get() method safely retrieves a value. If the key does not exist, it returns None by default.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } print(employee.get("name")) print(employee.get("salary"))
You can also provide a default value.
print(employee.get("salary", 0))
Practical Rule: Use data[key] when the key must exist. Use get() when the key may be missing.
Adding a New Key-Value Pair
You can add a new entry by assigning a value to a new key.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } employee["department"] = "Data Engineering" print(employee)
Updating an Existing Value
Assigning a value to an existing key replaces its current value.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } employee["name"] = "David" print(employee)
The same syntax is used for both adding new keys and updating existing keys.
Using update()
The update() method can add or update multiple key-value pairs.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } employee.update({ "department": "IT", "location": "Chennai" }) print(employee)
Removing an Item with pop()
pop() removes a specified key and returns its value.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } removed = employee.pop("department") print(removed) print(employee)
You can also provide a default value when the key may not exist.
removed = employee.pop("salary", 0) print(removed)
Removing the Last Inserted Item with popitem()
popitem() removes and returns the last inserted key-value pair.
data = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } item = data.popitem() print(item) print(data)
Deleting a Key with del
The del statement can remove a specific dictionary entry.
data = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } del data["department"] print(data)
Clearing a Dictionary
The clear() method removes all key-value pairs from a dictionary.
data = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } data.clear() print(data)
Checking Whether a Key Exists
The in operator checks dictionary keys.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } print("name" in employee) print("salary" in employee) print("salary" not in employee)
Important: When used directly with a dictionary, in checks for keys, not values.
Checking Whether a Value Exists
To check values, use values().
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } print("John" in employee.values()) print(101 in employee.values())
Getting Dictionary Keys
The keys() method returns a view containing the dictionary's keys.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } print(employee.keys())
You can loop through the keys.
for key in employee.keys(): print(key)
Getting Dictionary Values
The values() method provides access to the dictionary's values.
for value in employee.values(): print(value)
Getting Key-Value Pairs with items()
The items() method returns key-value pairs. This is one of the most useful methods when looping through a dictionary.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } for key, value in employee.items(): print(key, value)
items() ↓ (key, value) ↓ "id" 101 "name" "John" "department" "IT"
Looping Through a Dictionary
There are several ways to iterate through a dictionary depending on what you need.

data = { "id": 101, "name": "Laptop", "quantity": 25 } # Keys for key in data: print(key) # Values for value in data.values(): print(value) # Keys and values for key, value in data.items(): print(key, value)
Dictionary Length
Use len() to find the number of key-value pairs.
data = { "id": 101, "name": "Laptop", "quantity": 25 } print(len(data))
Nested Dictionaries
A dictionary can contain another dictionary as a value. This creates a nested dictionary.
employees = { "emp101": { "name": "John", "department": "IT" }, "emp102": { "name": "Alice", "department": "HR" } } print(employees["emp101"]["name"])
Nested dictionaries are useful for representing hierarchical data.
Dictionary Containing Lists
A dictionary value can also be a list.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "skills": ["Python", "SQL", "Spark"] } print(employee["skills"]) print(employee["skills"][0])
List of Dictionaries
A very common structure in Data Engineering is a list containing dictionaries, where each dictionary represents one record.

records = [ {"id": 101, "name": "Laptop", "quantity": 25}, {"id": 102, "name": "Monitor", "quantity": 10}, {"id": 103, "name": "Keyboard", "quantity": 50} ] for record in records: print(record["id"], record["name"], record["quantity"])

Data Engineering Connection: JSON data is commonly represented in Python using dictionaries and lists. A JSON object maps naturally to a Python dictionary, while a JSON array commonly maps to a Python list.
Dictionary as a Record
Dictionaries are excellent for representing records because each value has a meaningful name.
record = { "part_number": "2YNZK4-BGK-BL", "store_code": "BM11", "quantity": 150, "status": "Available" } print(record["part_number"]) print(record["store_code"]) print(record["quantity"])
This is often easier to understand than using positional values such as a tuple.
Dictionary from Two Lists
The zip() function can combine keys and values, and dict() can create a dictionary from them.
keys = ["id", "name", "quantity"] values = [101, "Laptop", 25] data = dict(zip(keys, values)) print(data)
This technique is useful when keys and values are already stored separately.
Dictionary Copying
Assigning one dictionary to another variable does not create an independent copy.
a = {"name": "John"} b = a b["name"] = "David" print(a) print(b)
Both variables refer to the same dictionary object.
Use copy() when you need a shallow copy.
a = {"name": "John"} b = a.copy() b["name"] = "David" print(a) print(b)
Dictionary Data in Data Engineering

Dictionaries are extremely important in Data Engineering because they are frequently used to represent structured records, configuration data, API responses, JSON objects, metadata, and intermediate processing results.
record = { "customer_id": 1001, "customer_name": "John", "country": "India", "orders": 15 } if record.get("orders", 0) > 10: print("High-value customer")
Using Dictionaries for Lookup
A dictionary can act as a lookup table where one value maps directly to another.
store_names = { "BM11": "Chennai", "BM12": "Bangalore", "BM13": "Hyderabad" } store_code = "BM11" print(store_names.get(store_code))
This pattern is useful when you repeatedly need to convert a code into a corresponding name or attribute.
Counting Values with a Dictionary
Dictionaries can be used to build simple frequency counters.
parts = ["A100", "B200", "A100", "C300", "B200", "A100"] counts = {} for part in parts: counts[part] = counts.get(part, 0) + 1 print(counts)
The result stores each unique part number as a key and its occurrence count as the value.
Data Engineering Connection: This basic counting pattern is useful for grouping and frequency analysis before learning more advanced tools such as Pandas and SQL aggregation.
Dictionary vs List vs Tuple vs Set

FeatureListTupleSetDictionary
StructureValuesValuesUnique valuesKey-value pairs
OrderedYesYesNoYes, insertion order is preserved
MutableYesNoYesYes
DuplicatesAllowedAllowedNoKeys unique, values may duplicate
AccessIndexIndexMembershipKey
Main UseCollection of valuesFixed collectionUnique valuesNamed data / lookup
Common Mistakes
# Mistake 1: Accessing a dictionary using an index employee = {"id": 101, "name": "John"} # print(employee[0])
Dictionaries are accessed using keys, not positional indexes.
# Correct print(employee["id"])
# Mistake 2: Assuming values are checked by 'in' data = {"name": "John", "city": "Chennai"} print("John" in data) # False print("John" in data.values()) # True
# Mistake 3: Accessing a missing key directly # print(data["salary"]) # Safer when the key may be missing print(data.get("salary"))
# Mistake 4: Accidentally replacing an existing value data = {"status": "Pending"} data["status"] = "Completed" print(data)
Assignment to an existing key updates the value instead of creating another key.
Quick Memory Rule
DICTIONARY ↓ Key → Value ↓ Fast lookup by key ↓ Add / Update / Remove ↓ Useful for records, JSON, APIs, and lookup tables
Remember: If you want to describe an object or record using meaningful field names, think dictionary = key → value.
Summary

• Dictionaries store key-value pairs.
  • Keys must be unique.
  • Values can be duplicated.
  • Dictionaries are mutable.
  • Access values using keys.
  • Use get() when a key may be missing.
  • Use keys(), values(), and items() to access dictionary data.
  • Use update() to add or update multiple entries.
  • Use pop(), popitem(), del, and clear() to remove data.
  • Dictionaries can contain lists and other dictionaries.
  • Lists of dictionaries are common representations of structured records.
  • Dictionaries are heavily used when working with JSON, APIs, configurations, and Data Engineering pipelines.
practice: Step 1: Create a dictionary containing an employee ID, name, department, and salary. Print the dictionary.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "Data Engineering", "salary": 50000 } print(employee)
Step 2: Access individual values using their keys.
print(employee["id"]) print(employee["name"]) print(employee["department"])
Step 3: Add a new key called location and update the department.
employee["location"] = "Chennai" employee["department"] = "Data Engineering" print(employee)
Step 4: Use get() to safely access a key that may not exist.
print(employee.get("salary")) print(employee.get("experience", 0))
Step 5: Loop through the dictionary and print every key and value.
for key, value in employee.items(): print(key, value)
Step 6: Create a list of dictionaries representing inventory records and print each part number and quantity.

inventory = [ {"part_number": "A100", "store_code": "BM11", "quantity": 50}, {"part_number": "B200", "store_code": "BM12", "quantity": 25}, {"part_number": "C300", "store_code": "BM11", "quantity": 75} ] for record in inventory: print(record["part_number"], record["quantity"])
Step 7: Create a dictionary that maps store codes to store names and perform a lookup.
stores = { "BM11": "Chennai", "BM12": "Bangalore", "BM13": "Hyderabad" } store_code = "BM11" print(stores.get(store_code))
Step 8: Count how many times each part number appears in a list.
parts = ["A100", "B200", "A100", "C300", "B200", "A100"] counts = {} for part in parts: counts[part] = counts.get(part, 0) + 1 print(counts)
Step 9: Compare two inventory records represented as dictionaries and access their quantities using keys.

record1 = { "part_number": "A100", "quantity": 50 } record2 = { "part_number": "B200", "quantity": 75 } print(record1["part_number"], record1["quantity"]) print(record2["part_number"], record2["quantity"])
Step 10: Create a nested dictionary representing a company and access a value from the nested structure.
company = { "name": "Example Company", "employee": { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } } print(company["employee"]["name"])
Practice Goal: Be able to create, access, update, remove, iterate through, and use dictionaries to represent real-world records and lookup data.

qna.a: get() allows you to safely retrieve a value and can return a default value when the key is missing.

qna.a: Assign a value to a new key, such as data["status"] = "Active".

qna.a: Assign a new value to its existing key.

qna.a: update() adds new key-value pairs and updates existing keys.

items.title: Mutable vs Immutable Objects
explanation: What Does Mutable and Immutable Mean?
In Python, mutability describes whether an object's value can be changed after the object has been created.
A mutable object can be changed in place. An immutable object cannot be changed after creation; when you appear to change its value, Python creates or uses another object instead.
Definition: Mutable = object can be modified after creation. Immutable = object's value cannot be modified after creation.
Mutable Object ↓ Can change its contents ↓ Same object can be modified Immutable Object ↓ Cannot change its value ↓ A new value/object is required
Python's data model explicitly distinguishes mutable objects such as lists and dictionaries from immutable objects such as numbers, strings, and tuples. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
Common Mutable Types

• list
  • dict
  • set
  • bytearray
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers[0] = 100 print(numbers)
The list itself was modified. This is an example of mutation.
Common Immutable Types

• int
  • float
  • bool
  • str
  • tuple
  • frozenset
name = "John" # A string cannot be modified character by character # name[0] = "D"
Strings are immutable, so operations that appear to change a string produce another string rather than modifying the original string. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
Mutable vs Immutable — Quick Comparison

FeatureMutableImmutable
Can change after creation?YesNo
ExamplesList, Dictionary, SetInteger, String, Tuple
Can modify contents?YesNo
Can be used as dictionary key?Generally noOften yes, if hashable
Example: Mutable List
data = [10, 20, 30] print(data) data.append(40) print(data)
The same list can be modified using methods such as append(), remove(), or by assigning to an index. Python's documentation describes lists as mutable. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
Example: Immutable Integer
x = 10 x = x + 5 print(x)
It is important to understand that the integer object containing 10 was not changed into 15. The expression produces the value 15, and the variable x is then bound to that value.
Important: Variables are names referring to objects. Mutability belongs to the object, not to the variable name.
Variables Point to Objects
One of the most important ideas for understanding mutability is that a variable does not contain the object itself in the simple conceptual model. It refers to an object.
numbers = [10, 20, 30]
numbers ↓ [10, 20, 30] ↑ list object
The variable numbers refers to a list object.
Two Variables Can Refer to the Same Mutable Object
a = [10, 20, 30] b = a b.append(40) print(a) print(b)
Both variables refer to the same list, so changing the list through b is visible through a.
Key Point: b = a does not create a new list. It creates another reference to the same list object.
Changing vs Reassigning
This distinction is extremely important.
Changing means modifying the existing mutable object.
a = [10, 20, 30] b = a b.append(40) print(a)
Reassigning means making a variable refer to a different object.
a = [10, 20, 30] b = a b = [100, 200] print(a) print(b)
Here, a still refers to the original list. Only b was reassigned.
Using id() to Understand Object Identity
The built-in id() function returns an identity value for an object. It can help demonstrate when two variables refer to the same object.
a = [10, 20, 30] b = a print(id(a)) print(id(b))
The two values are the same because a and b refer to the same list object.
a = [10, 20, 30] b = [10, 20, 30] print(a == b) print(a is b)
== checks whether the values are equal, while is checks whether both names refer to the same object.
== vs is

OperatorChecks
==Whether two objects have equal values
isWhether two references point to the same object
a = [10, 20] b = [10, 20] print(a == b) # True print(a is b) # False
The lists contain the same values, but they are two different list objects.
Immutable Objects and Reassignment
x = 10 y = x x = 20 print(x) print(y)
Changing x to 20 does not change y. The variable x is simply rebound to another integer value.
Before: x ──┐ ↓ 10 ← y After x = 20: x → 20 y → 10
Why Strings Are Immutable
You cannot modify an individual character of a Python string.
name = "Python" # name[0] = "J" # TypeError
Instead, create a new string.
name = "Python" name = "J" + name[1:] print(name)
The original string was not modified in place.
Why Tuples Are Immutable
data = (10, 20, 30) # data[0] = 100 # TypeError
A tuple cannot have its individual elements reassigned. However, a tuple can contain mutable objects such as lists. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
Important: Immutable Container Does Not Mean Deeply Immutable
This is a common point of confusion.
data = ([10, 20], "Python") data[0].append(30) print(data)
The tuple itself is immutable, but the list stored inside the tuple is mutable. Therefore, the list can change.
Tuple ↓ ([10, 20], "Python") ↓ mutable list ↓ [10, 20, 30]

Important: Immutability of a container does not automatically make the objects referenced by that container immutable. Python's data model explicitly notes this behavior. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}
Mutable Objects and Function Arguments
When a mutable object is passed to a function, the function can modify that object.
def add_item(data): data.append(40) numbers = [10, 20, 30] add_item(numbers) print(numbers)
The function modified the same list object that the caller passed.
Immutable Objects and Function Arguments
An immutable value cannot be changed in place by the function.
def add_value(x): x = x + 10 number = 20 add_value(number) print(number)
The original integer remains unchanged because integers are immutable.
Copying Mutable Objects
If you need an independent list or dictionary, assigning another variable is not enough.
original = [10, 20, 30] copy_data = original.copy() copy_data.append(40) print(original) print(copy_data)
The two lists are now separate objects.
Rule: For mutable collections, use an appropriate copying technique when you need an independent object.
Shallow Copy
A shallow copy creates a new outer collection, but nested objects are still shared.
data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] copy_data = data.copy() copy_data[0].append(99) print(data) print(copy_data)
The outer lists are different, but the nested list is shared.
data ─────→ [ ──→ [1, 2, 99], [3, 4] ] ↑ copy_data ─────────┘ Outer objects → different Nested object → shared
Deep Copy
When nested mutable objects must also be independently copied, Python provides copy.deepcopy().
import copy data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] copy_data = copy.deepcopy(data) copy_data[0].append(99) print(data) print(copy_data)
Now the nested structures are copied as well.
Remember: Shallow copy copies the outer structure. Deep copy recursively copies nested objects.
Mutability and Dictionary Keys
Dictionary keys must be hashable. Mutable objects such as lists and dictionaries cannot normally be used as dictionary keys because their contents can change.
# Invalid # data = {[1, 2]: "value"}

Immutable hashable objects such as strings, numbers, and suitable tuples can be used as dictionary keys. Python's documentation explains that hashability is required for dictionary keys and set members. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
data = { "name": "John", (101, "BM11"): "Inventory Record" } print(data)
Mutability and Sets
Set elements also need to be hashable, so mutable lists and dictionaries cannot be stored directly as set elements.
# Invalid # data = {[1, 2], [3, 4]}
A tuple containing only hashable elements can be used as a set element.
data = {(1, 2), (3, 4)} print(data)

Connection: Dictionary keys and set elements need stable hash values. This is why mutable containers such as lists and dictionaries cannot be used directly as keys or set members. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}
Data Engineering Example — Shared Mutable Data
Suppose you have a common configuration dictionary and accidentally assign it directly to another variable.
config = { "store_code": "BM11", "status": "Active" } pipeline_config = config pipeline_config["status"] = "Completed" print(config)
The original config also changes because both variables refer to the same dictionary.
For independent processing, create a copy when appropriate.
config = { "store_code": "BM11", "status": "Active" } pipeline_config = config.copy() pipeline_config["status"] = "Completed" print(config) print(pipeline_config)
Data Engineering Example — Why This Matters
Data pipelines frequently pass lists, dictionaries, and nested records between functions. If those objects are modified unexpectedly, later pipeline steps can receive incorrect data.
def clean_record(record): record["status"] = "cleaned" return record record = { "id": 101, "status": "raw" } clean_record(record) print(record)
Here the function changes the original dictionary. This behavior can be useful when intentional, but dangerous when the caller expects the original record to remain unchanged.
Data Engineering Connection: Understanding mutability helps prevent accidental modification of shared records, configuration objects, pipeline state, and nested data structures.
Hashable vs Mutable
Hashable means an object has a hash value that does not change during its lifetime and can therefore be used in contexts such as dictionary keys and set members.

ObjectMutable?Usually Hashable?
intNoYes
strNoYes
tupleNoYes, if its elements are hashable
listYesNo
dictYesNo
setYesNo
frozensetNoYes, if its elements are hashable
Python's glossary defines hashability in terms of a stable hash value and explains its role in dictionary keys and set members. :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}
Common Mistakes
# Mistake 1: Thinking assignment creates a copy original = [1, 2, 3] new_data = original new_data.append(4) print(original)
Both variables reference the same list.
# Mistake 2: Confusing == and is a = [1, 2] b = [1, 2] print(a == b) # True print(a is b) # False
# Mistake 3: Thinking tuple means everything inside is immutable data = ([1, 2], 10) data[0].append(3) print(data)
# Mistake 4: Using a mutable object as a dictionary key # data = {[1, 2]: "value"}
Quick Memory Rule
MUTABLE List / Dict / Set ↓ Can modify object IMMUTABLE Int / Float / Bool / String / Tuple ↓ Cannot modify object ↓ Create or use another value
Best Memory Trick: If you can change the contents of the existing object without creating a replacement object, it is mutable. If you cannot change its value after creation, it is immutable.
Summary

• Mutability describes whether an object's value can change after creation.
  • Lists, dictionaries, and sets are mutable.
  • Numbers, strings, and tuples are immutable.
  • Variables are names that refer to objects.
  • Two variables can refer to the same mutable object.
  • == compares values, while is checks object identity.
  • Assignment does not automatically create a copy of a mutable object.
  • Use copy() for a shallow copy when appropriate.
  • Use copy.deepcopy() when nested mutable objects also need independent copies.
  • Immutable and hashable objects can generally be used as dictionary keys or set elements.
  • Understanding mutability is important when processing lists, dictionaries, nested records, and configuration data in Data Engineering.
practice: Step 1: Create a list and modify one of its elements. Observe that the list itself changes.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers[0] = 100 print(numbers)
Step 2: Create a string and try to modify one character. Observe the error and understand why strings are immutable.
name = "Python" # name[0] = "J"
Step 3: Assign one list to another variable and modify the second variable. Check what happens to the first variable.
a = [10, 20, 30] b = a b.append(40) print(a) print(b) print(a is b)
Step 4: Create two separate lists with the same values and compare them using == and is.
a = [10, 20, 30] b = [10, 20, 30] print(a == b) print(a is b)
Step 5: Create a dictionary, assign it to another variable, modify the second variable, and observe the shared mutation.
data = {"status": "Pending"} other = data other["status"] = "Completed" print(data) print(other)
Step 6: Repeat the previous exercise using copy() so that the original dictionary does not change.
data = {"status": "Pending"} other = data.copy() other["status"] = "Completed" print(data) print(other)
Step 7: Create a tuple containing a list and modify the list inside the tuple. Understand why this is possible even though the tuple is immutable.
data = ([10, 20], "Python") data[0].append(30) print(data)
Step 8: Create a nested list, make a shallow copy, modify an inner list, and observe the result.
data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] copy_data = data.copy() copy_data[0].append(99) print(data) print(copy_data)
Step 9: Use deepcopy() and repeat the previous exercise.
import copy data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] copy_data = copy.deepcopy(data) copy_data[0].append(99) print(data) print(copy_data)
Step 10: Create a small Data Engineering example where a pipeline configuration dictionary is copied before modifying it.
config = { "store_code": "BM11", "status": "Active" } pipeline_config = config.copy() pipeline_config["status"] = "Completed" print("Original:", config) print("Pipeline:", pipeline_config)

Practice Goal: Be able to identify mutable and immutable objects, understand references and shared objects, distinguish mutation from reassignment, and avoid accidental data changes in Python programs and Data Engineering pipelines.

qna.q: Q1. What does mutable mean in Python?
qna.a: Mutable means an object's value or contents can be changed after the object is created.

qna.q: Q2. What does immutable mean?
qna.a: Immutable means an object's value cannot be changed after it is created.

qna.q: Q3. Give examples of mutable Python objects.
qna.a: Lists, dictionaries, and sets are common mutable objects.

qna.q: Q4. Give examples of immutable Python objects.
qna.a: Integers, floats, booleans, strings, and tuples are common immutable objects.

qna.q: Q5. Is a list mutable?
qna.a: Yes. List elements can be added, removed, or changed.

qna.q: Q6. Is a tuple mutable?
qna.a: No. A tuple itself is immutable.

qna.q: Q7. Are strings mutable?
qna.a: No. Strings are immutable.

qna.q: Q8. What happens when two variables are assigned to the same list?
qna.a: Both variables refer to the same list object, so a mutation through one variable is visible through the other.

qna.q: Q9. Does b = a create a copy of a list?
qna.a: No. It creates another reference to the same list object.

qna.q: Q10. What is the difference between == and is?
qna.a: == compares values for equality, while is checks whether two variables refer to the same object.

qna.q: Q11. What does id() help you understand?
qna.a: id() can help demonstrate the identity of an object and whether two variables refer to the same object.

qna.q: Q12. What is mutation?
qna.a: Mutation is changing the contents of an existing mutable object.

qna.q: Q13. What is reassignment?
qna.a: Reassignment makes a variable refer to another object or value.

qna.q: Q14. Can an immutable tuple contain a mutable list?
qna.a: Yes. The tuple cannot be structurally changed, but the mutable list stored inside it can be changed.

qna.q: Q15. Why can't a list normally be used as a dictionary key?
qna.a: Lists are mutable and therefore do not have the stable hash behavior required for dictionary keys.

qna.q: Q16. Why can a string be used as a dictionary key?
qna.a: Strings are immutable and hashable, so they can be used as dictionary keys.

qna.q: Q17. What is a shallow copy?
qna.a: A shallow copy creates a new outer collection while nested objects may still be shared.

qna.q: Q18. What is a deep copy?
qna.a: A deep copy recursively copies nested objects so that the copied structure does not share those nested mutable objects with the original.

qna.q: Q19. Why is mutability important in Data Engineering?
qna.a: Data pipelines often pass lists and dictionaries between functions. Unexpected mutation can change shared records or configuration and produce incorrect downstream results.

qna.q: Q20. What is the most important rule to remember about mutable objects?
qna.a: If multiple variables reference the same mutable object, changing the object through one reference can affect what the other references see.

items.title: Accessing and Modifying Data
explanation: What Does Accessing and Modifying Data Mean?
In Python, accessing data means retrieving values from a data structure, while modifying data means changing, adding, or removing values when the data structure supports modification.
Definition: Accessing = getting data. Modifying = changing, adding, or removing data.
The way you access or modify data depends on the Python data structure you are using.
LIST → index TUPLE → index SET → membership / iteration DICTIONARY → key STRING → index
Accessing Data from a List
Lists are ordered, so elements are accessed using their indexes. The first element has index 0.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM", "SSD", "GPU"] print(parts[0]) print(parts[1]) print(parts[3])
parts = ["CPU", "RAM", "SSD", "GPU"] ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ index 0 1 2 3
Negative Indexing in Lists
Negative indexes access elements from the end of the list.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM", "SSD", "GPU"] print(parts[-1]) print(parts[-2])
-1 refers to the last element, -2 to the second-last element, and so on.
Modifying a List Element
Because lists are mutable, an existing element can be changed using its index.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM", "SSD"] parts[1] = "Memory" print(parts)
The element at index 1 is replaced.
Adding Data to a List
Use append() to add one item to the end of a list.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM"] parts.append("SSD") print(parts)
Use insert() when you need to add an item at a specific position.
parts = ["CPU", "SSD"] parts.insert(1, "RAM") print(parts)
Use extend() to add multiple elements from another iterable.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM"] parts.extend(["SSD", "GPU"]) print(parts)
Removing Data from a List
Python provides several ways to remove list elements.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM", "SSD", "GPU"] parts.remove("RAM") print(parts)
remove() removes the first matching value.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM", "SSD", "GPU"] removed = parts.pop(2) print(removed) print(parts)
pop() removes and returns an element. If no index is supplied, it removes the last element.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM", "SSD"] del parts[1] print(parts)
del can remove an element using its index.
Accessing Multiple List Elements with Slicing
Slicing retrieves a range of elements.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM", "SSD", "GPU", "HDD"] print(parts[1:4]) print(parts[:3]) print(parts[2:])
The original list is not modified by normal slicing.
Accessing Data from a Tuple
Tuples are ordered, so they use indexing and slicing in the same way as lists.
record = (101, "Laptop", 25) print(record[0]) print(record[1]) print(record[-1])
However, tuples are immutable, so their existing elements cannot be modified.
record = (101, "Laptop", 25) # record[2] = 50 # TypeError
Key Difference: Lists allow access and modification. Tuples allow access but not direct modification.
Accessing Data from a Set
Sets are unordered and do not support indexing. You cannot use set_data[0] to retrieve an element.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM", "SSD"} # print(parts[0]) # TypeError
Instead, use membership checking or iterate through the set.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM", "SSD"} print("RAM" in parts) for part in parts: print(part)
Modifying a Set
Sets are mutable, so elements can be added or removed.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM"} parts.add("SSD") parts.discard("RAM") print(parts)
Because sets are unordered, you modify them by value rather than by position.
Accessing Data from a Dictionary
Dictionaries store key-value pairs, so values are accessed using their keys.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } print(employee["id"]) print(employee["name"]) print(employee["department"])
employee ↓ "id" → 101 "name" → "John" "department" → "IT"
Safe Dictionary Access with get()
If a key might not exist, get() is safer than direct indexing.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } print(employee.get("name")) print(employee.get("salary")) print(employee.get("salary", 0))
Direct access with employee["salary"] would raise a KeyError when the key is missing.
Modifying a Dictionary Value
Dictionaries are mutable. Assigning a new value to an existing key updates that value.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "status": "Active" } employee["status"] = "Completed" print(employee)
Adding a New Dictionary Entry
Assigning a value to a key that does not exist adds a new key-value pair.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } employee["department"] = "Data Engineering" print(employee)
Removing Dictionary Data
Use pop(), del, or popitem() depending on the requirement.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } employee.pop("department") print(employee)
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } del employee["department"] print(employee)
Accessing Dictionary Keys and Values
Use keys(), values(), and items() when you need to work with dictionary contents.
data = { "id": 101, "name": "Laptop", "quantity": 25 } print(data.keys()) print(data.values()) print(data.items())
items() is particularly useful for accessing both the key and value while looping.
for key, value in data.items(): print(key, value)
Accessing String Data
Strings are sequences of characters, so individual characters can be accessed using indexes.
name = "Python" print(name[0]) print(name[-1]) print(name[1:4])
Strings are immutable, so individual characters cannot be directly replaced.
name = "Python" # name[0] = "J" # TypeError
Instead, create a new string.
name = "Python" name = "J" + name[1:] print(name)
Accessing Nested Data
Real-world data often contains multiple levels of lists and dictionaries. You can access nested data by chaining indexes and keys.
employee = { "name": "John", "skills": ["Python", "SQL", "Spark"] } print(employee["skills"][0]) print(employee["skills"][2])
employee ↓ "skills" ↓ ["Python", "SQL", "Spark"] ↓ [0] → "Python"
Modifying Nested Data
If the nested object is mutable, you can modify it directly.
employee = { "name": "John", "skills": ["Python", "SQL"] } employee["skills"].append("Spark") print(employee)
The dictionary and its nested list are both mutable.
List of Dictionaries
A list of dictionaries is a very common structure for representing multiple records.

records = [ {"id": 101, "name": "Laptop", "quantity": 25}, {"id": 102, "name": "Monitor", "quantity": 10}, {"id": 103, "name": "Keyboard", "quantity": 50} ] print(records[0]["name"]) print(records[1]["quantity"])
records ↓ [0] → {"id": 101, "name": "Laptop", "quantity": 25} ↓ ["name"] ↓ "Laptop"
Modifying a Record in a List of Dictionaries
records = [ {"id": 101, "name": "Laptop", "quantity": 25}, {"id": 102, "name": "Monitor", "quantity": 10} ] records[0]["quantity"] = 30 print(records)
First, records[0] accesses the first dictionary. Then ["quantity"] accesses its quantity value.
Nested Dictionaries
Dictionaries can contain other dictionaries, allowing hierarchical data to be represented.
company = { "employee": { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } } print(company["employee"]["name"])
Modifying Nested Dictionaries
company = { "employee": { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } } company["employee"]["department"] = "Data Engineering" print(company)
Accessing Data While Looping
When processing multiple records, loops are commonly combined with indexing or dictionary keys.
records = [ {"id": 101, "name": "Laptop", "quantity": 25}, {"id": 102, "name": "Monitor", "quantity": 10} ] for record in records: print(record["id"], record["name"], record["quantity"])
This pattern is fundamental when processing collections of records in Python.
Modifying Data While Looping
You can modify individual mutable records while iterating through them when the modification is intentional.
records = [ {"id": 101, "status": "Pending"}, {"id": 102, "status": "Pending"} ] for record in records: record["status"] = "Processed" print(records)

Caution: Modifying a collection while iterating over it can produce unexpected behavior in some situations, especially when adding or removing elements from the collection itself. Be careful when changing the structure of a collection during iteration.
Accessing Data from Function Results
Functions often return collections. You can immediately access the returned data if you know its structure.
def get_record(): return { "id": 101, "name": "Laptop", "quantity": 25 } record = get_record() print(record["name"])
Accessing Data Safely in Real Pipelines
When processing external or changing data, some keys or fields may be missing. Defensive access can prevent unnecessary failures.

record = { "part_number": "A100", "quantity": 50 } part_number = record.get("part_number") store_code = record.get("store_code", "UNKNOWN") quantity = record.get("quantity", 0) print(part_number) print(store_code) print(quantity)

Data Engineering Connection: Source data may contain missing fields, optional fields, or unexpected records. Knowing when to use direct access versus safe access is important when building reliable data-processing code.
Accessing and Modifying Data — Data Structure Guide

Data TypeAccess UsingCan Modify?Typical Operation
ListIndex / SliceYesChange, append, remove
TupleIndex / SliceNoRead / unpack
SetMembership / iterationYesAdd / remove
DictionaryKeyYesAdd / update / remove
StringIndex / SliceNoCreate new string
Common Mistakes
# Mistake 1: Trying to index a set parts = {"CPU", "RAM", "SSD"} # print(parts[0])
# Mistake 2: Trying to modify a tuple record = (101, "Laptop", 25) # record[2] = 50
# Mistake 3: Accessing a missing dictionary key record = {"id": 101} # print(record["name"]) # Safer when the key may be missing print(record.get("name"))
# Mistake 4: Confusing a list index with a dictionary key records = [ {"id": 101, "name": "Laptop"} ] print(records[0]["name"])
Here 0 is the list index, while "name" is the dictionary key.
Quick Memory Rule
LIST → data[index] TUPLE → data[index] SET → value in data DICTIONARY → data[key] STRING → data[index]
Remember: Always identify the data structure first. Then choose the correct way to access or modify its data.
Summary

• Lists are accessed using indexes and can be modified.
  • Tuples are accessed using indexes but cannot be directly modified.
  • Sets do not support indexing; use membership checks or iteration.
  • Dictionaries are accessed using keys and can be modified.
  • Strings support indexing and slicing but are immutable.
  • Nested data requires combining indexes and keys.
  • Lists of dictionaries are common when working with collections of records.
  • get() is useful when dictionary keys may be missing.
  • Understanding access and modification is essential before working with larger Data Engineering datasets.
practice: Step 1: Create a list of five part numbers. Access the first, third, and last elements.
parts = ["A100", "B200", "C300", "D400", "E500"] print(parts[0]) print(parts[2]) print(parts[-1])
Step 2: Modify the second part number and add a new part number.
parts[1] = "B250" parts.append("F600") print(parts)
Step 3: Create a tuple representing a fixed product record and access each value.
record = (101, "Laptop", 25) print(record[0]) print(record[1]) print(record[2])
Step 4: Create a set of store codes and check whether a particular store exists.
stores = {"BM11", "BM12", "BM13"} print("BM11" in stores) print("BM20" in stores)
Step 5: Add and remove store codes from the set.
stores.add("BM14") stores.discard("BM12") print(stores)
Step 6: Create an inventory dictionary and access its values using keys.
inventory = { "part_number": "A100", "store_code": "BM11", "quantity": 50 } print(inventory["part_number"]) print(inventory["quantity"])
Step 7: Modify the quantity and add a new status field to the inventory dictionary.
inventory["quantity"] = 75 inventory["status"] = "Available" print(inventory)
Step 8: Create a list of inventory dictionaries and print each record's part number and quantity.

inventory = [ {"part_number": "A100", "quantity": 50}, {"part_number": "B200", "quantity": 25}, {"part_number": "C300", "quantity": 75} ] for record in inventory: print(record["part_number"], record["quantity"])
Step 9: Modify the quantity of the first inventory record.
inventory[0]["quantity"] = 100 print(inventory)
Step 10: Build a small data-processing example that safely reads an optional store code and updates the record status.
record = { "part_number": "A100", "quantity": 50 } store_code = record.get("store_code", "UNKNOWN") record["status"] = "Processed" print("Store:", store_code) print("Record:", record)

Practice Goal: Be able to identify the correct data-access method for lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, and strings, and confidently modify mutable data structures without accidentally changing immutable data.

qna.q: Q1. What does accessing data mean?
qna.a: Accessing data means retrieving a value from a data structure.

qna.q: Q2. What does modifying data mean?
qna.a: Modifying data means changing, adding, or removing data when the data structure supports those operations.

qna.q: Q3. How do you access an element in a list?
qna.a: Use its index, such as data[0].

qna.q: Q4. How do you modify a list element?
qna.a: Assign a new value to its index, such as data[0] = 100.

qna.q: Q5. Can a tuple be modified directly?
qna.a: No. Tuples are immutable.

qna.q: Q6. How do you access elements in a set?
qna.a: Sets do not support indexing. Use membership checking or iterate through the set.

qna.q: Q7. How do you add an element to a set?
qna.a: Use the add() method.

qna.q: Q8. How do you access a dictionary value?
qna.a: Use its key, such as data["name"].

qna.q: Q9. What happens if a dictionary key does not exist and you use square brackets?
qna.a: Python raises a KeyError.

qna.q: Q10. How can you safely access a possibly missing dictionary key?
qna.a: Use the get() method, optionally providing a default value.

qna.q: Q11. How do you add a new key-value pair to a dictionary?
qna.a: Assign a value to a new key, such as data["status"] = "Active".

qna.q: Q12. How do you update an existing dictionary value?
qna.a: Assign a new value to its existing key.

qna.q: Q13. How do you remove an item from a dictionary?
qna.a: You can use pop(), del, or popitem() depending on the requirement.

qna.q: Q14. Can strings be modified directly?
qna.a: No. Strings are immutable. You must create a new string.

qna.q: Q15. How do you access nested data?
qna.a: Combine indexes and keys according to the structure, such as records[0]["name"].

qna.q: Q16. What is a list of dictionaries?
qna.a: It is a list where each element is a dictionary, commonly used to represent multiple structured records.

qna.q: Q17. Why is records[0]["name"] valid?
qna.a: records[0] accesses the first list element, which is a dictionary, and ["name"] then accesses the dictionary value.

qna.q: Q18. What is the difference between modifying a list and modifying a tuple?
qna.a: A list can be changed after creation, while a tuple cannot be directly changed.

qna.q: Q19. Why is accessing and modifying data important in Data Engineering?
qna.a: Data pipelines constantly read, transform, validate, and update structured records, so understanding how Python data structures behave is fundamental.

qna.q: Q20. What is the most important rule for accessing Python data?
qna.a: First identify the data structure, then use its appropriate access method: index for lists and tuples, membership for sets, and keys for dictionaries.

items.title: List, Tuple, Set and Dictionary Methods
explanation: Why Learn Collection Methods?
Python provides built-in methods for working with lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries. These methods make it easier to add, remove, search, update, and process data.
Definition: A method is a function associated with an object that performs an operation on that object.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers.append(40) print(numbers)
Here, append() is a list method that modifies the list.
Collection Methods at a Glance

Data StructureImportant MethodsMain Purpose
Listappend(), extend(), insert(), remove(), pop(), clear(), index(), count(), sort(), reverse(), copy()Store and modify ordered collections
Tuplecount(), index()Work with fixed ordered collections
Setadd(), update(), remove(), discard(), pop(), clear(), union(), intersection(), difference()Unique values and set operations
Dictionaryget(), keys(), values(), items(), update(), pop(), popitem(), clear(), copy()Work with key-value data
List Methods
Lists are mutable, so they provide many methods for modifying and organizing their contents.
1. append()
append() adds one element to the end of a list.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers.append(40) print(numbers)
Result:
[10, 20, 30, 40]
Remember: append() adds exactly one object to the end of the list.
2. extend()
extend() adds each element from another iterable to the end of the list.
numbers = [10, 20] numbers.extend([30, 40, 50]) print(numbers)
Unlike append(), extend() adds the elements individually.
numbers = [10, 20] numbers.append([30, 40]) print(numbers) numbers = [10, 20] numbers.extend([30, 40]) print(numbers)
3. insert()
insert() adds an element at a specified index.
parts = ["CPU", "SSD"] parts.insert(1, "RAM") print(parts)
The existing elements are shifted to make room for the new element.
4. remove()
remove() removes the first matching value from a list.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM", "SSD", "RAM"] parts.remove("RAM") print(parts)
Only the first matching RAM is removed.
Important: remove() works with a value, not an index.
pop() removes and returns an element. If no index is supplied, it removes the last element.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] value = numbers.pop() print(value) print(numbers)
You can also specify an index.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] value = numbers.pop(1) print(value) print(numbers)
clear() removes all elements from a list.
numbers = [10, 20, 30] numbers.clear() print(numbers)
The list becomes empty.
index() returns the index of the first matching value.
parts = ["CPU", "RAM", "SSD", "GPU"] position = parts.index("SSD") print(position)
If the value does not exist, Python raises a ValueError.
count() returns the number of times a value appears in a list.
parts = ["RAM", "SSD", "RAM", "CPU", "RAM"] print(parts.count("RAM"))
Data Engineering Use: count() can help with simple frequency checks before moving to more advanced aggregation techniques.
sort() sorts the existing list in place.
numbers = [40, 10, 30, 20] numbers.sort() print(numbers)
You can sort in descending order using reverse=True.
numbers = [40, 10, 30, 20] numbers.sort(reverse=True) print(numbers)
10. reverse()
reverse() reverses the order of the existing list in place.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] numbers.reverse() print(numbers)
Important: reverse() reverses the current order. It does not sort the values.
copy() creates a shallow copy of the list.
original = [10, 20, 30] new_data = original.copy() new_data.append(40) print(original) print(new_data)
The two outer lists are independent.
List Methods — Quick Reference

MethodPurposeModifies List?
append(x)Add one item at the endYes
extend(iterable)Add multiple itemsYes
insert(i, x)Add item at indexYes
remove(x)Remove first matching valueYes
pop(i)Remove and return itemYes
clear()Remove all itemsYes
index(x)Find first matching indexNo
count(x)Count occurrencesNo
sort()Sort list in placeYes
reverse()Reverse list in placeYes
copy()Create shallow copyNo
Tuple Methods
Tuples are immutable, so they have far fewer methods than lists. The two main tuple methods are count() and index().
count() returns the number of occurrences of a value.
data = (10, 20, 20, 30, 20) print(data.count(20))
index() returns the index of the first occurrence of a value.
data = (10, 20, 30, 40) print(data.index(30))
Remember: Tuples cannot be changed, so methods such as append(), remove(), and sort() are not available for tuples.
Tuple Methods — Quick Reference

MethodPurposeModifies Tuple?
count(x)Count occurrencesNo
index(x)Find first matching indexNo
Set Methods
Sets are mutable and focused on unique values. Their methods are especially useful for adding, removing, and comparing collections.
add() adds one element to a set.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM"} parts.add("SSD") print(parts)
If the value already exists, the set remains unchanged.
2. update()
update() adds multiple elements from an iterable.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM"} parts.update(["SSD", "GPU"]) print(parts)
3. remove()
remove() removes a specified element. If the element does not exist, it raises a KeyError.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM", "SSD"} parts.remove("RAM") print(parts)
4. discard()
discard() removes an element if it exists. If it does not exist, nothing happens.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM", "SSD"} parts.discard("RAM") parts.discard("GPU") print(parts)
Remember: remove() raises an error for a missing element; discard() does not.
pop() removes and returns an arbitrary element from a set.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM", "SSD"} value = parts.pop() print(value) print(parts)
Do not depend on which specific element pop() removes.
clear() removes all elements from a set.
parts = {"CPU", "RAM", "SSD"} parts.clear() print(parts)
union() returns a new set containing unique elements from both sets.
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {3, 4, 5} result = a.union(b) print(result)
The | operator can also perform union.
result = a | b print(result)
8. intersection()
intersection() returns elements common to both sets.
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {3, 4, 5} result = a.intersection(b) print(result)
The & operator performs the same operation.
9. difference()
difference() returns elements present in the first set but not in the other set.
source = {101, 102, 103, 104} target = {101, 102, 104, 105} missing = source.difference(target) print(missing)
The - operator can also be used.
10. symmetric_difference()
symmetric_difference() returns values that are in either set but not in both.
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {3, 4, 5} result = a.symmetric_difference(b) print(result)
The ^ operator provides the same operation.
11. issubset()
issubset() checks whether every element of one set exists in another set.
small = {1, 2} big = {1, 2, 3, 4} print(small.issubset(big))
12. issuperset()
issuperset() checks whether one set contains every element of another set.
small = {1, 2} big = {1, 2, 3, 4} print(big.issuperset(small))
13. isdisjoint()
isdisjoint() checks whether two sets have no common elements.
a = {1, 2, 3} b = {4, 5, 6} print(a.isdisjoint(b))
Set Methods — Quick Reference

MethodPurpose
add(x)Add one element
update(iterable)Add multiple elements
remove(x)Remove element; error if missing
discard(x)Remove element without error if missing
pop()Remove and return an arbitrary element
clear()Remove all elements
union()Combine unique elements
intersection()Find common elements
difference()Find elements only in first set
symmetric_difference()Find elements in either set but not both
issubset()Check subset relationship
issuperset()Check superset relationship
isdisjoint()Check whether sets have no common elements
Dictionary Methods
Dictionaries store key-value pairs, so their methods focus on retrieving, updating, and removing key-value data.
get() retrieves a value using a key without raising an error when the key is missing.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } print(employee.get("name")) print(employee.get("salary")) print(employee.get("salary", 0))
keys() provides a view of the dictionary's keys.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } print(employee.keys())
It is commonly used while iterating through dictionary keys.
3. values()
values() provides a view of the dictionary's values.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } print(employee.values())
items() provides the dictionary's key-value pairs.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } for key, value in employee.items(): print(key, value)
5. update()
update() adds new key-value pairs and updates existing keys.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } employee.update({ "department": "IT", "name": "David" }) print(employee)
pop() removes a specified key and returns its value.
employee = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } removed = employee.pop("department") print(removed) print(employee)
7. popitem()
popitem() removes and returns the last inserted key-value pair.
data = { "id": 101, "name": "John", "department": "IT" } item = data.popitem() print(item) print(data)
clear() removes all key-value pairs from the dictionary.
data = { "id": 101, "name": "John" } data.clear() print(data)
copy() creates a shallow copy of the dictionary.
original = { "name": "John", "department": "IT" } new_data = original.copy() new_data["department"] = "Data Engineering" print(original) print(new_data)
10. setdefault()
setdefault() returns the value for a key if it exists. If the key does not exist, it inserts the key with the supplied default value and returns that value.
data = { "name": "John" } value = data.setdefault("department", "IT") print(value) print(data)
If the key already exists, its existing value is returned and is not replaced.
data = { "name": "John", "department": "HR" } value = data.setdefault("department", "IT") print(value) print(data)
Practical Note: setdefault() is useful for initializing a missing dictionary key, but use it only when that behavior is actually required because it can modify the dictionary.
Dictionary Methods — Quick Reference

MethodPurposeModifies Dictionary?
get(key)Safely retrieve a valueNo
keys()Get keysNo
values()Get valuesNo
items()Get key-value pairsNo
update()Add or update entriesYes
pop(key)Remove key and return valueYes
popitem()Remove and return last inserted pairYes
clear()Remove all entriesYes
copy()Create shallow copyNo
setdefault()Get existing value or create default entrySometimes
Methods That Modify vs Methods That Return Data
A useful concept is knowing whether a method changes the existing collection or returns information/new data.

LIST ↓ append() / remove() / sort() → Modify existing list index() / count() → Return information SET ↓ add() / remove() / clear() → Modify existing set union() / intersection() → Return a new set DICTIONARY ↓ update() / pop() / clear() → Modify existing dictionary get() / keys() / values() → Retrieve information
Important: Many Mutating Methods Return None
Methods such as append(), sort(), reverse(), and update() modify the object in place and generally return None.
numbers = [30, 10, 20] result = numbers.sort() print(numbers) print(result)
The list is sorted, but result is None.
Common Rule: If a list method changes the list in place, do not expect the method itself to return the modified list.
sort() vs sorted()
sort() is a list method that modifies the list. sorted() is a built-in function that returns a new sorted list.
numbers = [30, 10, 20] numbers.sort() print(numbers)
numbers = [30, 10, 20] result = sorted(numbers) print(numbers) print(result)

OperationEffect
list.sort()Changes the existing list
sorted(list)Returns a new sorted list
Methods in Data Engineering

Collection methods are frequently used while preparing records, checking data, building lookup structures, and performing basic transformations before using specialized tools such as Pandas, SQL, Spark, or Airflow.

records = [ {"part": "A100", "store": "BM11"}, {"part": "B200", "store": "BM12"}, {"part": "A100", "store": "BM11"} ] unique_parts = set() for record in records: unique_parts.add(record["part"]) print(unique_parts)
Here, a set method is used to collect unique part numbers from a collection of records.
Data Reconciliation Example
Set methods are especially useful when comparing IDs from source and target systems.

source_ids = {101, 102, 103, 104} target_ids = {101, 102, 104, 105} missing = source_ids.difference(target_ids) extra = target_ids.difference(source_ids) common = source_ids.intersection(target_ids) print("Missing:", missing) print("Extra:", extra) print("Common:", common)
Data Engineering Connection: difference() and intersection() are useful for basic source-to-target reconciliation and identifying missing or unexpected records.
Dictionary as a Lookup Table
Dictionary methods are useful when converting codes into meaningful values.
store_names = { "BM11": "Chennai", "BM12": "Bangalore", "BM13": "Hyderabad" } store_code = "BM11" print(store_names.get(store_code, "Unknown"))
This pattern appears frequently in data transformation logic.
Building a Frequency Dictionary
Dictionary methods can also be used to count occurrences.
parts = ["A100", "B200", "A100", "C300", "B200", "A100"] counts = {} for part in parts: counts[part] = counts.get(part, 0) + 1 print(counts)
Here, get() provides a default count of zero for a part that has not appeared before.
Common Mistakes
# Mistake 1: Using append() on a tuple numbers = (10, 20, 30) # numbers.append(40)
Tuples are immutable and do not provide list modification methods.
# Mistake 2: Confusing append() and extend() data = [1, 2] data.append([3, 4]) print(data) # Result: [1, 2, [3, 4]]
If you want the individual values added, use extend().
# Mistake 3: Expecting sort() to return a sorted list numbers = [3, 1, 2] result = numbers.sort() print(result) # None
# Mistake 4: Removing a missing set element with remove() parts = {"CPU", "RAM"} # parts.remove("GPU")
Use discard() when a missing value should not raise an error.
# Mistake 5: Confusing dictionary keys and values data = {"id": 101, "name": "John"} print("name" in data) # True print("John" in data) # False print("John" in data.values()) # True
Quick Memory Map

LIST append → one item extend → many items insert → specific position remove → value pop → index + return sort → sort in place reverse → reverse in place TUPLE count → occurrences index → position SET add → one item update → many items remove / discard → remove item union → combine intersection → common difference → only in first DICTIONARY get → safe lookup keys → keys values → values items → key + value update → add/update pop → remove by key
Final Rule: Learn the purpose of each method rather than memorizing every method. First identify the collection type, then choose the method that matches the operation you need.
Summary

• Lists have many modification and ordering methods.
  • Tuples mainly provide count() and index() because they are immutable.
  • Sets provide methods for unique-value management and mathematical set operations.
  • Dictionaries provide methods for key-value lookup, updating, and removal.
  • append() adds one object, while extend() adds elements from an iterable.
  • sort() modifies a list, while sorted() returns a new sorted list.
  • remove() and discard() behave differently when a set value is missing.
  • get() is useful for safely reading dictionary values.
  • Many mutating methods modify an object in place and return None.
  • These methods form the foundation for basic Python data processing before moving to Pandas, SQL, Spark, and production Data Engineering tools.
practice: Step 1: Create a list and practice append(), extend(), and insert().
numbers = [10, 20] numbers.append(30) numbers.extend([40, 50]) numbers.insert(1, 15) print(numbers)
Step 2: Practice remove(), pop(), and clear() on a list.
numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40] numbers.remove(20) removed = numbers.pop() print("Removed:", removed) print(numbers) numbers.clear() print(numbers)
Step 3: Create a list with duplicate part numbers and use count() and index().
parts = ["A100", "B200", "A100", "C300", "A100"] print(parts.count("A100")) print(parts.index("C300"))
Step 4: Practice sort() and reverse().
numbers = [40, 10, 30, 20] numbers.sort() print(numbers) numbers.reverse() print(numbers)
Step 5: Create a tuple and use both available tuple methods.
data = (10, 20, 20, 30, 20) print(data.count(20)) print(data.index(30))
Step 6: Create two sets and practice add(), update(), remove(), and discard().
parts = {"CPU", "RAM"} parts.add("SSD") parts.update(["GPU", "HDD"]) parts.remove("RAM") parts.discard("Monitor") print(parts)
Step 7: Create two sets of IDs and find their union, intersection, and differences.

source_ids = {101, 102, 103, 104} target_ids = {101, 102, 104, 105} print("Union:", source_ids.union(target_ids)) print("Common:", source_ids.intersection(target_ids)) print("Missing:", source_ids.difference(target_ids)) print("Extra:", target_ids.difference(source_ids))
Step 8: Create an inventory dictionary and practice get(), update(), pop(), and items().

inventory = { "part_number": "A100", "store_code": "BM11", "quantity": 50 } print(inventory.get("quantity", 0)) inventory.update({"quantity": 75, "status": "Available"}) for key, value in inventory.items(): print(key, value) inventory.pop("status") print(inventory)
Step 9: Build a frequency dictionary using get() to count repeated part numbers.
parts = ["A100", "B200", "A100", "C300", "B200", "A100"] counts = {} for part in parts: counts[part] = counts.get(part, 0) + 1 print(counts)
Step 10: Build a small source-to-target reconciliation program using set methods and print missing and extra IDs.

source_ids = {101, 102, 103, 104, 105} target_ids = {101, 102, 104, 106} missing = source_ids.difference(target_ids) extra = target_ids.difference(source_ids) common = source_ids.intersection(target_ids) print("Missing IDs:", missing) print("Extra IDs:", extra) print("Common IDs:", common)

Practice Goal: Be able to recognize the main methods of lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries, understand which methods modify the object, and choose the correct method for common Data Engineering data-processing tasks.

qna.q: Q1. What is a method in Python?
qna.a: A method is a function associated with an object that performs an operation on that object.

qna.q: Q2. What does list append() do?
qna.a: append() adds one object to the end of a list.

qna.q: Q3. What is the difference between append() and extend()?
qna.a: append() adds one object as a single element, while extend() adds each element from an iterable.

qna.q: Q4. What does insert() do?
qna.a: insert() adds an element at a specified index in a list.

qna.q: Q5. What does remove() do on a list?
qna.a: It removes the first matching value from the list.

qna.q: Q6. What does pop() do on a list?
qna.a: It removes and returns an element. Without an index, it removes the last element.

qna.q: Q7. What does clear() do?
qna.a: It removes all elements from the collection. For lists, sets, and dictionaries, it leaves an empty collection.

qna.q: Q8. What do index() and count() do?
qna.a: index() finds the first matching position, while count() returns how many times a value occurs.

qna.q: Q9. What is the difference between sort() and sorted()?
qna.a: sort() modifies a list in place, while sorted() returns a new sorted list.

qna.q: Q10. What are the main tuple methods?
qna.a: The main tuple methods are count() and index().

qna.q: Q11. Why do tuples have fewer methods than lists?
qna.a: Tuples are immutable, so methods that modify the collection are not available.

qna.q: Q12. What does set add() do?
qna.a: It adds one element to a set.

qna.q: Q13. What is the difference between set remove() and discard()?
qna.a: remove() raises KeyError if the element is missing, while discard() does nothing when the element is missing.

qna.q: Q14. What does set union() do?
qna.a: It returns a set containing the unique elements from both sets.

qna.q: Q15. What does set intersection() do?
qna.a: It returns the elements that are common to both sets.

qna.q: Q16. What does set difference() do?
qna.a: It returns elements present in the first set but not in the other set.

qna.q: Q17. What does dictionary get() do?
qna.a: It retrieves a value by key and can return a default value instead of raising KeyError when the key is missing.

qna.q: Q18. What are keys(), values(), and items() used for?
qna.a: keys() provides keys, values() provides values, and items() provides key-value pairs.

qna.q: Q19. What does dictionary update() do?
qna.a: It adds new key-value pairs and updates existing keys.

qna.q: Q20. Why are collection methods important in Data Engineering?
qna.a: They provide the basic operations needed to clean, transform, search, compare, organize, and process data before using larger tools such as SQL, Pandas, Spark, and data pipeline frameworks.

items.title: Nested Lists and Dictionaries
explanation: 1. What Are Nested Data Structures?

A nested data structure is a collection that contains another collection as one of its values. In Python, a list can contain lists, a dictionary can contain dictionaries, and lists and dictionaries can be combined with each other.
Nested structures are very common when working with real-world data because data usually has multiple levels of information.
