  • Calling read() after the file has already been closed.
  • Expecting read() to automatically create a list or dictionary.
  • Calling read() twice and expecting the same data both times without using seek().
  • Using read() on a huge file without considering memory usage.
  • Forgetting that read() reads from the current file position.
Important Example: Calling read() Twice

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    first = file.read()
    second = file.read()

print(first)
print(second)
first contains the file content, while second will normally be an empty string because the file position is already at the end.
To read it again, move the position back:

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    first = file.read()
    file.seek(0)
    second = file.read()
Data Engineering Example
Imagine a small configuration file containing a pipeline environment value.

with open("config.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    environment = file.read().strip()

print("Running environment:", environment)
The flow is:

config.txt
    |
    v
with open()
    |
    v
read()
    |
    v
Text content
    |
    v
strip()
    |
    v
Python variable
    |
    v
Pipeline logic
This demonstrates an important Data Engineering pattern: read raw input first, then transform or validate the value before using it.
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
read()Reads content from the current file position.
read() without argumentReads all remaining content.
read(n)Reads up to the requested amount from the current position.
Return valueText content is returned as a string.
File positionReading moves the current position forward.
seek(0)Moves the position back to the beginning.
Large filesAvoid loading the entire file when memory usage is a concern.
practice: Step 1: Create a file named data.txt with three lines and read the complete file using read().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

print(data)
Step 2: Print the type of the value returned by read().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

print(type(data))
Step 3: Read only the first 10 characters from the file.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read(10)

print(data)
Step 4: Read the first five characters and then read the remaining content.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    first = file.read(5)
    remaining = file.read()

print("First:", first)
print("Remaining:", remaining)
Step 5: Use seek(0) to read the same file twice.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    first = file.read()
    file.seek(0)
    second = file.read()

print(first)
print(second)
Step 6: Read a file and count the number of characters it contains.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

print("Characters:", len(data))
Step 7: Read a text file and check whether it contains the word ERROR.

with open("application.log", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

if "ERROR" in data:
    print("Error found")
else:
    print("No error found")
Step 8: Read a small file and convert its contents into a list of lines using splitlines().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

lines = data.splitlines()
print(lines)
Step 9: Create a large text file and compare reading the complete file with processing it line by line. Observe the difference in approach and memory usage.

# Complete file
with open("large_file.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

# Line by line
with open("large_file.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())

Practice Goal: You should understand what read() returns, how read(n) works, how file position affects repeated reads, how seek() can reset the position, and when reading the entire file may be inappropriate for large data.

qna.q: Q1. What does read() do?
qna.a: It reads data from the current file position and returns it. For a text file, the returned value is a string.

qna.q: Q2. What happens when read() is called without an argument?
qna.a: It reads all remaining content from the current file position.

qna.q: Q3. What does read(10) mean?
qna.a: It requests up to 10 characters from the current file position when the file is opened in text mode.

qna.q: Q4. What does read() return for a text file?
qna.a: It returns a Python string containing the text that was read.

qna.q: Q5. What happens if you call read() twice?
qna.a: The second call reads from the new current position. If the first call consumed the entire file, the second call normally returns an empty string.

qna.q: Q6. How can you read the file again after calling read()?
qna.a: Use seek(0) to move the file position back to the beginning and then call read() again.

qna.q: Q7. Does read() automatically convert CSV or JSON text into Python objects?
qna.a: No. read() reads the file content as text. Parsing structured formats requires the appropriate libraries or parsing logic.

qna.q: Q8. Why can read() be a problem for very large files?
qna.a: Without a size limit, it attempts to load all remaining content into memory, which can consume significant memory for large files.

qna.q: Q9. What is the difference between read() and readline()?
qna.a: read() reads all remaining content or a requested amount, while readline() reads one line at a time.

qna.q: Q10. Why is read() useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It provides a simple way to load the contents of small configuration files, text files, logs, and other raw inputs before performing validation or transformation.

items.title: readline()
explanation: What is readline()?
readline() is a file object method used to read one line at a time from an opened file. It reads from the current file position until it reaches a line ending or the end of the file.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line = file.readline()

print(line)
Definition: readline() reads the next line from a file and returns it as a string. Each call advances the file position to the next line.
Basic Syntax
file.readline()
The file should normally be opened using with open().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line = file.readline()
    print(line)
Reading the First Line
Suppose data.txt contains:

Python
SQL
Data Engineering
The first call to readline() reads only the first line.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line = file.readline()

print(line)
The result is approximately "Python\n". The newline character is normally included in the returned string.
Reading Multiple Lines
You can call readline() multiple times. Each call continues from the current file position.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line1 = file.readline()
    line2 = file.readline()
    line3 = file.readline()

print(line1)
print(line2)
print(line3)

data.txt
   |
   v
Python\n
SQL\n
Data Engineering\n
   |
   v
readline() → Python\n
   |
   v
readline() → SQL\n
   |
   v
readline() → Data Engineering\n
Why Does readline() Move Forward?
A file object maintains a current position. After readline() reads one line, the position moves to the beginning of the next line.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    print(file.readline())
    print(file.readline())
The first call reads the first line and the second call reads the next line.
Newline Character \n
When a line ends with a newline character, readline() normally includes that newline in the returned string.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line = file.readline()

print(repr(line))
Using repr() makes special characters such as \n visible.
'Python\n'
If you want to remove the surrounding whitespace and newline, you can use strip().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line = file.readline().strip()

print(line)
What Happens at End of File?
When there is no more data to read, readline() returns an empty string.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    while True:
        line = file.readline()
        if line == "":
            break
        print(line.strip())
Important: An empty string returned by readline() indicates that the end of the file has been reached.
Using readline() with a Loop
You can use readline() repeatedly until the end of the file.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    while True:
        line = file.readline()
        if not line:
            break
        print(line.strip())
This works because a non-empty string is truthy, while the empty string returned at end-of-file is falsy.
readline() vs read()

MethodBehaviorTypical Use
read()Reads all remaining content or a specified amount.Small files or when complete content is needed.
readline()Reads one line at a time.Controlled line-by-line processing.
readlines()Reads remaining lines into a list.When a list of lines is required.
for line in fileIterates through lines directly.Common approach for processing large text files.
readline() vs for line in file
Both approaches can process a file line by line. A for loop is generally simpler and is the usual approach when you simply want to process every line.

# Using readline()
with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    while True:
        line = file.readline()
        if not line:
            break
        print(line.strip())

# Using direct iteration
with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())
Practical Rule: Learn readline() because it explains how line-by-line file reading works. For straightforward processing of every line, for line in file is usually cleaner.
Using readline() for a Header
A useful practical case is reading the first line separately when it contains metadata or a header.

with open("employees.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    header = file.readline().strip()
    first_record = file.readline().strip()

print("Header:", header)
print("First record:", first_record)
This technique is useful for understanding how file streams can be consumed in stages.
Using readline() with a Size Argument
readline() can optionally receive a size argument that limits the amount returned.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line = file.readline(5)

print(line)
The size argument limits how much data is returned from that line; it does not mean 'read five complete lines'.
Data Engineering Example
Imagine a raw text file where the first line contains a source name and subsequent lines contain records.

with open("source_data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    source = file.readline().strip()

    print("Source:", source)

    for line in file:
        record = line.strip()
        if record:
            print("Processing:", record)

source_data.txt
       |
       v
readline()
       |
       v
Read first line
       |
       v
Store metadata
       |
       v
Process remaining lines
       |
       v
Pipeline logic
This pattern demonstrates how a pipeline can consume the first line separately and then continue processing the remaining records.
Memory Consideration
readline() reads one line at a time rather than loading the entire file into memory. This can be useful when working with large text files.

with open("large_log.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    while True:
        line = file.readline()
        if not line:
            break

        # Process one line
        if "ERROR" in line:
            print(line.strip())
However, for normal line-by-line processing, direct iteration using for line in file is usually simpler.
Common Mistakes

• Forgetting that readline() returns the newline character when one is present.
  • Calling readline() repeatedly and forgetting that each call advances the file position.
  • Expecting readline() to return a list of lines.
  • Forgetting to handle the empty string at end-of-file when using a manual while loop.
  • Using readline() when a simple for line in file loop would be clearer.
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
readline()Reads the next line from the current file position.
Return valueReturns a string in text mode.
NewlineThe returned line normally includes its newline character when present.
File positionEach call advances the position.
End of fileReturns an empty string when there is no more data.
Large filesCan process one line at a time without loading the whole file.
Common alternativefor line in file is usually simpler for processing every line.
practice: Step 1: Create a file named data.txt containing three lines and read only the first line using readline().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line = file.readline()

print(line)
Step 2: Call readline() three times and observe which line each call returns.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line1 = file.readline()
    line2 = file.readline()
    line3 = file.readline()

print(line1)
print(line2)
print(line3)
Step 3: Use strip() to remove the newline character from a line.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line = file.readline().strip()

print(line)
Step 4: Keep calling readline() until the end of the file is reached.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    while True:
        line = file.readline()
        if line == "":
            break
        print(line.strip())
Step 5: Read the first line as a header and then process the remaining lines.

with open("employees.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    header = file.readline().strip()
    print("Header:", header)

    for line in file:
        print("Record:", line.strip())
Step 6: Create a log file and use readline() to find the first line containing ERROR.

with open("application.log", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    while True:
        line = file.readline()
        if not line:
            break

        if "ERROR" in line:
            print("First error:", line.strip())
            break
Step 7: Compare readline() with for line in file for processing the same file.

# readline()
with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    while True:
        line = file.readline()
        if not line:
            break
        print(line.strip())

# Direct iteration
with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())

Practice Goal: You should understand how readline() reads one line, how the file position advances, how end-of-file is detected, and when direct iteration is simpler for Data Engineering file processing.

qna.q: Q1. What does readline() do?
qna.a: It reads the next line from the current file position and returns it as a string.

qna.q: Q2. Does readline() read the entire file?
qna.a: No. It reads one line at a time.

qna.q: Q3. Does readline() include the newline character?
qna.a: Normally yes, if the line in the file ends with a newline character.

qna.q: Q4. How can you remove the newline from the returned line?
qna.a: You can use strip(), for example line = file.readline().strip().

qna.q: Q5. What does readline() return at the end of the file?
qna.a: It returns an empty string, "", when there is no more data to read.

qna.q: Q6. What happens to the file position after calling readline()?
qna.a: The file position advances past the line that was read, so the next call reads the following line.

qna.q: Q7. What is the difference between read() and readline()?
qna.a: read() reads all remaining content or a requested amount, while readline() reads the next line.

qna.q: Q8. Is readline() useful for large files?
qna.a: Yes. It allows processing one line at a time instead of loading the complete file into memory.

qna.q: Q9. Which is usually simpler for processing every line: readline() or for line in file?
qna.a: for line in file is usually simpler for straightforward line-by-line processing, although readline() is useful when you need explicit control over individual reads.

qna.q: Q10. Can readline() be used to read a header separately from the remaining records?
qna.a: Yes. You can call readline() once for the header and then continue iterating over the remaining lines.

items.title: readlines()
explanation: What is readlines()?
readlines() is a file object method used to read all remaining lines from a file and return them as a Python list.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

print(lines)
Definition: readlines() reads all remaining lines from the current file position and returns them as a list of strings.
Basic Syntax
file.readlines()
The file should normally be opened using with open().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

print(lines)
Example
Suppose data.txt contains:

Python
SQL
Data Engineering
Using readlines():

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

print(lines)
The result will be similar to:
["Python\n", "SQL\n", "Data Engineering"]
Each line becomes one element in the list. The newline character is normally included when it exists in the file.
Return Type

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

print(type(lines))
The result is a Python list.
Remember: read() returns the file content as a string, while readlines() returns the lines as a list of strings.
Processing the Returned List
Because readlines() returns a list, you can use normal list operations and loops on the result.

with open("employees.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

for line in lines:
    print(line.strip())
Removing Newline Characters
The strings returned by readlines() may contain \n. You can remove it while processing each line.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

for line in lines:
    print(line.strip())
You can also create a new cleaned list:

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

clean_lines = [line.strip() for line in lines]
print(clean_lines)
The list comprehension used here is only a simple example. List comprehensions will be covered more deeply later in the roadmap.
Reading from the Current File Position
readlines() reads from the current file position, not necessarily from the beginning.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    first = file.readline()
    remaining = file.readlines()

print("First:", first)
print("Remaining:", remaining)

data.txt
   |
   v
Python\n
SQL\n
Data Engineering\n
   |
   v
readline()
   |
   v
Python\n
   |
   v
readlines()
   |
   v
["SQL\n", "Data Engineering\n"]
Since readline() already consumed the first line, readlines() reads only the remaining lines.
Using readlines() from the Beginning
If you want to read all lines again after another read operation, move the file position back to the beginning with seek(0).

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.readline()
    file.seek(0)
    lines = file.readlines()

print(lines)
readlines() vs read()

MethodReturn ValueExample Result
read()String"Python SQL "
readlines()List of strings["Python ", "SQL "]
Use read() when you want the content as one string. Use readlines() when you specifically need the lines as a list.
readlines() vs readline()

MethodReadsReturn Type
readline()One linestr
readlines()All remaining lineslist

# One line
with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    line = file.readline()

# All remaining lines
with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()
readlines() vs Direct File Iteration
Both approaches can process lines, but they behave differently in terms of how the data is held in memory.

# readlines(): creates a list containing the lines
with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

for line in lines:
    print(line.strip())

# Direct iteration: process lines as the file is iterated
with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())

Practical Rule: Use readlines() when you actually need all the remaining lines as a list. For simply processing a large file line by line, direct iteration with for line in file is generally more appropriate.
Memory Consideration
readlines() stores all returned lines in a list. Therefore, a very large file can require a significant amount of memory.

# Potentially memory-heavy for a very large file
with open("large_file.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()
For large Data Engineering workloads, it is often better to process the file incrementally.

with open("large_file.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        process_line = line.strip()
        print(process_line)
Using len() with readlines()
Because the result is a list, you can use len() to find how many lines were read.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

print("Number of lines:", len(lines))
Accessing Individual Lines
Since readlines() returns a list, individual lines can be accessed using list indexing.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

print(lines[0])
print(lines[1])
Remember that Python uses zero-based indexing, so lines[0] represents the first line.
Checking Whether a Line Exists

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

if lines:
    print("First line:", lines[0].strip())
else:
    print("File is empty")
An empty file produces an empty list, so checking if lines can determine whether any lines were returned.
Data Engineering Example
Suppose a small configuration or mapping file contains a manageable number of records. You can load all lines into a list and then inspect or process them.

with open("source_list.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

for line in lines:
    source = line.strip()
    if source:
        print("Processing source:", source)

source_list.txt
       |
       v
readlines()
       |
       v
List of lines
       |
       v
Loop through list
       |
       v
Clean / validate
       |
       v
Process data
This is suitable when the file is reasonably small and keeping all lines in memory is acceptable.
When Should You Use readlines()?

SituationRecommended Approach
Need the complete text as one stringread()
Need one specific next linereadline()
Need all lines as a listreadlines()
Need to process a large file line by linefor line in file
Common Mistakes

• Expecting readlines() to return one string instead of a list.
  • Forgetting that newline characters may be present in each returned line.
  • Using readlines() on a huge file without considering memory usage.
  • Forgetting that it reads from the current file position.
  • Calling readlines() twice without resetting the file position and expecting the same result.
  • Using readlines() when direct iteration would be simpler and more memory-efficient.
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
readlines()Reads all remaining lines from the current file position.
Return typeReturns a list of strings.
NewlineLines normally retain their newline character when present.
File positionReading starts from the current position.
MemoryAll returned lines are stored in a list.
Large filesPrefer direct line-by-line iteration when appropriate.
Empty fileReturns an empty list.
practice: Step 1: Create a file named data.txt with three lines and read all lines using readlines().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

print(lines)
Step 2: Print the type of the value returned by readlines().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

print(type(lines))
Step 3: Print each line without its newline character.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

for line in lines:
    print(line.strip())
Step 4: Find the number of lines in the file.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

print("Number of lines:", len(lines))
Step 5: Access the first and second lines using list indexing.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

print("First:", lines[0].strip())
print("Second:", lines[1].strip())
Step 6: Read the first line using readline() and then read all remaining lines using readlines().

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    first_line = file.readline()
    remaining_lines = file.readlines()

print("First:", first_line.strip())
print("Remaining:", remaining_lines)
Step 7: Use seek(0) to reset the file position and call readlines() again.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.readline()
    file.seek(0)
    lines = file.readlines()

print(lines)
Step 8: Compare readlines() with direct file iteration using a small log file.

# readlines()
with open("application.log", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    lines = file.readlines()

for line in lines:
    print(line.strip())

# Direct iteration
with open("application.log", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())
Step 9: Think about whether readlines() is appropriate for a 10 MB file versus a multi-GB log file. Explain why the approach may differ.

Practice Goal: You should understand that readlines() returns a list of all remaining lines, how the current file position affects its result, how to work with the returned list, and why direct iteration is generally preferable for very large files.

qna.q: Q1. What does readlines() do?
qna.a: It reads all remaining lines from the current file position and returns them as a list of strings.

qna.q: Q2. What is the return type of readlines()?
qna.a: It returns a Python list containing strings, with each string representing one line.

qna.q: Q3. Does readlines() include newline characters?
qna.a: Normally yes. If a line in the file ends with a newline character, that newline is normally included in the corresponding string.

qna.q: Q4. What does readlines() return for an empty file?
qna.a: It returns an empty list, [].

qna.q: Q5. What is the difference between read() and readlines()?
qna.a: read() returns the remaining file content as a string, while readlines() returns the remaining lines as a list of strings.

qna.q: Q6. What is the difference between readline() and readlines()?
qna.a: readline() reads one line, while readlines() reads all remaining lines and returns them as a list.

qna.q: Q7. Can readlines() read from the middle of a file?
qna.a: Yes. It starts reading from the current file position. If earlier operations already consumed some data, only the remaining lines are returned.

qna.q: Q8. Why can readlines() be inefficient for very large files?
qna.a: It stores all returned lines in a list, which can require significant memory for a large file.

qna.q: Q9. What is generally better for processing a large file line by line?
qna.a: Using for line in file is generally preferable because it processes the file incrementally instead of first creating a list containing all lines.

qna.q: Q10. When would you intentionally use readlines()?
qna.a: When you specifically need all remaining lines as a list and the amount of data is reasonably small enough to keep in memory.

items.title: write()
explanation: What is write()?
write() is a file object method used to write data into a file. In text mode, it writes a string to the current file position and returns the number of characters written.

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Python")
Definition: write() writes the supplied data to the file at the current file position. When writing text, the supplied value must be a string.
Basic Syntax
file.write(data)
For a text file, data should normally be a string.

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Hello Python")
Writing Multiple Lines
write() does not automatically add a new line. If you want each piece of data on a separate line, explicitly include \n.

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Python\n")
    file.write("SQL\n")
    file.write("Data Engineering\n")
The file will contain:

Python
SQL
Data Engineering
Important: write() writes exactly the string you provide. It does not automatically add spaces or newline characters.
Writing a String Variable

message = "Data Engineering"

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write(message)
This is useful when the data to be written is stored in a Python variable.
Writing Numbers
In text mode, write() expects a string. You cannot directly pass an integer or float.

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write(100)
The above produces a TypeError because 100 is an integer, not a string.
Convert the value to a string first:

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write(str(100))
You can also use an f-string when constructing text:

count = 100

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write(f"Total records: {count}\n")
Writing Several Values
A single write() call accepts one object. To write multiple pieces of text, combine them into a string or make multiple calls.

name = "Ravi"
age = 25

with open("employee.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Name: " + name + "\n")
    file.write("Age: " + str(age) + "\n")
Using an f-string is often cleaner:

name = "Ravi"
age = 25

with open("employee.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write(f"Name: {name}\n")
    file.write(f"Age: {age}\n")
Return Value of write()
In text mode, write() returns the number of characters written.

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    result = file.write("Python")

print(result)
The result is 6 because the string "Python" contains six characters.
Remember: The return value of write() is not the written content. It reports how many characters were written in text mode.
write() with "w" Mode
When a file is opened using "w", writing starts with a new or truncated file. If the file already exists, its previous contents are removed.

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("New data")

Existing data.txt
       |
       v
open(..., "w")
       |
       v
Existing content removed
       |
       v
write("New data")
       |
       v
New file content
Warning: Be careful with "w" mode. Opening an existing file in this mode truncates its contents before writing.
write() with "a" Mode
Use "a" mode when you want to add new data to the end of an existing file without replacing its existing content.

with open("pipeline.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Pipeline completed\n")
If the file already contains:
Pipeline started
the new content is added after the existing content.

Pipeline started
Pipeline completed
Writing to a File Using with open()
The recommended pattern is:

with open("output.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Some data")
The with statement ensures that the file is properly closed after the writing operation.
Writing Data with Newlines
For text-based files, \n is commonly used to separate records or lines.

records = ["101,Ravi", "102,Anil", "103,Sita"]

with open("employees.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for record in records:
        file.write(record + "\n")
This produces one record per line.
Writing Empty Strings
Writing an empty string does not add any characters to the file.

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    result = file.write("")

print(result)
# 0
Writing Large Amounts of Data
When writing many records, repeatedly calling write() can be useful for processing data incrementally.

records = [
    "101,Ravi",
    "102,Anil",
    "103,Sita"
]

with open("output.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for record in records:
        file.write(record + "\n")
For very large datasets, specialized data-processing and file-format tools are generally used later in the Data Engineering roadmap.
Writing a Simple Pipeline Result
A basic Python pipeline might process some records and write the results to an output file.

records = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Sita"]

with open("output.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for name in records:
        file.write(f"Processed: {name}\n")

Input Records
     |
     v
Python Processing
     |
     v
write()
     |
     v
output.txt
Data Engineering Connection: Writing output files is one part of a basic ETL flow: read input → transform data → write output. Later ETL and data-format topics will cover more scalable approaches.
write() vs writelines()
Python also provides writelines(), which can write multiple strings from an iterable. It does not automatically add newline characters.

lines = ["Python\n", "SQL\n", "Data Engineering\n"]

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.writelines(lines)

MethodPurpose
write()Writes one string.
writelines()Writes multiple strings from an iterable.
Important: Neither write() nor writelines() automatically adds a newline. Add \n yourself when separate lines are required.
Common Mistakes

• Using "w" mode when you intended to preserve existing data.
  • Forgetting to add \n between lines.
  • Passing an integer, list, or dictionary directly to write() in text mode.
  • Assuming write() automatically converts Python objects into JSON, CSV, or other formats.
  • Forgetting to use with open() or otherwise close the file.
  • Assuming the return value is the written data instead of the number of characters written.
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
write()Writes a string to a file.
Text modeThe value supplied should be a string.
\nMust be added explicitly to create a new line.
"w"Writes from a new/truncated file.
"a"Adds data to the end of the file.
Return valueNumber of characters written in text mode.
writelines()Writes multiple strings from an iterable.
practice: Step 1: Create a file named data.txt and write a simple message into it.

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Hello Python")
Step 2: Write three separate lines into the file using \n.

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Python\n")
    file.write("SQL\n")
    file.write("Data Engineering\n")
Step 3: Store a name and age in variables and write them to a file using an f-string.

name = "Ravi"
age = 25

with open("employee.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write(f"Name: {name}\n")
    file.write(f"Age: {age}\n")
Step 4: Write a number to a text file after converting it to a string.

count = 100

with open("count.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write(str(count))
Step 5: Check the return value of write().

with open("data.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    result = file.write("Python")

print("Characters written:", result)
Step 6: Create a log file using "w" mode and then append another record using "a" mode.

with open("pipeline.log", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Pipeline started\n")

with open("pipeline.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Pipeline completed\n")
Step 7: Create a list of simple records and write each record to a separate line.

records = ["101,Ravi", "102,Anil", "103,Sita"]

with open("employees.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    for record in records:
        file.write(record + "\n")
Step 8: Read the file you created and verify that the written content is correct.

with open("employees.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

print(data)
Step 9: Practice the difference between overwriting and appending. Write one message using "w", append another using "a", then read the final file.

with open("pipeline.log", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Run 1\n")

with open("pipeline.log", "a", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Run 2\n")

with open("pipeline.log", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    print(file.read())

Practice Goal: You should be comfortable using write() to create and update text files, adding newlines, converting values to strings, understanding its return value, and distinguishing overwrite mode from append mode.

qna.q: Q1. What does write() do?
qna.a: It writes the supplied data to the file at the current file position. In text mode, the supplied value should be a string.

qna.q: Q2. Does write() automatically add a newline?
qna.a: No. If you want a new line, you must explicitly include \n in the string.

qna.q: Q3. What does write() return in text mode?
qna.a: It returns the number of characters written.

qna.q: Q4. Can you directly write an integer using write() in text mode?
qna.a: No. Convert it to a string first, for example file.write(str(100)).

qna.q: Q5. What happens when write() is used with "w" mode?
qna.a: If the file already exists, opening it in "w" mode truncates its existing contents before writing.

qna.q: Q6. What is the difference between "w" and "a" when using write()?
qna.a: "w" writes to a new or truncated file, while "a" preserves existing content and writes new data at the end.

qna.q: Q7. Can write() write multiple lines?
qna.a: Yes. You can make multiple write() calls or include multiple \n characters in one string.

qna.q: Q8. What is the difference between write() and writelines()?
qna.a: write() writes one string, while writelines() writes multiple strings from an iterable. Neither method automatically adds newline characters.

qna.q: Q9. Why should write() normally be used inside with open()?
qna.a: The with statement ensures that the file is properly closed after the writing block finishes.

qna.q: Q10. How is write() relevant to Data Engineering?
qna.a: It provides a basic way to create output files, write processed records, generate simple pipeline results, and append simple log or status information.

items.title: File Paths
explanation: What is a File Path?
A file path tells Python where a file or folder is located in the computer's file system. Whenever you use open(), Python needs a path to know which file it should access.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()
Definition: A file path is the location of a file or directory in a file system. It can be relative to the current working directory or an absolute path from the root of the file system.
Why File Paths Matter

Data Engineering programs frequently work with input files, output files, logs, configuration files, temporary data, and project directories. Correct path handling is therefore an important basic skill.

Python Program
      |
      v
   File Path
      |
      v
File System
      |
      +---- data/
      |       +---- input.csv
      |       +---- output.csv
      |
      +---- logs/
              +---- pipeline.log
Relative Path
A relative path describes a location relative to the program's current working directory.

with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()
If the current working directory contains data.txt, Python can open it using this simple relative path.
You can also refer to files inside folders:

with open("data/input.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()
Relative Path: A path interpreted from the current working directory rather than from the root of the file system.
Absolute Path
An absolute path specifies the complete location of a file starting from the root of the file system or drive.
For example, on Windows:

with open("C:\\Users\\Ravi\\Documents\\data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()
On Linux:

with open("/home/ravi/data/data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()
Absolute Path: A complete path that identifies the location of a file or directory independently of the current working directory.
Relative vs Absolute Paths

FeatureRelative PathAbsolute Path
Starting pointCurrent working directoryRoot/drive location
Exampledata/input.txt/home/user/data/input.txt
PortabilityUsually easier to move with a projectOften tied to a specific machine/location
Typical project useCommonly preferredUseful when a fixed external location is required
Current Working Directory
A relative path depends on the process's current working directory. Python provides os.getcwd() to find it.

import os

print(os.getcwd())
You can also use pathlib:

from pathlib import Path

print(Path.cwd())
Important: The current working directory is not necessarily the folder containing your Python file. It depends on how the program was started and the environment from which it was run.
Parent Directory: ..
The special path component .. refers to the parent directory.

with open("../data/input.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

project/
├── data/
│   └── input.txt
└── scripts/
    └── process.py

From scripts/:
../data/input.txt
      |
      v
Move one directory up
      |
      v
data/input.txt
Current Directory: .
The special path component . represents the current directory.

with open("./data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()
In many cases, data.txt and ./data.txt refer to the same location.
Windows Paths and Backslashes
Windows commonly uses backslashes in paths. Backslash is also used for Python escape sequences, so care is required.

path = "C:\\data\\input.txt"
print(path)
A raw string can make Windows paths easier to write:

path = r"C:\data\input.txt"

with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()
Tip: Raw strings are useful for Windows paths and other strings containing many backslashes. They are not a universal solution for every possible path-string situation.
Using Forward Slashes
Python also accepts forward slashes in many Windows file-path APIs.

path = "C:/data/input.txt"

with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()
Using pathlib is generally a cleaner approach when you want path handling that works across operating systems.
Using pathlib
pathlib provides an object-oriented way to work with file system paths.

from pathlib import Path

file_path = Path("data") / "input.txt"

with open(file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()
The / operator joins path components in a platform-aware way.
Recommended Practice: For new Python projects, learn pathlib instead of manually constructing complex paths with string concatenation.
Creating a Path with Multiple Directories

from pathlib import Path

file_path = Path("project") / "data" / "raw" / "input.txt"

print(file_path)
This creates a path representing:
project/data/raw/input.txt
Checking Whether a Path Exists
pathlib can check whether a file or directory exists.

from pathlib import Path

file_path = Path("data/input.txt")

if file_path.exists():
    print("File exists")
else:
    print("File does not exist")
Checking File vs Directory

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/input.txt")

print(path.exists())
print(path.is_file())
print(path.is_dir())

MethodPurpose
exists()Checks whether the path exists.
is_file()Checks whether the path represents a file.
is_dir()Checks whether the path represents a directory.
Creating Directories with pathlib
Path.mkdir() can create directories.

from pathlib import Path

output_dir = Path("output")
output_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
exist_ok=True prevents an error when the directory already exists.
For nested directories:

from pathlib import Path

output_dir = Path("output") / "daily" / "2026"
output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
Joining Paths Correctly
Avoid manually joining paths using string concatenation.

# Avoid for general path construction
path = "data" + "/" + "input.txt"
Prefer:

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data") / "input.txt"
This lets Python handle the appropriate path separator for the operating system.
File Paths in a Data Engineering Project
A Data Engineering project may organize files into separate directories for raw data, processed data, logs, and configuration.

data_pipeline/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── processed/
├── logs/
├── config/
└── scripts/
    └── pipeline.py
You can construct these paths using pathlib:

from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path("data_pipeline")
RAW_DIR = BASE_DIR / "data" / "raw"
PROCESSED_DIR = BASE_DIR / "data" / "processed"
LOG_DIR = BASE_DIR / "logs"

input_file = RAW_DIR / "input.txt"
output_file = PROCESSED_DIR / "output.txt"
Data Engineering Connection: Separating raw, processed, output, and log paths makes pipeline projects easier to organize and maintain. Later ETL and pipeline topics will build on this structure.
Path and File Operations
A path identifies the location; file operations such as open() determine what you do with the file.

Path
 |
 +---- Identify location
 |
 v
open(path, mode)
 |
 +---- Read
 +---- Write
 +---- Append
 +---- Process
Common Path Errors

• FileNotFoundError: The specified file or path cannot be found.
  • NotADirectoryError: A path component expected to be a directory is actually a file.
  • PermissionError: The program does not have the required permission.
  • Incorrect relative path: The path is interpreted from a different current working directory than expected.
  • Windows backslash issues: Backslashes can interact with Python escape sequences when written as ordinary strings.
Useful Path Information

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/input.txt")

print(path.name)
print(path.parent)
print(path.suffix)

ExpressionExample Result
path.nameinput.txt
path.parentdata
path.suffix.txt
Quick Summary

ConceptKey Point
File pathSpecifies the location of a file or directory.
Relative pathInterpreted relative to the current working directory.
Absolute pathSpecifies the complete location.
.Represents the current directory.
..Represents the parent directory.
Path.cwd()Returns the current working directory as a Path.
Path / "file.txt"Builds a path using pathlib.
exists()Checks whether a path exists.
is_file()Checks whether a path is a file.
is_dir()Checks whether a path is a directory.
practice: Step 1: Print the current working directory using both os and pathlib.

import os
from pathlib import Path

print(os.getcwd())
print(Path.cwd())
Step 2: Create a relative path to a file named input.txt inside a data folder.

from pathlib import Path

file_path = Path("data") / "input.txt"
print(file_path)
Step 3: Check whether the path exists and whether it is a file.

from pathlib import Path

file_path = Path("data") / "input.txt"

print("Exists:", file_path.exists())
print("Is file:", file_path.is_file())
Step 4: Create a project directory structure for a small data pipeline.

from pathlib import Path

base = Path("data_pipeline")
raw = base / "data" / "raw"
processed = base / "data" / "processed"
logs = base / "logs"

raw.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
processed.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
logs.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
Step 5: Create an input file inside the raw-data directory and write some data to it.

from pathlib import Path

raw_dir = Path("data_pipeline") / "data" / "raw"
input_file = raw_dir / "input.txt"

with open(input_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("101,Ravi\n102,Anil\n")
Step 6: Read the file using the Path object instead of manually constructing an absolute path.

from pathlib import Path

input_file = Path("data_pipeline") / "data" / "raw" / "input.txt"

with open(input_file, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    print(file.read())
Step 7: Practice using . and .. to understand current and parent directories.

from pathlib import Path

current = Path(".")
parent = Path("..")

print(current.resolve())
print(parent.resolve())
Step 8: Inspect the name, parent directory, and extension of a file path.

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/raw/input.csv")

print("Name:", path.name)
print("Parent:", path.parent)
print("Suffix:", path.suffix)
Step 9: Create a simple pipeline folder structure with raw, processed, and logs directories and explain why each directory exists.

Practice Goal: You should understand relative and absolute paths, the current working directory, . and .., Windows path considerations, and how to use pathlib to build and inspect paths for Data Engineering projects.

qna.q: Q1. What is a file path?
qna.a: A file path specifies the location of a file or directory in a file system.

qna.q: Q2. What is the difference between a relative path and an absolute path?
qna.a: A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory, while an absolute path specifies the complete location from the root or drive.

qna.q: Q3. What does Path.cwd() return?
qna.a: It returns the current working directory as a pathlib.Path object.

qna.q: Q4. What do . and .. represent?
qna.a: . represents the current directory, while .. represents the parent directory.

qna.q: Q5. Why is pathlib useful?
qna.a: It provides a clear, object-oriented and platform-aware way to construct, inspect, and work with file system paths.

qna.q: Q6. How do you join paths using pathlib?
qna.a: Use the / operator, for example Path("data") / "input.txt".

qna.q: Q7. How can you check whether a path exists?
qna.a: Use path.exists() when working with a pathlib.Path object.

qna.q: Q8. How can you check whether a path is a file or directory?
qna.a: Use path.is_file() for files and path.is_dir() for directories.

qna.q: Q9. Why can hard-coded absolute paths be a problem in projects?
qna.a: They may depend on a specific user's machine or directory structure, making the project harder to move or run in another environment.

qna.q: Q10. Why are file paths important in Data Engineering?
qna.a: Data pipelines regularly read raw data and write processed data, logs, configurations, and outputs. Reliable path handling helps organize and locate these resources correctly.

items.title: pathlib
explanation: What is pathlib?

pathlib is a Python standard-library module used to work with files and directories through Path objects. It provides a cleaner and more platform-independent approach to handling file system paths than manually building path strings.

from pathlib import Path

file_path = Path("data") / "input.txt"
print(file_path)
Definition: pathlib provides object-oriented tools for representing and working with file system paths.
Why Use pathlib?
Without pathlib, developers often construct paths manually using strings. This can become difficult when projects contain many nested directories or need to run on different operating systems.

# String-based path
path = "data/raw/input.txt"

# pathlib
from pathlib import Path
path = Path("data") / "raw" / "input.txt"
pathlib makes path construction, checking, and file-system operations easier to read and maintain.
Importing pathlib
The most commonly used class is Path.
from pathlib import Path
You can then create a Path object:

path = Path("data/input.txt")
print(path)
Creating a Path

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/input.txt")
print(path)
A Path object represents the location. It does not mean that the file must already exist.
Important: Creating Path("data/input.txt") creates a path object in Python. It does not automatically create the file or directory on disk.
Joining Paths
One of the most useful features of pathlib is joining path components with the / operator.

from pathlib import Path

base = Path("data")
file_path = base / "raw" / "input.txt"

print(file_path)

Path("data")
     |
     +--- / "raw"
              |
              +--- / "input.txt"
                       |
                       v
              data/raw/input.txt
This is generally clearer than manually concatenating strings.
Current Working Directory
Path.cwd() returns the current working directory.

from pathlib import Path

current_directory = Path.cwd()
print(current_directory)
Remember: Relative paths are interpreted based on the process's current working directory. The current working directory is not necessarily the directory containing your Python script.
Absolute Path
A path can be converted to an absolute path using resolve().

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/input.txt")
absolute_path = path.resolve()

print(absolute_path)
This is useful when you need to see the complete location represented by a relative path.
Checking Whether a Path Exists

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/input.txt")

if path.exists():
    print("Path exists")
else:
    print("Path does not exist")
exists() returns True when the path exists and False otherwise.
Checking for a File

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/input.txt")

if path.is_file():
    print("This is a file")
is_file() checks whether the path refers to a regular file.
Checking for a Directory

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data")

if path.is_dir():
    print("This is a directory")
is_dir() checks whether the path refers to a directory.
Creating Directories
mkdir() creates a directory represented by a Path.

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("output")
path.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
exist_ok=True prevents an error if the directory already exists.
For nested directories, use parents=True:

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data") / "processed" / "2026"
path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
Parameter Meaning: parents=True allows missing parent directories to be created. exist_ok=True avoids an error when the target directory already exists.
Opening a File with a Path Object
A Path object can be passed directly to open().

from pathlib import Path

file_path = Path("data") / "input.txt"

with open(file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

print(data)
This works naturally with the with open() pattern learned in the previous topics.
Reading with Path.open()
A Path object also provides an open() method.

from pathlib import Path

file_path = Path("data/input.txt")

with file_path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()

print(data)
Both open(file_path, ...) and file_path.open(...) can be used.
Writing Using Path.open()

from pathlib import Path

output_file = Path("output.txt")

with output_file.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Data Engineering")
Reading and Writing Text Directly
For simple text files, Path provides convenient methods such as read_text() and write_text().

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data.txt")

path.write_text("Python\nSQL\nData Engineering", encoding="utf-8")

data = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
print(data)
Practical Tip: read_text() and write_text() are convenient for simple text files. For more control over file modes, incremental processing, or larger files, use open() with a context manager.
Getting the File Name

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/raw/input.csv")

print(path.name)
Output:
input.csv
Getting the Parent Directory

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/raw/input.csv")

print(path.parent)
Output:
data/raw
Getting the File Extension

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/raw/input.csv")

print(path.suffix)
Output:
.csv
You can also get the complete suffix sequence using suffixes.

path = Path("backup.tar.gz")

print(path.suffix)
print(path.suffixes)
Getting the File Stem
stem returns the final file name without its final suffix.

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/input.csv")

print(path.stem)
Output:
input
Checking File Metadata
A Path object can provide basic file information using stat().

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/input.txt")

if path.exists():
    info = path.stat()
    print("Size:", info.st_size, "bytes")
This can be useful when checking input files before processing them.
Listing Files in a Directory
iterdir() returns the items directly inside a directory.

from pathlib import Path

data_dir = Path("data")

for item in data_dir.iterdir():
    print(item)
You can check what type each item is:

from pathlib import Path

data_dir = Path("data")

for item in data_dir.iterdir():
    if item.is_file():
        print("File:", item)
    elif item.is_dir():
        print("Directory:", item)
Finding Files with glob()
glob() can find paths matching a pattern inside a directory.

from pathlib import Path

data_dir = Path("data")

for file_path in data_dir.glob("*.csv"):
    print(file_path)
This finds CSV files directly inside the data directory.
For example:

data/
├── employees.csv
├── sales.csv
└── notes.txt
The pattern "*.csv" matches employees.csv and sales.csv.
Recursive File Searching with rglob()
rglob() searches recursively through subdirectories.

from pathlib import Path

base = Path("data")

for file_path in base.rglob("*.csv"):
    print(file_path)

data/
├── raw/
│   ├── sales.csv
│   └── users.csv
└── processed/
    └── sales.csv

rglob("*.csv")
        |
        v
Find CSV files recursively
        |
        v
raw/sales.csv
raw/users.csv
processed/sales.csv
Renaming a File
rename() can rename or move a path.

from pathlib import Path

old_path = Path("data/old.txt")
new_path = Path("data/new.txt")

old_path.rename(new_path)
Deleting a File
unlink() removes a file.

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("temporary.txt")

if path.exists():
    path.unlink()
Warning: File deletion is destructive. Always verify the path and your conditions before using unlink() in automation or production code.
Data Engineering Project Structure
pathlib becomes particularly useful when organizing a Data Engineering project into predictable directories.

data_engineering_project/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   ├── processed/
│   └── output/
├── logs/
├── config/
├── scripts/
└── tests/

from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path("data_engineering_project")
RAW_DIR = BASE_DIR / "data" / "raw"
PROCESSED_DIR = BASE_DIR / "data" / "processed"
OUTPUT_DIR = BASE_DIR / "data" / "output"
LOG_DIR = BASE_DIR / "logs"
CONFIG_DIR = BASE_DIR / "config"

RAW_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
PROCESSED_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

Data Engineering Connection: Pipelines often need predictable locations for raw input, transformed data, outputs, logs, and configuration. pathlib provides a clean foundation for managing these locations.
Common Mistakes

• Assuming creating a Path object creates the file or directory automatically.
  • Confusing the current working directory with the directory containing the Python script.
  • Hard-coding machine-specific absolute paths into reusable projects.
  • Forgetting parents=True when creating multiple missing directory levels.
  • Using write_text() for very large files when incremental writing would be more appropriate.
  • Deleting files with unlink() without verifying the path.
  • Using complicated manual string concatenation instead of path operations.
Quick Summary

Method / AttributePurpose
Path()Creates a path object.
Path.cwd()Gets the current working directory.
/Joins path components.
resolve()Gets a resolved absolute path.
exists()Checks whether a path exists.
is_file()Checks whether the path is a file.
is_dir()Checks whether the path is a directory.
mkdir()Creates directories.
read_text()Reads a text file.
write_text()Writes text to a file.
nameGets the final file or directory name.
parentGets the parent path.
suffixGets the final file extension.
stemGets the file name without its final suffix.
iterdir()Lists direct children of a directory.
glob()Finds paths matching a pattern.
rglob()Recursively finds paths matching a pattern.
rename()Renames or moves a path.
unlink()Deletes a file.
practice: Step 1: Import Path and create a path for a file named input.txt inside a data directory.

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data") / "input.txt"
print(path)
Step 2: Print the current working directory and convert the relative file path into a resolved path.

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("data/input.txt")

print("Current:", Path.cwd())
print("Resolved:", path.resolve())
Step 3: Create data/raw and data/processed directories.

from pathlib import Path

raw_dir = Path("data") / "raw"
processed_dir = Path("data") / "processed"

raw_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
processed_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
Step 4: Create a text file inside the raw directory and write some sample records.

from pathlib import Path

input_file = Path("data") / "raw" / "input.txt"

with input_file.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("101,Ravi\n102,Anil\n103,Sita\n")
Step 5: Check whether the file exists and whether it is actually a file.

print(input_file.exists())
print(input_file.is_file())
Step 6: Print the file name, parent directory, suffix, and stem.

print("Name:", input_file.name)
print("Parent:", input_file.parent)
print("Suffix:", input_file.suffix)
print("Stem:", input_file.stem)
Step 7: Find all .txt files directly inside the raw-data directory.

for file_path in raw_dir.glob("*.txt"):
    print(file_path)
Step 8: Search recursively for all CSV files inside a project data directory.

from pathlib import Path

base = Path("data")

for file_path in base.rglob("*.csv"):
    print(file_path)
Step 9: Build a small Data Engineering directory structure using pathlib instead of manually concatenating strings.

from pathlib import Path

base = Path("pipeline")

folders = [
    base / "data" / "raw",
    base / "data" / "processed",
    base / "data" / "output",
    base / "logs",
    base / "config"
]

for folder in folders:
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

Practice Goal: You should be comfortable creating Path objects, joining paths, checking files and directories, creating folders, reading and writing files, finding files with patterns, and using pathlib to organize Data Engineering project directories.

qna.q: Q1. What is pathlib?
qna.a: pathlib is a Python standard-library module that provides object-oriented tools for working with file system paths.

qna.q: Q2. What is Path?
qna.a: Path is the main class commonly used from pathlib to represent and manipulate file system paths.

qna.q: Q3. Does creating a Path object create the actual file?
qna.a: No. Creating Path("data/input.txt") only creates a path representation in Python. The file must be created separately.

qna.q: Q4. How do you join paths using pathlib?
qna.a: Use the / operator, for example Path("data") / "raw" / "input.txt".

qna.q: Q5. What does Path.cwd() return?
qna.a: It returns the current working directory as a Path object.

qna.q: Q6. What is the difference between exists(), is_file(), and is_dir()?
qna.a: exists() checks whether the path exists, is_file() checks whether it is a file, and is_dir() checks whether it is a directory.

qna.q: Q7. What does mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) do?
qna.a: It creates the requested directory along with missing parent directories and does not raise an error if the directory already exists.

qna.q: Q8. What is the difference between glob() and rglob()?
qna.a: glob() searches according to a pattern within the directory and its specified path scope, while rglob() performs the pattern search recursively through subdirectories.

qna.q: Q9. Can a Path object be used with open()?
qna.a: Yes. For example, open(Path("data/input.txt"), "r") works, and a Path object also provides its own open() method.

qna.q: Q10. Why is pathlib useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: Data Engineering projects frequently work with raw data, processed data, output files, logs, and configuration directories. pathlib provides a clean and maintainable way to construct and manage these paths.

items.title: Basic File Exceptions
explanation: What Are File Exceptions?
When Python works with files, operations such as opening, reading, writing, or accessing paths can fail. Python reports these problems using exceptions.

with open("missing.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    data = file.read()
If missing.txt does not exist, Python raises a FileNotFoundError.
Definition: A file exception is an exception raised when a file or directory operation cannot be completed successfully.
Why Handle File Exceptions?
A data pipeline should not unexpectedly stop just because an input file is missing, a path is invalid, or the program does not have permission to access a resource.

Python Program
      |
      v
File Operation
      |
      +---- Success ----> Continue
      |
      +---- Failure ----> Exception
                              |
                              v
                         Handle Error
                              |
                              v
                       Continue / Stop Safely
try and except
The basic mechanism for handling an exception is try and except.

try:
    with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found")
Python executes the code inside try. If the specified exception occurs, Python executes the matching except block.
FileNotFoundError
FileNotFoundError occurs when a requested file or directory cannot be found at the specified path.

try:
    with open("input.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("input.txt was not found")
This is one of the most common exceptions when working with relative paths.
PermissionError
PermissionError occurs when the operating system denies the requested file or directory operation because the program does not have the required permission.

try:
    with open("protected.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        file.write("Test")
except PermissionError:
    print("Permission denied")
The exact circumstances depend on the operating system, file permissions, and how the file or directory is configured.
IsADirectoryError
IsADirectoryError can occur when an operation expects a file but the specified path refers to a directory.

try:
    with open("data", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except IsADirectoryError:
    print("The path points to a directory, not a file")
NotADirectoryError
NotADirectoryError can occur when part of a path is expected to be a directory but is actually a file.

try:
    with open("data.txt/input.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except NotADirectoryError:
    print("A path component is not a directory")
UnicodeDecodeError
When a text file is opened with an encoding that cannot correctly decode its contents, Python can raise a UnicodeDecodeError while reading.

try:
    with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except UnicodeDecodeError:
    print("The file could not be decoded using UTF-8")
Important: The correct encoding depends on the actual file data. Do not automatically assume that changing the encoding will fix every file-processing problem.
IsADirectoryError vs NotADirectoryError

ExceptionMeaning
IsADirectoryErrorThe path expected to be a file points to a directory.
NotADirectoryErrorA path component expected to be a directory is actually not a directory.
OSError
OSError is a broader exception for operating-system-related errors. Several more specific file and operating-system exceptions inherit from it.

try:
    with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except OSError as error:
    print("File operation failed:", error)

Practical Rule: Prefer catching a specific exception such as FileNotFoundError when you know exactly what problem you want to handle. Use a broader OSError when handling a wider range of operating-system file errors is appropriate.
Multiple File Exceptions
You can handle different file-related exceptions separately.

try:
    with open("input.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File does not exist")
except PermissionError:
    print("Permission denied")
except UnicodeDecodeError:
    print("Unable to decode the file")
Python checks the except blocks and executes the first matching handler.
Using the Exception Object
You can store the exception in a variable using as and inspect its message.

try:
    with open("missing.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError as error:
    print("Error:", error)
This is useful for debugging and logging because the exception object contains information about the failure.
Using else
The optional else block runs only when no exception occurs in the try block.

try:
    with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found")
else:
    print("File read successfully")
This can make successful processing separate from error handling.
Using finally
The finally block runs whether an exception occurs or not.

try:
    with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found")
finally:
    print("File operation finished")
When using with open(), file closing is already handled automatically. Therefore, you usually do not need finally just to close the file.
Important: Do not add manual file.close() inside finally when using with open() simply to close the file. The context manager already handles that cleanup.
Checking Before Opening
You can use pathlib to check whether a file exists before opening it.

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("input.txt")

if path.exists():
    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
else:
    print("File does not exist")
This can be useful when you want to give a clear message or take an alternative action.

Important: Checking first does not guarantee that the later operation will succeed. The file system can change between the check and the operation, so exceptions should still be handled when failure matters.
File Exceptions and Data Pipelines
In Data Engineering, an input file may be missing, corrupted, inaccessible, or located somewhere different from what the pipeline expects.

Pipeline
   |
   v
Find Input File
   |
   +---- Missing ------> Handle FileNotFoundError
   |
   +---- No Permission -> Handle PermissionError
   |
   +---- Wrong Type ----> Handle File/Directory Error
   |
   +---- Invalid Text --> Handle Decode Error
   |
   v
Read and Process Data
Handling these failures explicitly makes the pipeline easier to debug and prevents unexpected crashes.
Practical Data Engineering Example
Suppose a pipeline expects a daily input file. If the file is missing, the pipeline can report the problem clearly.

from pathlib import Path

input_file = Path("data/raw/daily_sales.txt")

try:
    with input_file.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"Input file not found: {input_file}")
except PermissionError:
    print(f"Permission denied: {input_file}")
else:
    print("Input file loaded successfully")
Data Engineering Connection: File exceptions are basic building blocks for reliable pipelines. Later topics such as logging, data quality, ETL, and pipeline monitoring will build on this foundation.
Common Mistakes

• Catching every exception with except Exception: when a specific exception can be handled instead.
  • Ignoring the actual exception message and making debugging harder.
  • Using path.exists() as if it guarantees that a later file operation cannot fail.
  • Manually closing files unnecessarily when using with open().
  • Silently ignoring missing input files when the pipeline actually requires them.
  • Changing the encoding blindly instead of understanding the file's actual encoding.
Quick Summary

ExceptionBasic Meaning
FileNotFoundErrorRequested file or directory cannot be found.
PermissionErrorOperation is not permitted by the operating system.
IsADirectoryErrorA path expected to be a file refers to a directory.
NotADirectoryErrorA path component expected to be a directory is not a directory.
UnicodeDecodeErrorText could not be decoded using the selected encoding.
OSErrorBroader category of operating-system-related errors.
try/exceptUsed to handle exceptions.
elseRuns when the try block succeeds without an exception.
finallyRuns whether an exception occurs or not.
practice: Step 1: Try to open a file that does not exist and observe the FileNotFoundError.

with open("missing.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    print(file.read())
Step 2: Handle the missing file using try and except.

try:
    with open("missing.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        print(file.read())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found")
Step 3: Capture the exception object and print its message.

try:
    with open("missing.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        print(file.read())
except FileNotFoundError as error:
    print("Error:", error)
Step 4: Practice handling more than one file-related exception.

try:
    with open("input.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found")
except PermissionError:
    print("Permission denied")
except UnicodeDecodeError:
    print("Encoding problem")
Step 5: Use pathlib to check whether a file exists before reading it.

from pathlib import Path

path = Path("input.txt")

if path.exists():
    with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        print(file.read())
else:
    print("Input file does not exist")
Step 6: Add an else block to report successful file processing.

try:
    with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found")
else:
    print("File loaded successfully")
Step 7: Add a finally block and observe that it runs whether the operation succeeds or fails.

try:
    with open("data.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("File not found")
finally:
    print("Operation finished")
Step 8: Build a small input-file validation program that checks whether a required file exists, reads it, and reports missing-file or permission errors.

from pathlib import Path

input_file = Path("data/raw/input.txt")

try:
    with input_file.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        data = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"Missing input: {input_file}")
except PermissionError:
    print(f"Permission denied: {input_file}")
else:
    print("Input loaded")

Practice Goal: You should be able to recognize common file exceptions, handle specific exceptions with try/except, use else and finally correctly, and build basic error handling for Data Engineering file inputs.

qna.q: Q1. What is a file exception?
qna.a: It is an exception raised when a file or directory operation cannot be completed successfully.

qna.q: Q2. What is FileNotFoundError?
qna.a: It occurs when Python cannot find the requested file or directory at the specified path.

qna.q: Q3. What is PermissionError?
qna.a: It occurs when the operating system denies the requested file or directory operation because the required permission is unavailable.

qna.q: Q4. What is IsADirectoryError?
qna.a: It occurs when an operation expects a file but the specified path refers to a directory.

qna.q: Q5. What is NotADirectoryError?
qna.a: It occurs when a component of a path is expected to be a directory but is actually not a directory.

qna.q: Q6. What is UnicodeDecodeError in file handling?
qna.a: It can occur when Python tries to decode text using an encoding that cannot correctly decode the file's contents.

qna.q: Q7. Why should specific exceptions be caught when possible?
qna.a: Specific exceptions allow the program to respond appropriately to known failure cases instead of hiding unrelated problems.

qna.q: Q8. What is the purpose of else in exception handling?
qna.a: The else block runs when the try block completes without raising an exception.

qna.q: Q9. What is the purpose of finally?
qna.a: The finally block runs whether an exception occurs or not. With with open(), you normally do not need it merely to close the file.

qna.q: Q10. Why are file exceptions important in Data Engineering?
qna.a: Data pipelines depend on external files and directories. Handling missing, inaccessible, incorrectly typed, or incorrectly decoded files helps pipelines fail in a controlled and understandable way.

items.title: try
explanation: What is try?

The try statement is used to place code that may cause an exception inside a protected block. If an exception occurs, Python can transfer control to an appropriate except block instead of immediately stopping the program.
The basic structure is:

try:
    # Code that may cause an exception
    risky_operation()
except:
    # Handle the exception
    handle_error()

Start
              |
              v
        +-------------+
        |  try block  |
        +-------------+
          |         |
       No error   Error occurs
          |         |
          v         v
       Continue   except block
          |         |
          +----+----+
               |
               v
            Continue
Why Do We Use try?
Without exception handling, an unexpected error can terminate the current execution flow. The try statement allows potentially failing operations to be handled explicitly.
This is especially useful in Data Engineering because pipelines commonly work with files, databases, APIs, network resources, and external systems where failures can occur.
Simple Example

try:
    number = int("abc")
except:
    print("Conversion failed")
The statement int("abc") cannot convert the text "abc" into an integer. Python raises an exception, and control moves to the except block.

try:
    number = int("100")
except:
    print("Conversion failed")

print("Program continues")
Here, no exception occurs, so the except block is skipped and execution continues after the exception-handling structure.
What Happens When an Exception Occurs?
<ol>
• Python starts executing the statements inside try.
• If no exception occurs, the remaining try statements execute normally.
• If an exception occurs, Python stops executing the remaining statements inside that try block.
• Python looks for a matching except handler.
• If a matching handler exists, its code executes.
• Execution then continues after the exception-handling structure.
Example: File Operation

try:
    file = open("data.csv", "r", encoding="utf-8")
    data = file.read()
    file.close()
except:
    print("Unable to read the file")
If the file does not exist or another file-related exception occurs, Python can enter the except block.
Important: try does not prevent an exception from occurring. It provides a controlled place from which the exception can be handled.
Only Put Risky Code Inside try
A common mistake is putting a large amount of unrelated code inside one try block. It is generally clearer to protect only the operation that may fail.

# Less precise
try:
    data = read_file()
    result = process_data(data)
    save_result(result)
except:
    print("Something went wrong")
The above structure makes it difficult to know which operation failed.

# More focused
try:
    data = read_file()
except:
    print("File could not be read")

result = process_data(data)
save_result(result)
As you learn except, you will learn how to handle specific exception types rather than catching every exception broadly.
try Is Not a Replacement for Validation
Exception handling and input validation solve different problems. Validation checks whether data meets expected rules, while exception handling deals with operations that actually raise exceptions.

age = input("Enter age: ")

try:
    age = int(age)
except ValueError:
    print("Age must be a number")
Here, conversion is an operation that can raise an exception, so it is appropriate to protect it with try.
Data Engineering Example
