items.title: `zip()`
explanation: 1. What is zip()?
zip() is a Python built-in function used to combine elements from two or more iterables into pairs or groups.
It is especially useful when you need to process corresponding values from multiple lists or other iterables at the same time.

names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]
scores = [85, 90, 95]

result = zip(names, scores)

print(list(result))
Output:
[("Ravi", 85), ("Anil", 90), ("Priya", 95)]
Key Idea: zip() combines the first item from each iterable, then the second item from each iterable, and continues in the same way.
2. Basic Syntax
zip(iterable1, iterable2, ...)
You can provide two or more iterables.

names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]
ages = [25, 28, 24]
cities = ["Bangalore", "Hyderabad", "Tirupati"]

result = list(zip(names, ages, cities))

print(result)
Output:
[("Ravi", 25, "Bangalore"), ("Anil", 28, "Hyderabad"), ("Priya", 24, "Tirupati")]
3. zip() Returns an Iterator
zip() does not directly return a list. It returns a zip object that can be iterated over.

names = ["Ravi", "Anil"]
scores = [85, 90]

result = zip(names, scores)

print(result)
If you want to see all pairs immediately, convert it to a list:
print(list(result))
Remember: zip() produces an iterator. Use list(), tuple(), or a loop when you need to consume its values.
4. Pairing Two Lists
The most common use is pairing corresponding elements from two lists.

products = ["Laptop", "Phone", "Tablet"]
prices = [50000, 20000, 15000]

for product, price in zip(products, prices):
    print(product, price)
Output:

Laptop 50000
Phone 20000
Tablet 15000
5. Creating a Dictionary with zip()
zip() is commonly used with dict() to combine a list of keys and a list of values.

keys = ["name", "age", "city"]
values = ["Ravi", 25, "Bangalore"]

person = dict(zip(keys, values))

print(person)
Output:
{"name": "Ravi", "age": 25, "city": "Bangalore"}
Useful Pattern: dict(zip(keys, values)) is a simple way to construct a dictionary when you have separate keys and values.
6. Using zip() with a Dictionary Comprehension
zip() can also be combined with dictionary comprehensions.

ids = [101, 102, 103]
names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]

customers = {
    customer_id: name
    for customer_id, name in zip(ids, names)
}

print(customers)
Output:
{101: "Ravi", 102: "Anil", 103: "Priya"}
7. Using zip() with a List Comprehension
You can use zip() when you need to create a list from corresponding values.

products = ["Laptop", "Phone", "Tablet"]
prices = [50000, 20000, 15000]

result = [
    f"{product}: {price}"
    for product, price in zip(products, prices)
]

print(result)
Output:
["Laptop: 50000", "Phone: 20000", "Tablet: 15000"]
8. Unequal Length Iterables
By default, zip() stops when the shortest iterable is exhausted.

names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]
scores = [85, 90]

result = list(zip(names, scores))

print(result)
Output:
[("Ravi", 85), ("Anil", 90)]
The third name is not included because there is no third score.
Important: Standard zip() silently stops at the shortest iterable. Always consider whether your input collections are expected to have the same length.
9. Checking Lengths Before Using zip()
If corresponding data must have the same number of elements, you can validate the lengths first.

names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]
scores = [85, 90]

if len(names) != len(scores):
    raise ValueError("Names and scores must have the same length")

result = list(zip(names, scores))
This is useful when missing data could cause an incorrect transformation.
10. Strict zip()
Modern Python provides a strict option that can detect unequal-length iterables.

names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]
scores = [85, 90]

result = zip(names, scores, strict=True)
When the iterables have different lengths, consuming the zip object raises a ValueError.
Data Engineering Use: strict=True can be useful when two datasets are expected to contain exactly matching numbers of records and silently dropping values would be undesirable.
11. Unzipping Data
You can reverse a zipped structure using zip(*).

data = [
    ("Ravi", 25),
    ("Anil", 28),
    ("Priya", 24)
]

names, ages = zip(*data)

print(names)
print(ages)
Output:

("Ravi", "Anil", "Priya")
(25, 28, 24)
The * unpacks the tuples so that their corresponding elements can be passed separately to zip().
12. Understanding zip(*)

Original data

("Ravi", 25)
("Anil", 28)
("Priya", 24)
       │
       │ zip(*)
       ▼
("Ravi", "Anil", "Priya")
(25, 28, 24)
This technique is often called unzipping because it separates paired or grouped values back into individual sequences.
13. Data Engineering Example — Combining Columns
Imagine data extracted from separate sources:

customer_ids = [101, 102, 103]
customer_names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]
customer_cities = ["Bangalore", "Hyderabad", "Tirupati"]

customers = [
    {
        "id": customer_id,
        "name": name,
        "city": city
    }
    for customer_id, name, city
    in zip(customer_ids, customer_names, customer_cities)
]

print(customers)
This produces:

[
    {"id": 101, "name": "Ravi", "city": "Bangalore"},
    {"id": 102, "name": "Anil", "city": "Hyderabad"},
    {"id": 103, "name": "Priya", "city": "Tirupati"}
]
Data Engineering Use: This pattern can be useful when combining related columns or parallel datasets into structured records before further transformation.
14. Data Engineering Example — Comparing Two Datasets
You can process corresponding values from two collections to compare them.

source_values = [100, 200, 300]
target_values = [100, 180, 300]

comparison = [
    source == target
    for source, target in zip(source_values, target_values)
]

print(comparison)
Output:
[True, False, True]
This basic pattern can help demonstrate record-level comparisons between source and target data.
15. Data Engineering Example — Calculating Differences

source = [100, 200, 300]
target = [90, 220, 300]

differences = [
    source_value - target_value
    for source_value, target_value
    in zip(source, target)
]

print(differences)
Output:
[10, -20, 0]
This can be useful as a simple example of comparing corresponding metrics during data validation.
16. zip() with Three or More Iterables
You can pass more than two iterables.

ids = [101, 102, 103]
names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]
status = ["ACTIVE", "INACTIVE", "ACTIVE"]

records = list(zip(ids, names, status))

print(records)
Output:

[
    (101, "Ravi", "ACTIVE"),
    (102, "Anil", "INACTIVE"),
    (103, "Priya", "ACTIVE")
]
17. zip() with Strings
Strings are iterable, so zip() can pair their characters.

letters1 = "ABC"
letters2 = "123"

result = list(zip(letters1, letters2))

print(result)
Output:
[("A", "1"), ("B", "2"), ("C", "3")]
Although this is useful for understanding zip(), in Data Engineering you will more commonly use it with structured data collections.
18. Common Mistakes

• Forgetting that zip() returns an iterator rather than a list.
  • Assuming unequal-length iterables automatically raise an error.
  • Not noticing that standard zip() stops at the shortest iterable.
  • Using zip() when the values are not actually positionally related.
  • Forgetting that a zip iterator is consumed after iteration.
19. Zip Iterators Are Consumed
A zip object is an iterator. Once its values have been consumed, iterating over it again does not produce the same values.

names = ["Ravi", "Anil"]
scores = [85, 90]

result = zip(names, scores)

print(list(result))
print(list(result))
The second list(result) is empty because the iterator has already been consumed.
Remember: If you need to reuse the result multiple times, convert it to a list or another reusable collection first.
20. Quick Summary

# Pair two lists
list(zip(names, scores))

# Loop through paired values
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(name, score)

# Create a dictionary
dict(zip(keys, values))

# Dictionary comprehension
{k: v for k, v in zip(keys, values)}

# Unzip
names, scores = zip(*data)

# Detect unequal lengths
zip(names, scores, strict=True)

Data Engineering Takeaway: zip() is a useful tool for combining corresponding values, constructing records, comparing parallel datasets, and building dictionaries. Always understand how it handles unequal lengths before using it in a data pipeline.
practice: Step 1: Combine two lists of names and ages using zip() and print each pair.

names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]
ages = [25, 28, 24]

for name, age in zip(names, ages):
    print(name, age)
Step 2: Create a dictionary from separate lists of keys and values.

keys = ["name", "age", "city"]
values = ["Ravi", 25, "Bangalore"]

person = dict(zip(keys, values))
print(person)
Step 3: Use zip() with a dictionary comprehension to create a customer lookup.

ids = [101, 102, 103]
names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]

customers = {
    customer_id: name
    for customer_id, name in zip(ids, names)
}

print(customers)
Step 4: Combine three lists into structured records.

ids = [101, 102, 103]
names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Priya"]
status = ["ACTIVE", "INACTIVE", "ACTIVE"]

records = [
    {"id": customer_id, "name": name, "status": customer_status}
    for customer_id, name, customer_status
    in zip(ids, names, status)
]

print(records)
Step 5: Compare corresponding values from two lists and identify whether they match.

source = [100, 200, 300, 400]
target = [100, 180, 300, 450]

matches = [
    source_value == target_value
    for source_value, target_value in zip(source, target)
]

print(matches)
Step 6: Calculate the difference between corresponding source and target values.

source = [100, 200, 300]
target = [90, 220, 300]

differences = [
    source_value - target_value
    for source_value, target_value in zip(source, target)
]

print(differences)
Step 7: Practice unzipping a list of tuples back into separate sequences.

records = [
    (101, "Ravi"),
    (102, "Anil"),
    (103, "Priya")
]

ids, names = zip(*records)

print(ids)
print(names)
Step 8: Build a small Data Engineering validation task. Combine source IDs and target IDs and identify mismatched pairs.

source_ids = [101, 102, 103, 104]
target_ids = [101, 102, 105, 104]

mismatches = [
    (source_id, target_id)
    for source_id, target_id in zip(source_ids, target_ids)
    if source_id != target_id
]

print(mismatches)
Step 9: Repeat the previous validation using strict=True with deliberately unequal-length lists and observe the error.

source_ids = [101, 102, 103]
target_ids = [101, 102]

result = zip(source_ids, target_ids, strict=True)
print(list(result))
Practice Goal: Be able to use zip() to pair multiple collections, create dictionaries and records, compare parallel datasets, unzip data, and recognize the risks of unequal-length inputs.

qna.q: Q1. What is zip()?
qna.a: zip() is a built-in Python function that combines corresponding elements from two or more iterables.

qna.q: Q2. What does zip() return?
qna.a: It returns a zip iterator containing tuples of corresponding elements.

qna.q: Q3. How do you see all values returned by zip()?
qna.a: You can convert the zip object to a list using list(zip(...)) or iterate over it with a loop.

qna.q: Q4. What happens when the input iterables have different lengths?
qna.a: Standard zip() stops when the shortest iterable is exhausted, so unmatched values from longer iterables are not included.

qna.q: Q5. How can you detect unequal lengths with zip()?
qna.a: Use zip(..., strict=True) when the input iterables are expected to have the same length.

qna.q: Q6. How can zip() be used to create a dictionary?
qna.a: Use dict(zip(keys, values)) to pair keys with their corresponding values.

qna.q: Q7. What does zip(*) do?
qna.a: It can be used to unzip an iterable of tuples by unpacking the tuples and passing their corresponding elements back to zip().

qna.q: Q8. Can zip() combine more than two iterables?
qna.a: Yes. You can pass three or more iterables to zip().

qna.q: Q9. Why is zip() useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It can help combine related columns, construct records, compare source and target data, and perform transformations on parallel datasets.

qna.q: Q10. Can a zip object be reused after iteration?
qna.a: No. A zip object is an iterator and is consumed as its values are iterated. Convert it to a list if you need to reuse the results.

items.title: sorted()
explanation: What is sorted()?
sorted() is a Python built-in function used to return a new sorted list from an iterable such as a list, tuple, set, string, dictionary, or other iterable.
The important point is that sorted() does not modify the original iterable. It creates and returns a new list containing the elements in sorted order.

numbers = [5, 2, 9, 1, 7]

result = sorted(numbers)

print(result)
print(numbers)
Output:\n[1, 2, 5, 7, 9]\n[5, 2, 9, 1, 7]
Definition: sorted() returns a new list containing the elements of an iterable arranged in sorted order.
Basic Syntax

sorted(iterable)

sorted(iterable, reverse=False)

sorted(iterable, key=None, reverse=False)

ParameterMeaning
iterableThe collection or iterable that you want to sort.
keyOptional function used to decide what value should be used for sorting.
reverseOptional boolean. False sorts ascending; True sorts descending.
Sorting Numbers
Numbers are sorted from smallest to largest by default.

numbers = [50, 10, 30, 20, 40]

sorted_numbers = sorted(numbers)

print(sorted_numbers)
Output:\n[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
Sorting in Descending Order
Use reverse=True when you want the largest values first.

numbers = [50, 10, 30, 20, 40]

result = sorted(numbers, reverse=True)

print(result)
Output:\n[50, 40, 30, 20, 10]
Sorting Strings
Strings are sorted according to their ordering rules, generally based on Unicode code points.

names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "Kiran", "Bala"]

result = sorted(names)

print(result)
Output:\n['Anil', 'Bala', 'Kiran', 'Ravi']
Sorting a Tuple
You can pass a tuple to sorted(), but the result is always a list.

numbers = (40, 10, 30, 20)

result = sorted(numbers)

print(result)
print(type(result))
Output:\n[10, 20, 30, 40]\n<class 'list'>
Sorting Using key
The key parameter is one of the most important features of sorted(). It tells Python which value should be used when comparing elements.
For example, suppose you have names and want to sort them according to their length.

names = ["Nethaji", "Ram", "Alexander", "Sai"]

result = sorted(names, key=len)

print(result)
Output:\n['Ram', 'Sai', 'Nethaji', 'Alexander']
Here, len is used as the key function. Python compares the length of each string instead of comparing the strings themselves.
Sorting Dictionaries by Value
A very common Data Engineering use case is sorting records according to a particular field.

employees = {
    "Ravi": 45000,
    "Anil": 30000,
    "Kiran": 50000
}

result = sorted(employees.items(), key=lambda item: item[1])

print(result)
Output:\n[('Anil', 30000), ('Ravi', 45000), ('Kiran', 50000)]
items() produces key-value pairs. The lambda expression uses item[1], the value, as the sorting key.
Sorting a List of Dictionaries
This is especially useful when working with structured records that come from APIs, JSON files, or databases.

employees = [
    {"name": "Ravi", "salary": 45000},
    {"name": "Anil", "salary": 30000},
    {"name": "Kiran", "salary": 50000}
]

result = sorted(employees, key=lambda employee: employee["salary"])

for employee in result:
    print(employee)

Output:
{'name': 'Anil', 'salary': 30000}
{'name': 'Ravi', 'salary': 45000}
{'name': 'Kiran', 'salary': 50000}
Sorting by Multiple Conditions
You can use a tuple as the sorting key to sort by multiple fields.

employees = [
    {"name": "Ravi", "department": "IT", "salary": 45000},
    {"name": "Anil", "department": "HR", "salary": 30000},
    {"name": "Kiran", "department": "IT", "salary": 40000}
]

result = sorted(
    employees,
    key=lambda employee: (employee["department"], employee["salary"])
)

for employee in result:
    print(employee)
Python first sorts by department. If two records have the same department, it then uses salary as the next sorting condition.
sorted() vs list.sort()
Python also provides the list method .sort(). The two approaches are related but behave differently.

Featuresorted()list.sort()
TypeBuilt-in functionList method
ReturnsNew sorted listNone
Changes original listNoYes
Works with many iterablesYesNo, list only

numbers = [30, 10, 20]

result = sorted(numbers)
print(result)
print(numbers)

# Original list remains unchanged

numbers = [30, 10, 20]

result = numbers.sort()

print(numbers)
print(result)
Output:\n[10, 20, 30]\nNone
Data Engineering Example
Suppose an ETL process reads transaction records and you want to process the highest-value transactions first.

transactions = [
    {"id": 101, "amount": 500},
    {"id": 102, "amount": 1500},
    {"id": 103, "amount": 800}
]

transactions = sorted(
    transactions,
    key=lambda row: row["amount"],
    reverse=True
)

for row in transactions:
    print(row)

Output:
{'id': 102, 'amount': 1500}
{'id': 103, 'amount': 800}
{'id': 101, 'amount': 500}

Raw Records
     │
     ▼
sorted(records, key=amount, reverse=True)
     │
     ▼
Highest Amount ─────────► Lowest Amount
     │                         │
     ▼                         ▼
Process important       Process remaining
transactions first      transactions
Important Points to Remember

• sorted() returns a new list.
  • The original iterable is not modified.
  • Default order is ascending.
  • Use reverse=True for descending order.
  • Use key when sorting according to a specific property.
  • The result of sorted() is always a list.
  • sorted() can work with many iterable types.
Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Expecting sorted() to modify the original list. It does not.

numbers = [3, 1, 2]
sorted(numbers)
print(numbers)

# Output: [3, 1, 2]
Mistake 2: Assigning the result of list.sort() to a variable and expecting a sorted list. sort() modifies the list in place and returns None.
Mistake 3: Using the wrong dictionary field in the key function. Make sure the field exists in every record being sorted.
Quick Summary

RequirementExample
Ascendingsorted(data)
Descendingsorted(data, reverse=True)
Sort by lengthsorted(data, key=len)
Sort records by fieldsorted(data, key=lambda x: x["salary"])
Multiple sort fieldssorted(data, key=lambda x: (x["department"], x["salary"]))

qna.q: Q1. What is sorted()?
qna.a: sorted() is a Python built-in function that returns a new list containing the elements of an iterable in sorted order.

qna.q: Q2. Does sorted() modify the original list?
qna.a: No. sorted() creates and returns a new sorted list. The original list remains unchanged.

qna.q: Q3. What is the default sorting order?

qna.a: sorted() returns a new sorted list and works with many iterables. list.sort() modifies the existing list in place and returns None.

qna.q: Q8. Can sorted() sort a list of dictionaries?

qna.q: Q9. What does sorted(data, key=lambda x: x["salary"]) mean?

qna.a: It can be used to organize records by timestamps, amounts, priorities, IDs, or other fields before processing, validation, reporting, or other pipeline operations.

items.title: any() and all()
explanation: What are any() and all()?
any() and all() are Python built-in functions used to check the truth values of elements in an iterable such as a list, tuple, set, or generator.
any(): Returns True if at least one element in the iterable is truthy.
all(): Returns True only if every element in the iterable is truthy.

any()

[False, False, True, False]
          │
          ▼
   At least one True?
          │
        YES
          │
          ▼
        True


all()

[True, True, True, True]
          │
          ▼
     Are ALL True?
          │
        YES
          │
          ▼
        True
Basic Syntax
any(iterable)\nall(iterable)
Both functions accept one iterable and return a Boolean value: True or False.
Using any()
any() checks whether at least one element is truthy.

values = [False, False, True, False]

result = any(values)

print(result)
Output:\nTrue
Only one True value is enough for any() to return True.
When any() Returns False
any() returns False when every element is falsy.
values = [False, False, False]\n\nprint(any(values))
Output:\nFalse
Using all()
all() checks whether every element in the iterable is truthy.

values = [True, True, True]

result = all(values)

print(result)
Output:\nTrue
When all() Returns False
If even one element is falsy, all() returns False.
values = [True, True, False, True]\n\nprint(all(values))
Output:\nFalse
Truthy and Falsy Values
These functions do not require the iterable to contain only True and False. Python evaluates each value according to its truthiness.

values = [1, 5, 10]
print(all(values))

values = [1, 0, 10]
print(all(values))

values = [0, 0, 5]
print(any(values))

Output:
True
False
True
Common falsy values include False, None, 0, 0.0, empty strings, and empty collections.
any() with Conditions
A very common pattern is using a generator expression inside any() to check whether at least one record satisfies a condition.

numbers = [10, 25, 40, 55]

result = any(number > 50 for number in numbers)

print(result)
Output:\nTrue
Because 55 > 50, at least one number satisfies the condition.
all() with Conditions
Use all() when every item must satisfy a condition.

numbers = [10, 25, 40, 55]

result = all(number > 0 for number in numbers)

print(result)
Output:\nTrue
Every number is greater than zero, so the result is True.
Difference Between any() and all()

FunctionQuestion It AnswersExample
any()Is at least one item true?any([False, True, False]) → True
all()Are all items true?all([True, True, True]) → True
Data Engineering Example — Data Validation
In a data pipeline, you may need to check whether at least one record contains an invalid value.

ages = [25, 31, 42, -5, 28]

invalid_found = any(age < 0 for age in ages)

print(invalid_found)
Output:\nTrue
Because -5 is invalid, any() detects that at least one invalid record exists.
Data Engineering Example — Checking Required Fields
Suppose an ETL pipeline receives customer records. You may want to check whether every record contains a non-empty customer ID.

customer_ids = ["C101", "C102", "C103", "C104"]

all_valid = all(customer_ids)

print(all_valid)
Output:\nTrue
If one ID is missing or represented by an empty string, all() will return False.
customer_ids = ["C101", "C102", "", "C104"]\n\nprint(all(customer_ids))
Output:\nFalse
Data Engineering Example — Checking Pipeline Records
Suppose every record must have a positive amount before loading it into a database.

transactions = [
    {"id": 101, "amount": 500},
    {"id": 102, "amount": 1200},
    {"id": 103, "amount": 800}
]

all_valid = all(row["amount"] > 0 for row in transactions)

print(all_valid)
Output:\nTrue
This pattern is useful for performing a quick validation check before continuing to another pipeline stage.
Data Engineering Example — Checking for Missing Values
any() can be used to quickly determine whether at least one required field is missing.

names = ["Ravi", "Anil", "", "Kiran"]

missing_name = any(name == "" for name in names)

print(missing_name)
Output:\nTrue
Here, any() answers the question: Does at least one record have a missing name?
Short-Circuit Behavior
any() and all() can stop checking as soon as the final result is known.
For any(), once a truthy value is found, the result must be True, so remaining elements do not need to be evaluated.
For all(), once a falsy value is found, the result must be False, so remaining elements do not need to be evaluated.

any():  False → False → True → STOP
                         │
                         ▼
                       True

all():  True → True → False → STOP
                         │
                         ▼
                       False
This behavior can be useful when checking large datasets or generator expressions because unnecessary checks may be avoided.
Empty Iterables
There is an important rule to remember when the iterable is empty.
print(any([]))\nprint(all([]))
Output:\nFalse\nTrue
any([]) is False because there is no truthy element. all([]) is True because there is no element that violates the requirement that all elements be truthy.
Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Using all() when you only need one matching record. Use any() when the requirement is "at least one".
Mistake 2: Using any() when every record must pass validation. Use all() for "every record" validation.
Mistake 3: Confusing any(numbers) with any(number > 100 for number in numbers). The first checks whether values themselves are truthy; the second checks a specific condition.
Quick Summary

RequirementUse
At least one value is truthyany(values)
Every value is truthyall(values)
At least one item satisfies a conditionany(condition for item in data)
Every item satisfies a conditionall(condition for item in data)
Check whether any invalid record existsany(invalid_condition for row in data)
Check whether all records are validall(valid_condition for row in data)

    {"id": 101, "amount": 500},

]

Practice Goal: Be able to recognize whether a requirement means "at least one" or "every", then use any() or all() to perform concise validation and condition checks in Python data-processing workflows.

qna.q: Q1. What does any() do?
qna.a: any() returns True if at least one element in the iterable is truthy. Otherwise, it returns False.

qna.q: Q2. What does all() do?
qna.a: all() returns True only when every element in the iterable is truthy. If any element is falsy, it returns False.

qna.q: Q3. What is the easiest way to remember the difference?
qna.a: any() means "at least one" and all() means "every one".

qna.q: Q4. What is the result of any([False, False, True])?
qna.a: The result is True because at least one element is truthy.

qna.q: Q5. What is the result of all([True, True, False])?
qna.a: The result is False because at least one element is falsy.

qna.q: Q6. Can any() and all() be used with conditions?
qna.a: Yes. A common pattern is any(condition for item in data) or all(condition for item in data).

qna.q: Q7. What happens with an empty iterable?
qna.a: any([]) returns False, while all([]) returns True.

qna.q: Q8. Why are any() and all() useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: They provide concise ways to perform validation checks, such as detecting whether any record is invalid or verifying whether every record satisfies a required condition.

qna.q: Q9. What is short-circuit behavior?
qna.a: any() can stop after finding the first truthy result, while all() can stop after finding the first falsy result.

qna.q: Q10. Which function should you use to check whether at least one transaction has an invalid amount?
qna.a: Use any(), for example: any(row["amount"] <= 0 for row in transactions).

items.title: map() Basics
explanation: What is map()?
map() is a Python built-in function used to apply a function to every item in an iterable and produce the transformed results.
It is useful when you want to perform the same transformation on every value in a collection.
Definition: map() applies a function to each item of an iterable and returns a map iterator containing the resulting values.

Input Data
   │
   ├── 10 ──► function ──► 20
   ├── 20 ──► function ──► 40
   ├── 30 ──► function ──► 60
   │
   ▼
Transformed Data
Basic Syntax
map(function, iterable)

PartMeaning
functionThe function that should be applied to every item.
iterableThe collection whose items should be processed.
Simple Example
Suppose you want to multiply every number by 2.

def double(number):
    return number * 2

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]

result = map(double, numbers)

print(list(result))
Output:\n[20, 40, 60, 80]
Here, double() is applied to every item in numbers.
Why Do We Use list()?
In Python 3, map() returns a map iterator, not a list.

numbers = [1, 2, 3]

result = map(lambda x: x * 2, numbers)

print(result)
The result is a map object. To see all transformed values as a list, convert it using list().
result = list(map(lambda x: x * 2, numbers))\n\nprint(result)
Output:\n[2, 4, 6]
Using lambda with map()
A common use of map() is combining it with a lambda function when the transformation is short.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

result = map(lambda x: x * 10, numbers)

print(list(result))
Output:\n[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
The expression lambda x: x * 10 is applied to each number.
Converting Strings to Integers
map() is commonly used when data arrives as strings but needs to be converted into another type.

values = ["10", "20", "30", "40"]

result = map(int, values)

print(list(result))
Output:\n[10, 20, 30, 40]
Here, the built-in int() function is applied to every string.
Converting Strings to Lowercase

names = ["RAVI", "ANIL", "KIRAN"]

result = map(str.lower, names)

print(list(result))
Output:\n['ravi', 'anil', 'kiran']
Here, str.lower is used as the function applied to every string.
Using map() with Multiple Iterables
map() can receive more than one iterable when the function accepts multiple arguments.

numbers1 = [10, 20, 30]
numbers2 = [1, 2, 3]

result = map(lambda x, y: x + y, numbers1, numbers2)

print(list(result))
Output:\n[11, 22, 33]
The first elements are passed together, then the second elements, and so on.

numbers1: 10 ─┐     20 ─┐     30 ─┐
              ├─ + ────┤        │
numbers2:  1 ─┘      2 ─┘      3 ─┘
              │         │         │
             11        22        33
map() with Data Engineering Data
In Data Engineering, raw data often arrives in string form. map() can perform simple transformations before the data moves to the next pipeline stage.

raw_amounts = ["500", "1200", "800", "2500"]

amounts = list(map(int, raw_amounts))

print(amounts)
Output:\n[500, 1200, 800, 2500]
After conversion, the values can be used for numerical calculations or validation.
Data Engineering Example — Cleaning Text
Suppose a source system sends customer names with inconsistent capitalization.

raw_names = ["  ravi  ", " ANIL", "kiran ", " SURESH "]

clean_names = list(
    map(lambda name: name.strip().title(), raw_names)
)

print(clean_names)
Output:\n['Ravi', 'Anil', 'Kiran', 'Suresh']
This demonstrates a simple transformation step that could occur while preparing source data.
map() vs List Comprehension
The same transformation can often be written using a list comprehension.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]

# map()
result1 = list(map(lambda x: x * 2, numbers))

# List comprehension
result2 = [x * 2 for x in numbers]
Both produce the same values. List comprehensions are often easier to read for simple Python transformations, while map() can be convenient when you already have a function to apply.

ApproachExample
map()list(map(int, values))
List comprehension[int(x) for x in values]
map() Is Lazy
The map object calculates values as they are requested rather than immediately creating the complete result list.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]

result = map(lambda x: x * 10, numbers)

print(result)
The transformation is represented by a map iterator. You can consume it using a loop or convert it to a list.
for value in result:\n    print(value)

Output:
10
20
30
40
Important: A map iterator is consumed as you iterate over it. If you need to use the transformed results multiple times, store them in a collection such as a list.
When to Use map()

• Converting values from one type to another.
  • Applying the same simple transformation to every item.
  • Cleaning or normalizing simple values.
  • Applying an existing function to every item.
  • Processing multiple iterables element by element.
When Not to Force map()
Do not use map() simply because it exists. If a list comprehension is much clearer, use the clearer approach.
# Clear\npositive = [x for x in numbers if x > 0]
This example contains filtering logic. A list comprehension communicates the intention more directly. More advanced filtering with filter() will be covered separately.
Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Expecting map() to return a list directly. In Python 3, it returns a map iterator. Use list() when you need a list.
Mistake 2: Forgetting that the function is applied to every element. The function must accept the number of arguments corresponding to the number of iterables supplied.
Mistake 3: Trying to reuse an already-consumed map iterator.

numbers = [1, 2, 3]
result = map(lambda x: x * 2, numbers)

print(list(result))
print(list(result))

# Second result is empty because the iterator was already consumed.
Quick Summary

RequirementExample
Apply a function to every itemmap(function, data)
Convert strings to integerslist(map(int, values))
Use a short transformationlist(map(lambda x: x * 2, values))
Process two lists togethermap(function, list1, list2)
Get a list from the resultlist(map(...))

Step 7: Compare map() with a list comprehension for the same transformation.

Practice Goal: Be able to use map() for simple transformations, type conversions, text cleaning, and element-by-element processing of source data in Python-based Data Engineering workflows.

qna.q: Q1. What is map()?
qna.a: map() is a Python built-in function that applies a function to every item in an iterable and returns a map iterator containing the results.

qna.q: Q2. What is the syntax of map()?
qna.a: The basic syntax is map(function, iterable).

qna.q: Q3. Does map() return a list?
qna.a: No. In Python 3, map() returns a map iterator. Use list() if you need the results as a list.

qna.q: Q4. Why is map(int, values) useful?
qna.a: It applies int() to every item, which is useful when numeric data arrives as strings and needs to be converted into integers.

qna.q: Q5. Can map() work with multiple iterables?
qna.a: Yes. The function must accept the corresponding number of arguments, and map() processes the iterables element by element.

qna.q: Q6. What is the difference between map() and a list comprehension?
qna.a: Both can perform transformations. map() applies a function to each item and returns an iterator, while a list comprehension directly creates a list.

qna.q: Q7. Why is map() called lazy?
qna.a: Because the transformed values are produced when the map iterator is consumed rather than creating the complete result immediately.

qna.q: Q8. Can a map iterator be reused after it has been consumed?
qna.a: No. Once the iterator has been consumed, iterating over it again produces no remaining values.

qna.q: Q9. How can map() be useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It can perform simple transformations such as type conversion, text normalization, and element-by-element processing while preparing source data.

qna.q: Q10. When should you avoid forcing the use of map()?
qna.a: If a list comprehension or another approach expresses the transformation more clearly, prefer the clearer approach rather than using map() unnecessarily.

items.title: filter() Basics
explanation: What is filter()?
filter() is a Python built-in function used to select elements from an iterable that satisfy a given condition.
Unlike map(), which transforms every item, filter() keeps only the items for which the filtering function returns a truthy value.
Definition: filter() returns an iterator containing only the elements of an iterable for which the provided function returns a truthy value.

Input Data
   │
   ├── 10 ──► condition ──► Keep
   ├── 5  ──► condition ──► Remove
   ├── 20 ──► condition ──► Keep
   ├── 3  ──► condition ──► Remove
   │
   ▼
Filtered Data
[10, 20]
Basic Syntax
filter(function, iterable)

PartMeaning
functionA function that determines whether each item should be kept.
iterableThe collection whose elements should be checked.
Simple Example
Suppose you want to keep only numbers greater than 10.

def greater_than_10(number):
    return number > 10

numbers = [5, 12, 8, 20, 15]

result = filter(greater_than_10, numbers)

print(list(result))
Output:\n[12, 20, 15]
The function returns True for values greater than 10, so those values are kept.
Using lambda with filter()
For short conditions, a lambda function is commonly used.

numbers = [5, 12, 8, 20, 15]

result = filter(lambda x: x > 10, numbers)

print(list(result))
Output:\n[12, 20, 15]
Here, x > 10 is the condition. Only values for which the condition is True are retained.
filter() Returns an Iterator
In Python 3, filter() returns a filter iterator rather than a list.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

result = filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, numbers)

print(result)
To obtain a list of the filtered values, use list().
result = list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, numbers))\n\nprint(result)
Output:\n[2, 4]
Filtering Even Numbers
A common example is keeping only even numbers.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]

result = list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, numbers))

print(result)
Output:\n[2, 4, 6, 8]
Filtering Odd Numbers

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]

result = list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 != 0, numbers))

print(result)
Output:\n[1, 3, 5, 7]
Filtering Strings
You can use filter() to select strings based on conditions such as length.

names = ["Ram", "Alexander", "Sai", "Nethaji", "Anil"]

result = filter(lambda name: len(name) > 4, names)

print(list(result))
Output:\n['Alexander', 'Nethaji']
Filtering Non-Empty Values
If the function argument is None, filter() removes falsy values and keeps truthy values.

values = ["Ravi", "", "Anil", "", "Kiran"]

result = list(filter(None, values))

print(result)
Output:\n['Ravi', 'Anil', 'Kiran']
This can be useful for removing empty strings or other falsy values, but remember that values such as 0 and False are also falsy.
Filtering a List of Dictionaries
This is especially useful when working with structured records from APIs, JSON files, or databases.

employees = [
    {"name": "Ravi", "salary": 45000},
    {"name": "Anil", "salary": 30000},
    {"name": "Kiran", "salary": 50000}
]

result = filter(
    lambda employee: employee["salary"] > 40000,
    employees
)

for employee in result:
    print(employee)
Output:\n{'name': 'Ravi', 'salary': 45000}\n{'name': 'Kiran', 'salary': 50000}
Data Engineering Example — Filtering Valid Records
In an ETL pipeline, you may receive records containing invalid transaction amounts. filter() can select only records that satisfy the validation rule.

transactions = [
    {"id": 101, "amount": 500},
    {"id": 102, "amount": -100},
    {"id": 103, "amount": 800},
    {"id": 104, "amount": 0}
]

valid_transactions = filter(
    lambda row: row["amount"] > 0,
    transactions
)

print(list(valid_transactions))

Output:
[
    {'id': 101, 'amount': 500},
    {'id': 103, 'amount': 800}
]

Source Transactions
        │
        ▼
   filter(amount > 0)
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
   │         │
 Valid     Invalid
   │         │
   ▼         ▼
Pipeline   Reject /
Next Step  Review
Data Engineering Example — Filtering Records by Status
Suppose an API returns many orders but only completed orders should continue to the next stage.

orders = [
    {"id": 101, "status": "completed"},
    {"id": 102, "status": "pending"},
    {"id": 103, "status": "completed"},
    {"id": 104, "status": "cancelled"}
]

completed = list(filter(
    lambda order: order["status"] == "completed",
    orders
))

print(completed)

Output:
[
    {'id': 101, 'status': 'completed'},
    {'id': 103, 'status': 'completed'}
]
filter() vs map()
The easiest way to understand the difference is:

map()
Input ──► Transform every item ──► Output

filter()
Input ──► Check every item ──► Keep matching items

FunctionPurposeExample
map()Transforms every itemmap(int, values)
filter()Selects matching itemsfilter(lambda x: x > 10, values)

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# map() → transforms every value
doubled = list(map(lambda x: x * 2, numbers))

# filter() → keeps only matching values
even = list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, numbers))

print(doubled)
print(even)
Output:\n[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]\n[2, 4]
filter() vs List Comprehension
The same filtering operation can usually be written using a list comprehension.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# filter()
result1 = list(filter(lambda x: x > 2, numbers))

# List comprehension
result2 = [x for x in numbers if x > 2]
Both produce the same result. List comprehensions are often easier to read for simple filtering, while filter() can be useful when you already have a filtering function.

ApproachExample
filter()list(filter(lambda x: x > 2, numbers))
List comprehension[x for x in numbers if x > 2]
filter() Is Lazy
Like map(), filter() returns an iterator. The filtering operation produces values as the iterator is consumed.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

result = filter(lambda x: x > 2, numbers)

for value in result:
    print(value)

Output:
3
4
5
Important: A filter iterator is consumed as you iterate over it. If you need to reuse the filtered results multiple times, convert it to a list or another suitable collection.
Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Expecting filter() to return a list directly. In Python 3, it returns a filter iterator. Use list() when a list is required.
Mistake 2: Using map() when the requirement is actually to remove or select records. Use filter() for selection.
Mistake 3: Forgetting that the filtering function should return a truthy or falsy result for each item.
Mistake 4: Using filter(None, data) without realizing that all falsy values, including 0, False, None, and empty strings, are removed.
Quick Summary

RequirementExample
Filter using a functionfilter(function, data)
Filter with a conditionfilter(lambda x: x > 10, data)
Get a listlist(filter(...))
Keep even numbersfilter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, numbers)
Filter records by fieldfilter(lambda x: x["status"] == "completed", records)
Remove falsy valuesfilter(None, values)

qna.a: filter() is a Python built-in function that selects elements from an iterable for which a filtering function returns a truthy value.

qna.q: Q2. What is the syntax of filter()?
qna.a: The basic syntax is filter(function, iterable).

qna.q: Q8. Can filter() work with dictionaries?
qna.a: Yes. You can filter a list of dictionaries using a condition based on one or more dictionary fields.

qna.q: Q9. Is filter() lazy?

items.title: Iterable vs Iterator
explanation: What is an Iterable?
An iterable is an object that can be traversed one item at a time. In simple terms, if you can use an object in a for loop, it is generally iterable.
Common Python iterables include lists, tuples, strings, sets, dictionaries, and files.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

for number in numbers:
    print(number)

Output:
10
20
30
Definition: An iterable is an object that can provide its elements one at a time, usually through an iterator.
What is an Iterator?
An iterator is an object that represents the process of traversing through an iterable one item at a time.
An iterator remembers its current position. You can retrieve the next value using the next() function.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

Output:
10
20
30
Definition: An iterator is an object that produces values one at a time and keeps track of its current position.
Iterable vs Iterator

Iterable
   │
   │ iter()
   ▼
Iterator
   │
   │ next()
   ▼
Value 1
   │
   │ next()
   ▼
Value 2
   │
   │ next()
   ▼
Value 3
   │
   │ next()
   ▼
StopIteration

FeatureIterableIterator
Can be looped overYesYes
Provides iter()YesYes
Provides next()Not necessarilyYes
Remembers current positionNot by itselfYes
Can be consumedNot necessarilyYes
Creating an Iterator with iter()
The iter() function takes an iterable and returns an iterator for it.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

iterator = iter(numbers)

print(type(numbers))
print(type(iterator))
The list is the iterable, while the object returned by iter() is the iterator.
Getting Values with next()
The next() function asks an iterator for its next available value.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]
iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

Output:
10
20
30
Every call to next() advances the iterator to the next position.
What Happens After the Iterator Is Exhausted?
Once there are no more values, calling next() raises StopIteration.

numbers = [10, 20]
iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

Output:
10
20
StopIteration
A for loop handles StopIteration automatically, which is why you normally do not see this exception while using a loop.
How a for Loop Uses an Iterator
When Python receives an iterable in a for loop, it obtains an iterator and repeatedly requests the next value until the iterator is exhausted.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

for number in numbers:
    print(number)
Conceptually, the loop behaves roughly like this:

numbers = [10, 20, 30]
iterator = iter(numbers)

while True:
    try:
        number = next(iterator)
        print(number)
    except StopIteration:
        break
You normally use the for loop instead of writing this manually, but understanding this process explains the relationship between iterables and iterators.
List: Iterable but Not Its Own Iterator
A list is an iterable. Calling iter() on the list creates an iterator.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

print(iter(numbers))
print(next(numbers))
The second operation fails because the list itself is not an iterator. You need to create an iterator first.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]
iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
Output:\n10
Iterator Is Also Iterable
An important relationship is that an iterator is itself iterable. This is why an iterator can also be used directly in a for loop.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]
iterator = iter(numbers)

for number in iterator:
    print(number)
However, the iterator is consumed as the loop progresses.
Iterable vs Iterator — Simple Example

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

# Iterable
print(numbers)

# Create iterator
iterator = iter(numbers)

# Consume iterator
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

numbers = [10, 20, 30]
      │
      │ iter()
      ▼
iterator
      │
      ├── next() → 10
      ├── next() → 20
      └── next() → 30
Generators Are Iterators
Generators are an important example of iterators in Python. A generator produces values one at a time instead of creating all values at once.

def numbers():
    yield 10
    yield 20
    yield 30

generator = numbers()

print(next(generator))
print(next(generator))
print(next(generator))

Output:
10
20
30
The generator remembers where it stopped and continues from there when next() is called again.
Why Iterators Matter in Data Engineering
Data Engineering often involves processing large amounts of data. Loading an entire dataset into memory at once can be expensive.
Iterators allow data to be processed one item at a time, which can reduce memory usage.

Large Data Source
       │
       ▼
    Iterator
       │
       ├── Record 1 ──► Process
       ├── Record 2 ──► Process
       ├── Record 3 ──► Process
       ├── Record 4 ──► Process
       │
       ▼
 Continue until data is exhausted
File Objects and Iteration
File objects are iterable. This makes it possible to process a file line by line instead of loading the entire file into memory.
with open("sales.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:\n    for line in file:\n        print(line.strip())
This pattern is useful when processing large log files, CSV-like text files, or other line-oriented data.
Iterators and Memory Efficiency
Consider a large sequence of values. A list stores all values in memory, while an iterator can produce values as they are requested.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
Only the requested values are retrieved through the iterator interface. This idea becomes particularly important with generators and large data-processing workflows.

Data Engineering Connection: Iterators and generators are useful when processing large files, streams, API results, or database records incrementally instead of requiring the entire dataset to be materialized in memory.
Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Assuming every iterable supports next() directly. A list is iterable but is not itself an iterator.
Mistake 2: Forgetting that an iterator has a current position. Calling next() advances that position.
Mistake 3: Trying to reuse an exhausted iterator. Once it reaches the end, it has no remaining values.
Mistake 4: Thinking that an iterator automatically stores all results. Its purpose is to provide values progressively.
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
IterableAn object that can provide elements for iteration.
IteratorAn object that produces the next value and remembers its position.
iter()Creates or obtains an iterator from an iterable.
next()Gets the next value from an iterator.
StopIterationSignals that the iterator has no more values.
GeneratorA convenient way to create an iterator using yield.

Step 3: Call next() one more time after the iterator is exhausted and observe the StopIteration exception.

iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

Step 4: Use a for loop with a list and understand that Python internally obtains an iterator.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

for number in numbers:
    print(number)
Step 5: Create an iterator from a list and partially consume it before using the iterator in a for loop.

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]
iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))

Step 6: Create a generator using yield and retrieve its values using next().

def numbers():
    yield 100
    yield 200
    yield 300

generator = numbers()

Step 7: Process a text file line by line using its iterable behavior instead of reading the entire file into memory.
with open("sales.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:\n    for line in file:\n        print(line.strip())
Step 8: Explain the difference between an iterable and an iterator using a list example.

# iter(numbers) → iterator

Practice Goal: Understand the relationship between iterables, iterators, iter(), next(), and StopIteration. This foundation is important for processing large datasets efficiently in Data Engineering.

qna.q: Q1. What is an iterable?
qna.a: An iterable is an object that can provide its elements one at a time and can generally be used in a for loop.

qna.q: Q2. What is an iterator?
qna.a: An iterator is an object that produces values one at a time and keeps track of its current position.

qna.q: Q3. What does iter() do?
qna.a: iter() obtains an iterator from an iterable.

qna.q: Q4. What does next() do?
qna.a: next() retrieves the next available value from an iterator and advances its position.

qna.q: Q5. Is a list an iterator?
qna.a: A list is an iterable, but a normal list is not itself an iterator. You can create an iterator from it using iter(list).

qna.q: Q6. What happens when an iterator has no more values?
qna.a: Calling next() raises StopIteration. A normal for loop handles this internally.

qna.q: Q7. Is an iterator also iterable?
qna.a: Yes. An iterator is also iterable, which is why it can be used directly in a for loop.

qna.q: Q8. Why are iterators useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: They allow data to be processed progressively, which can help avoid loading an entire large dataset into memory at once.

qna.q: Q9. What is a generator?
qna.a: A generator is a convenient way to create an iterator, commonly using the yield statement to produce values one at a time.

qna.q: Q10. What is the key difference between an iterable and an iterator?
qna.a: An iterable provides a way to obtain an iterator, while an iterator maintains the current traversal position and provides the next value through next().

items.title: iter()
explanation: What is iter()?
iter() is a Python built-in function used to obtain an iterator from an iterable object.
It is the bridge between an iterable such as a list and an iterator that can produce values one at a time using next().
Definition: iter() returns an iterator object for an iterable.

Iterable
[List / Tuple / String / File]
        │
        │ iter()
        ▼
    Iterator
        │
        │ next()
        ▼
     Value 1
        │
        │ next()
        ▼
     Value 2
Basic Syntax
iter(iterable)
The most common form takes one iterable and returns its iterator.
Creating an Iterator from a List

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

iterator = iter(numbers)

print(iterator)
The list is the iterable, while iterator is the iterator created from that list.
print(next(iterator))\nprint(next(iterator))\nprint(next(iterator))

Output:
10
20
30
iter() with Different Iterables
iter() can be used with many Python objects that are iterable.

# List
numbers = [10, 20, 30]
list_iterator = iter(numbers)

# Tuple
values = ("A", "B", "C")
tuple_iterator = iter(values)

# String
text = "ABC"
string_iterator = iter(text)

print(next(list_iterator))
print(next(tuple_iterator))
print(next(string_iterator))

Output:
10
A
A
iter() and next() Work Together
iter() creates or obtains the iterator, while next() retrieves values from that iterator.

numbers = [100, 200, 300]

iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

numbers = [100, 200, 300]
          │
          │ iter()
          ▼
       iterator
          │
          ├── next() → 100
          ├── next() → 200
          └── next() → 300
Iterator Position Is Maintained
An iterator remembers where it currently is. Each call to next() moves forward.

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]
iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
Output:\n10\n20
The next call continues from the current position rather than starting again.
print(next(iterator))\nprint(next(iterator))
Output:\n30\n40
What Happens When the Iterator Ends?
When the iterator has no more values, calling next() raises StopIteration.

numbers = [10, 20]
iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

Output:
10
20
StopIteration
A for loop normally handles StopIteration automatically.
Using iter() with a for Loop
You can explicitly create an iterator and then use it in a for loop.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]
iterator = iter(numbers)

for number in iterator:
    print(number)

Output:
10
20
30
The iterator is consumed as the loop runs.
Iterable vs Iterator
iter() helps demonstrate the difference between an iterable and an iterator.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

# numbers is an iterable
# iter(numbers) creates an iterator

iterator = iter(numbers)

ObjectRole
numbersIterable
iter(numbers)Iterator
next(iterator)Gets the next value
iter() Does Not Copy the Data
A common misunderstanding is that iter() creates a second copy of the entire collection. It does not.
numbers = [10, 20, 30]\niterator = iter(numbers)
The iterator provides a way to traverse the existing iterable. It does not mean that another complete list has been created.
iter() with Files
File objects are iterable. You can obtain an iterator from a file and retrieve lines one at a time.

with open("sales.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    iterator = iter(file)

    print(next(iterator).strip())
    print(next(iterator).strip())
This allows file data to be processed incrementally rather than loading the entire file into memory.
Data Engineering Example — Processing Records One at a Time
Suppose a collection contains transaction records. An iterator can be used to retrieve records progressively.

transactions = [
    {"id": 101, "amount": 500},
    {"id": 102, "amount": 800},
    {"id": 103, "amount": 1200}
]

iterator = iter(transactions)

record = next(iterator)
print(record)
Output:\n{'id': 101, 'amount': 500}
The next call retrieves the next record without restarting from the beginning.
Data Engineering Example — Large File Processing
In Data Engineering, large log or data files should often be processed incrementally rather than loading the complete file into memory.

with open("large_sales.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    iterator = iter(file)

    for line in iterator:
        line = line.strip()
        if line:
            print(line)

Large File
    │
    ▼
iter(file)
    │
    ├── Line 1 ──► Process
    ├── Line 2 ──► Process
    ├── Line 3 ──► Process
    └── ...
         │
         ▼
      End of File
Data Engineering Connection: iter() is useful when you need an iterator interface for incremental processing of files, records, or other large data sources.
Two-Argument Form of iter()
iter() also has a second form that repeatedly calls a zero-argument function until that function returns a specified sentinel value.
iter(callable, sentinel)
This is an advanced use of iter(). For example, the following repeatedly calls input() until the user enters stop.
for value in iter(lambda: input("Enter value: "), "stop"):\n    print("Received:", value)
When the function returns "stop", iteration ends and that sentinel value is not yielded.
For this roadmap: Understand the two-argument form conceptually. The one-argument form, iter(iterable), is the important foundation for normal iterator usage.
Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Calling next() directly on a list. Use iter() first: next(iter(numbers)).
Mistake 2: Expecting iter() to return the first value. It returns an iterator. Use next() to retrieve a value.
Mistake 3: Forgetting that the iterator maintains its position. Repeated calls to next() continue from where the previous call stopped.
Mistake 4: Calling next() after the iterator is exhausted without handling StopIteration.
Quick Summary

ConceptExample
Create iteratoriterator = iter(data)
Get next valuenext(iterator)
End of iteratorStopIteration
Iterate through valuesfor item in iterator
Iterable[10, 20, 30]
Iteratoriter([10, 20, 30])

Practice Goal: Be able to use iter() to obtain iterators from lists, strings, tuples, files, and other iterables, then use next() or a for loop to process values incrementally.

qna.a: It provides an iterator interface that supports incremental processing of data, which is useful for large files and other data sources where processing everything at once may be undesirable.

qna.q: Q9. What is the two-argument form of iter()?
qna.a: The form iter(callable, sentinel) repeatedly calls a zero-argument callable until it returns the specified sentinel value.

qna.q: Q10. Does iter() return the first value of an iterable?
qna.a: No. It returns an iterator. Use next() to retrieve the next value.

items.title: next()
explanation: What is next()?
next() is a Python built-in function used to retrieve the next value from an iterator.
Every time you call next(), the iterator moves forward and returns the next available value.
Definition: next() retrieves the next item from an iterator and advances the iterator's current position.

Iterator
   │
   ├── next() ──► Value 1
   │
   ├── next() ──► Value 2
   │
   ├── next() ──► Value 3
   │
   └── next() ──► StopIteration
Basic Syntax
next(iterator)
You can also provide a default value:
next(iterator, default)

ArgumentMeaning
iteratorThe iterator from which the next value should be retrieved.
defaultOptional value returned when the iterator is exhausted instead of raising StopIteration.
Basic Example
First create an iterator using iter().

numbers = [10, 20, 30]

iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

Output:
10
20
30
Each call to next() retrieves the next value and advances the iterator.
How the Iterator Position Changes

numbers = [100, 200, 300, 400]
iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))  # 100
print(next(iterator))  # 200
print(next(iterator))  # 300

Before next():
[100, 200, 300, 400]
  ▲
  │
 position

next() → 100

next() → 200

next() → 300

Remaining → 400
The iterator does not restart from the beginning after each call. It remembers its current position.
What Happens at the End?
When there are no more values available, calling next() normally raises StopIteration.

numbers = [10, 20]
iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

Output:
10
20
StopIteration
StopIteration tells Python that the iterator has reached its end.
Using a Default Value
You can provide a second argument to next(). If the iterator is exhausted, Python returns that default value instead of raising StopIteration.

numbers = [10, 20]
iterator = iter(numbers)

print(next(iterator, "No more data"))
print(next(iterator, "No more data"))
print(next(iterator, "No more data"))

Output:
10
20
No more data
Important: The default value is returned only when the iterator is exhausted. It does not replace a value that actually exists in the iterator.
next() with a String Iterator
Strings are iterable, so you can create an iterator from a string and retrieve characters one at a time.

text = "DATA"
iterator = iter(text)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

Output:
D
A
T
A
next() with a Tuple Iterator

values = ("Python", "SQL", "Spark")
iterator = iter(values)

print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))

Output:
Python
SQL
Spark
Using next() in a while Loop
You can manually consume an iterator using next() inside a loop.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]
iterator = iter(numbers)

while True:
    try:
        value = next(iterator)
        print(value)
    except StopIteration:
        break

Output:
10
20
30
This is conceptually similar to what a for loop does internally when it consumes an iterator.
next() vs for Loop
A for loop automatically handles iterator traversal and StopIteration. Use next() when you need explicit control over retrieving individual values.

ApproachUse Case
for loopProcess all values automatically.
next()Retrieve the next value manually and control the traversal.

# Automatic traversal
for number in numbers:
    print(number)

# Manual traversal
iterator = iter(numbers)
print(next(iterator))
print(next(iterator))
Data Engineering Example — Reading Records Sequentially
Suppose an ETL process receives transaction records and needs to retrieve records one at a time.

transactions = [
    {"id": 101, "amount": 500},
    {"id": 102, "amount": 800},
    {"id": 103, "amount": 1200}
]

iterator = iter(transactions)

first_record = next(iterator)
print(first_record)
Output:\n{'id': 101, 'amount': 500}
The next call retrieves the following record without starting from the beginning.
Data Engineering Example — Processing a File
File objects can be iterated line by line. next() can be useful when you need to read a specific first line or process a header before processing the remaining records.

with open("sales.csv", "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    iterator = iter(file)

    header = next(iterator)
    print("Header:", header.strip())

    for line in iterator:
        print("Data:", line.strip())
Here, next() consumes the header first. The following for loop continues from the next line rather than reading the header again.

sales.csv
   │
   ▼
next(iterator)
   │
   ▼
Header
   │
   ▼
for loop
   │
   ├── Row 1
   ├── Row 2
   ├── Row 3
   └── ...
Data Engineering Example — Getting the First Record
A default value can be useful when a data source may be empty.

records = []
iterator = iter(records)

first_record = next(iterator, None)

if first_record is None:
    print("No records available")
else:
    print(first_record)
Output:\nNo records available
This avoids an exception when there is no first record.
Iterators Are Consumed
Once a value has been retrieved with next(), that value is no longer the next value of the iterator.

numbers = [10, 20, 30]
iterator = iter(numbers)

first = next(iterator)
second = next(iterator)

print(first)
print(second)
print(next(iterator))

Output:
10
20
30
If you need to start again, create a new iterator.
iterator = iter(numbers)\nprint(next(iterator))
Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Calling next() on a normal list. A list is iterable but is not itself an iterator. Use next(iter(numbers)) or store the iterator first.
Mistake 2: Forgetting that every next() call advances the iterator.
Mistake 3: Calling next() after the iterator is exhausted without handling StopIteration or providing a default.
Mistake 4: Assuming next() starts from the beginning every time. It always continues from the iterator's current position.
Quick Summary

RequirementExample
Get next valuenext(iterator)
Get next value safelynext(iterator, None)
Create iterator firstiterator = iter(data)
End of iteratorStopIteration
Process remaining valuesfor item in iterator
Restart traversalCreate a new iterator with iter(data)

qna.q: Q1. What does next() do?
qna.a: next() retrieves the next value from an iterator and advances the iterator's position.

qna.q: Q2. What is the basic syntax of next()?
qna.a: The basic syntax is next(iterator). An optional default can be provided as next(iterator, default).

qna.q: Q3. Can you use next() directly on a list?
qna.a: No. A normal list is iterable but is not an iterator. You need to create an iterator first using iter(list).

qna.q: Q4. What happens when there are no more values?
qna.a: If no default value is provided, next() raises StopIteration when the iterator is exhausted.

qna.q: Q5. How can you avoid StopIteration?
qna.a: Provide a default value, for example next(iterator, None). The default is returned when the iterator has no more values.

qna.q: Q6. Does next() change the iterator's position?
qna.a: Yes. Each successful call to next() advances the iterator to the next position.

qna.q: Q7. How can next() be useful when reading a CSV file?
qna.a: It can be used to consume the header first, after which a for loop can process the remaining data rows.

qna.q: Q8. Why is next() useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It allows controlled, incremental retrieval of records from iterators, which can be useful when processing large files or other data sources progressively.

qna.q: Q9. What happens if you call next() twice on the same iterator?
qna.a: The first call returns the current next value and the second call returns the following value because the iterator advances after each successful call.

qna.q: Q10. How do you restart an iterator from the beginning?
qna.a: Create a new iterator from the original iterable using iter(data). An exhausted iterator itself cannot be reset with next().

items.title: Generators
explanation: What is a Generator?
A generator is a special type of Python iterator that produces values one at a time instead of creating all values at once.
Generators are created using a function containing the yield statement or by using a generator expression.
Definition: A generator is an iterator that produces values lazily, one value at a time, when requested.

Generator Function
      │
      │ yield
      ▼
   Value 1
      │
      │ next()
      ▼
   Value 2
      │
      │ next()
      ▼
   Value 3
      │
      ▼
 StopIteration
Why Do We Need Generators?
Suppose you need to generate one million numbers.
A normal list stores all one million values in memory. A generator can produce each value only when it is requested.

# List
numbers = [x for x in range(1000000)]

# Generator
numbers = (x for x in range(1000000))
The generator does not need to create the complete sequence before you start processing it.

Large Dataset
     │
     ▼
 Generator
     │
     ├── Record 1 → Process
     ├── Record 2 → Process
     ├── Record 3 → Process
     ├── Record 4 → Process
     └── ...
          │
          ▼
       End of Data
Key Idea: Generators are especially useful when data is large and you want to process it incrementally instead of loading everything into memory at once.
Creating a Generator Function
A generator function looks like a normal function, but it uses yield instead of returning all values at once.

def numbers():
    yield 10
    yield 20
    yield 30
Calling the function does not immediately execute all of its code. It returns a generator object.
result = numbers()\n\nprint(result)
Using next() with a Generator
A generator is an iterator, so you can use next() to retrieve its values.

def numbers():
    yield 10
    yield 20
    yield 30

generator = numbers()

print(next(generator))
print(next(generator))
print(next(generator))

Output:
10
20
30
Each next() call resumes the generator from where the previous yield stopped.
How yield Works
The yield statement temporarily pauses the generator function and sends a value to the caller.

def numbers():
    print("Before first yield")
    yield 10
    print("Before second yield")
    yield 20
    print("Before third yield")
    yield 30
    print("Finished")

generator = numbers()

print(next(generator))
print(next(generator))
print(next(generator))
After each yield, execution pauses. The next call resumes execution from that exact point.

next()
  │
  ▼
execute
  │
  ▼
yield 10
  │
  └── pause
       │
next()│
  │   ▼
  │ resume
  │   │
  │ yield 20
  │   │
  │   └── pause
  │
next()│
  ▼
resume → yield 30
yield vs return
The most important difference is that return ends a function, while yield pauses a generator and allows it to continue later.

def normal_function():
    return 10


def generator_function():
    yield 10
    yield 20

returnyield
Ends the function.Pauses the generator.
Returns a result.Produces a value.
Function execution ends.Execution can resume later.
Normally used for one final result.Can produce multiple values over time.
Using a Generator with a for Loop
You normally do not need to call next() manually. A for loop can consume the generator automatically.

def numbers():
    yield 10
    yield 20
    yield 30

for number in numbers():
    print(number)

Output:
10
20
30
Generator with a Loop
Generators become especially useful when producing a sequence dynamically.

def count_up_to(limit):
    number = 1

    while number <= limit:
        yield number
        number += 1

for value in count_up_to(5):
    print(value)

Output:
1
2
3
4
5
The generator produces each number only when the loop requests it.
Generators and Memory Efficiency
Consider generating one million numbers.

# Creates the complete list immediately
numbers = [x for x in range(1000000)]

# Produces values lazily
numbers = (x for x in range(1000000))
The list comprehension creates and stores a complete list. The generator expression produces values when they are requested.
Important: Generators can reduce memory usage because they do not need to materialize the entire result sequence at once.
Generators for Large Files
A common Data Engineering pattern is reading and processing a large file one line at a time.

def read_sales(file_path):
    with open(file_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as file:
        for line in file:
            yield line.strip()

for row in read_sales("sales.csv"):
    print(row)
The function does not create a list containing every line. It yields one line at a time.

Large sales.csv
       │
       ▼
 read_sales()
       │
       ├── yield row 1 → process
       ├── yield row 2 → process
       ├── yield row 3 → process
       └── ...
             │
             ▼
          End of file
Data Engineering Example — Processing Records
Suppose you have a large source of transaction records. A generator can produce only the records needed for processing.

def valid_transactions(transactions):
    for transaction in transactions:
        if transaction["amount"] > 0:
            yield transaction

transactions = [
    {"id": 101, "amount": 500},
    {"id": 102, "amount": -100},
    {"id": 103, "amount": 800}
]

for transaction in valid_transactions(transactions):
    print(transaction)
Output:\n{'id': 101, 'amount': 500}\n{'id': 103, 'amount': 800}
This pattern can be useful when building a processing stage that should emit only records meeting a condition.
Generator Pipeline
Generators can be chained together to create processing stages.

def read_numbers():
    for number in range(1, 6):
        yield number


def square(numbers):
    for number in numbers:
        yield number * number


for value in square(read_numbers()):
    print(value)

Output:
1
4
9
16
25

Source
  │
  ▼
read_numbers()
  │
  ▼
square()
  │
  ▼
Output

Each stage produces values incrementally.

Data Engineering Connection: Generator pipelines can represent a sequence of processing stages where data flows through transformations without requiring every intermediate result to be stored in memory.
Generator Expressions
A generator expression looks similar to a list comprehension, but uses parentheses instead of square brackets.

# List comprehension
numbers = [x * 2 for x in range(5)]

# Generator expression
numbers = (x * 2 for x in range(5))
The list comprehension creates a list immediately, while the generator expression creates a generator that produces values lazily.

numbers = (x * 2 for x in range(5))

for number in numbers:
    print(number)
Generator vs List

FeatureListGenerator
Stores resultsYesProduces values as needed
Memory usageCan be high for large dataUsually lower for sequential processing
ReusableYesNormally one-time consumption
Access by indexYesNo direct indexing
Lazy evaluationNoYes
When to Use Generators

• Processing large files.
  • Generating large sequences.
  • Reading records incrementally.
  • Building memory-efficient processing pipelines.
  • Streaming values through multiple processing stages.
  • Working with data where you do not need all results at the same time.
When a List Is Better
Generators are not always better. Use a list when you need random access, repeated iteration, or when the dataset is small enough that storing the complete result is practical.

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]

print(numbers[2])

# Direct indexing works with a list.
A generator does not support normal list-style indexing such as generator[2].
Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Thinking yield behaves exactly like return. yield pauses the generator so execution can resume later.
Mistake 2: Expecting a generator to be reusable like a list. Once consumed, you normally need to create a new generator.
Mistake 3: Converting a huge generator to a list without considering memory usage. list(generator) materializes all remaining values.
Mistake 4: Using a generator when you need random access or repeated traversal. A list may be more appropriate in those cases.
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
GeneratorAn iterator that produces values lazily.
yieldProduces a value and pauses execution.
next()Resumes the generator and retrieves its next value.
Generator expressionA compact generator syntax using parentheses.
Memory benefitValues can be processed without storing the complete sequence.
Data Engineering useLarge files, incremental processing, and pipeline stages.
