qna.a: Inheritance allows a child class to reuse and extend attributes and methods from a parent class.

qna.q: Q2. What is a parent class?
qna.a: A parent class, also called a base class, is the class whose attributes and methods can be inherited by another class.

qna.q: Q3. What is a child class?
qna.a: A child class, also called a derived class, is a class that inherits from another class.

qna.q: Q4. How do you create a child class in Python?
qna.a: Put the parent class name inside parentheses after the child class name, such as class DataEngineer(Employee):.

qna.q: Q5. Can a child class add its own methods?
qna.a: Yes. A child class can reuse inherited methods and define additional methods specific to the child.

qna.q: Q6. What happens if a child class does not define its own __init__()?
qna.a: It can use the inherited initializer from the parent class, assuming the inherited initializer is applicable to the way the child is being constructed.

qna.q: Q7. What is super() used for?
qna.a: super() provides a convenient way for a child class to access behavior from its parent class, commonly to reuse the parent's __init__().

qna.q: Q8. What is method overriding?
qna.a: Method overriding occurs when a child class defines a method with the same name as an inherited method, providing its own implementation.

qna.q: Q9. What does isinstance() check?
qna.a: It checks whether an object is an instance of a specified class or a compatible parent class.

qna.q: Q10. What does issubclass() check?
qna.a: It checks whether one class is derived from another class.

qna.q: Q11. What is an is-a relationship?
qna.a: It describes a relationship where the child represents a specialized type of the parent, such as DataEngineer is an Employee.

qna.q: Q12. How can inheritance be useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It can help model related components that share common behavior, such as different data-source classes or specialized pipeline classes that reuse common configuration and functionality.

items.title: Why Logging Instead of Only print()
explanation: What is Logging?
Logging is the practice of recording information about what a program is doing while it runs. Python provides the built-in logging module for this purpose.
Definition: Logging provides a structured way to record application events, errors, warnings, and useful diagnostic information while a program is running.
Why Not Use Only print()?
print() is useful for learning Python, quick debugging, and simple scripts. However, production applications and Data Engineering pipelines usually need more control over diagnostic information.

print("Pipeline started")
print("Reading data")
print("Transforming data")
print("Pipeline completed")
This works for a small script, but as an application grows, it becomes difficult to distinguish normal information, warnings, errors, and debugging details.
Logging Provides Log Levels
Logging allows messages to be categorized by importance, such as DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL.

import logging

logging.debug("Debug information")
logging.info("Pipeline started")
logging.warning("Input file is large")
logging.error("Database connection failed")
logging.critical("Pipeline cannot continue")
This classification makes logs easier to understand and control.
Logging Can Be Configured
Unlike simple print() statements, logging can be configured to control where messages go and which severity levels should be recorded.

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

logging.debug("Debug message")
logging.info("Pipeline started")
logging.warning("File is large")
With the level set to INFO, the debug message is normally not displayed, while INFO and higher-severity messages are eligible to be recorded.
Logging Can Include Useful Context
Log records can include information such as the timestamp, log level, logger name, and message.

import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s"
)

logging.info("Pipeline started")
A log record can therefore provide more operational context than a simple message printed to the console.
Logging Can Write to a File
Logging can be configured to write records to a file instead of displaying them only in the console.

import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    filename="pipeline.log",
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s"
)

logging.info("Pipeline started")
logging.info("Pipeline completed")
This allows log records to remain available after the program finishes, which is useful for troubleshooting and operational monitoring.
Logging Can Record Errors

import logging

try:
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    logging.error("Calculation failed")
Logging can record that an error occurred without relying on manually added print() statements throughout the program.
Logging with Exception Details
When handling an exception, logging.exception() can be useful because it records the error message together with traceback information.

import logging

try:
    result = 10 / 0
except Exception:
    logging.exception("Pipeline step failed")
This is especially useful when diagnosing failures because the traceback helps identify where the exception occurred.
print() vs Logging

print()Logging
Simple output.Structured application logging.
No built-in severity levels.Supports log levels such as DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL.
Usually writes directly to standard output.Can be configured for different handlers and destinations.
Limited formatting control.Supports configurable formats.
Useful for quick debugging and simple scripts.Better suited to applications and production workflows.
Not designed as an operational logging system.Designed for application and operational diagnostics.
Logging in a Data Engineering Pipeline

import logging

logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s"
)

logging.info("ETL pipeline started")
logging.info("Reading source data")
logging.info("Transforming records")
logging.info("Loading data into PostgreSQL")
logging.info("ETL pipeline completed")
This gives the pipeline a basic operational record of what happened during execution.
Example: Logging Record Counts

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

records = [101, 102, 103, 104]

logging.info("Records received: %d", len(records))
Logging supports formatted messages. Passing values separately from the message is the preferred logging style rather than constructing every message with an f-string.
Example: Logging Pipeline Errors

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

def load_data():
    try:
        # Database loading logic
        raise ConnectionError("Database unavailable")
    except ConnectionError:
        logging.exception("Failed to load data")

load_data()
This pattern is useful in Data Engineering because pipeline failures need enough information to investigate what went wrong.
Logging Helps During Production Troubleshooting

Data Pipeline
     |
     +-- Extract
     |     |
     |     +-- INFO: Source connected
     |     +-- INFO: 10,000 records read
     |
     +-- Transform
     |     |
     |     +-- INFO: Transformation started
     |     +-- WARNING: 25 invalid records
     |
     +-- Load
           |
           +-- ERROR: Database connection failed
A sequence of structured log messages can help an engineer understand which stage of a pipeline was reached before a failure occurred.
Logging Is Not a Replacement for Error Handling
Logging records what happened, while exception handling determines how the program responds to an exception.

import logging

try:
    process_data()
except Exception:
    logging.exception("Data processing failed")
    # Handle, retry, or propagate the error as appropriate
Logging and exception handling often work together: exception handling manages the failure, while logging provides diagnostic information about it.
When print() Is Still Useful
print() is not bad or forbidden. It is still appropriate for simple scripts, quick experiments, learning, and intentionally displaying output to a user.

name = input("Enter your name: ")
print(f"Hello, {name}")
For a simple interactive script like this, using the logging framework would usually add unnecessary complexity.
Practical Rule

Practical Rule: Use print() for user-facing output, simple scripts, and quick debugging. Use logging when you need structured, configurable, persistent, or operational information about program execution.
Common Mistakes

• Replacing every print() statement with logging without considering whether the message is actually a user-facing output.
  • Using only ERROR for every event instead of choosing an appropriate log level.
  • Logging sensitive information such as passwords, API keys, tokens, or confidential data.
  • Using logging.exception() outside an exception handler when traceback information is not appropriate.
  • Assuming logging automatically fixes or handles an error.

Data Engineering Connection: In real Data Engineering pipelines, logging helps track pipeline stages, source and target systems, record counts, validation results, warnings, failures, retries, and execution details. This becomes especially important when pipelines run automatically without a developer watching them.
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
print()Simple output mechanism useful for scripts, learning, and user-facing output.
LoggingStructured way to record application events and diagnostics.
Log levelIndicates the severity or importance of a log message.
ConfigurationControls logging level, format, and destinations.
File loggingStores log records for later investigation.
logging.exception()Logs an error with exception traceback information when used in an exception handler.
practice: Step 1: Replace simple pipeline print() messages with basic logging.

Step 3: Configure a useful log format containing the timestamp, level, and message.

logging.basicConfig(

    format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s"
)

logging.info("ETL pipeline started")
Step 4: Write pipeline logs to a file.

logging.basicConfig(
    filename="pipeline.log",
    level=logging.INFO,

try:
    value = 10 / 0

Step 6: Create a small Data Engineering-style pipeline that logs each stage and the number of processed records.

import logging

logging.info("Pipeline completed")

Practice Goal: Understand why print() is sufficient for simple output but logging is more suitable for structured diagnostics, production pipelines, errors, warnings, execution tracking, and troubleshooting.

qna.q: Q1. Why use logging instead of only print()?
qna.a: Logging provides structured and configurable diagnostic information, including severity levels, formatting, and different output destinations.

qna.q: Q2. Is print() bad practice?
qna.a: No. print() is useful for user-facing output, simple scripts, learning, and quick debugging. Logging is more appropriate when operational diagnostics are needed.

qna.q: Q3. What are the common Python logging levels?
qna.a: The commonly used levels are DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL.

qna.q: Q4. What does logging.basicConfig() do?
qna.a: It provides a simple way to configure the root logging system, such as the minimum level, message format, and optionally a log file.

qna.q: Q5. Can logging write messages to a file?
qna.a: Yes. For example, logging.basicConfig(filename="pipeline.log", ...) can configure file output.

qna.q: Q6. Why are log levels useful?
qna.a: They allow messages to be categorized by importance and make it possible to control which messages are recorded or displayed.

qna.q: Q7. What is logging.exception() used for?
qna.a: It is commonly used inside an exception handler to log an error message together with traceback information.

qna.q: Q8. Does logging handle an exception automatically?
qna.a: No. Logging records information about the event. Exception handling determines how the program responds to the exception.

qna.q: Q9. Why is logging important in Data Engineering?
qna.a: Automated pipelines need execution information that can be reviewed later. Logging can record stages, record counts, warnings, failures, and other diagnostic details.

qna.q: Q10. Should sensitive information be written to logs?
qna.a: No. Passwords, API keys, access tokens, and other sensitive information should not be unnecessarily written to logs.

items.title: Log Levels
explanation: What Are Log Levels?
Log levels tell you how important or severe a log message is. Python's logging module provides standard levels that help you control which messages are recorded or displayed.

DEBUG → INFO → WARNING → ERROR → CRITICAL
Low severity ←────────────────────→ High severity
Why Log Levels Are Important

In a real Data Engineering pipeline, thousands of events can happen during execution. You don't always need every message. Log levels allow you to separate normal information from warnings and failures.

import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) logging.debug("Reading configuration") logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.warning("Input file is larger than expected") logging.error("Database connection failed") logging.critical("Pipeline cannot continue")
With level=logging.INFO, the logger normally records INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL messages, while DEBUG messages are filtered out.
1. DEBUG
DEBUG is used for detailed information that is mainly useful when troubleshooting a program.
logging.debug("Starting database connection") logging.debug("SQL query prepared") logging.debug("Rows fetched: 5000")
DEBUG messages can be very useful during development, but production systems often use a higher logging level so the logs do not become unnecessarily large.
2. INFO
INFO is used for normal application or pipeline progress.
logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.info("Reading input file") logging.info("5000 records loaded") logging.info("Pipeline completed successfully")
For a Data Engineering pipeline, INFO logs can tell you what stage is currently running and whether important operations completed.
3. WARNING
WARNING indicates something unexpected or potentially problematic happened, but the program can usually continue.
logging.warning("Input file contains 25 invalid rows") logging.warning("API response time is higher than expected") logging.warning("Duplicate records detected")
A warning is not necessarily a failure. It tells you that something deserves attention.
4. ERROR
ERROR indicates that an operation failed, but the entire application or pipeline may still be able to continue.
try: connection = connect_to_database() except ConnectionError: logging.error("Unable to connect to database")
For example, one optional data source may fail while the remaining pipeline stages continue processing.
5. CRITICAL
CRITICAL represents a very serious problem that may prevent the application or pipeline from continuing correctly.
logging.critical("Source database is completely unavailable") logging.critical("Pipeline cannot continue")
CRITICAL should be reserved for severe failures rather than ordinary errors.
Log Level Comparison

LevelPurposeTypical Data Engineering Example
DEBUGDetailed troubleshooting informationSQL parameters, internal processing details
INFONormal execution informationPipeline started, 10,000 rows loaded
WARNINGPotential problem, execution can continue100 invalid records found
ERRORAn operation failedFailed to load a table
CRITICALSevere failure affecting continuationPipeline cannot start because the main database is unavailable
How the Logging Level Filters Messages
The configured logging level acts as a minimum level. Messages below that level are normally ignored.

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING) logging.debug("Debug message") logging.info("Info message") logging.warning("Warning message") logging.error("Error message") logging.critical("Critical message")
Here, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL are recorded, while DEBUG and INFO are filtered out.
Common Logging Level Values
DEBUG = 10 INFO = 20 WARNING = 30 ERROR = 40 CRITICAL = 50
These numeric values determine the severity ordering. You normally use the level names rather than writing the numbers directly.
Changing the Minimum Log Level
import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) logging.debug("Detailed debugging information") logging.info("Pipeline started")
Using DEBUG as the minimum level allows DEBUG and all higher-severity messages to be processed.
Data Engineering Example

import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) logging.info("ETL pipeline started") logging.info("Reading customers.csv") logging.warning("50 records contain missing email values") try: logging.info("Loading data into PostgreSQL") # database operation except Exception: logging.exception("Database load failed") logging.info("ETL pipeline finished")
This gives you a useful execution history: normal progress is recorded with INFO, data-quality concerns with WARNING, and failures with ERROR or exception logging.
Important Rule: Log Level Does Not Handle the Error
A log level only describes the severity of a message. It does not automatically fix the problem or replace exception handling.
try: process_data() except Exception: logging.exception("Data processing failed")
Here, try/except handles the exception and logging.exception() records the failure and traceback.
Common Mistakes

• Using DEBUG for every normal message.
  • Using ERROR for situations that are only warnings.
  • Using CRITICAL for ordinary failures.
  • Logging passwords, API keys, tokens, or other secrets.
  • Assuming a log message automatically handles an exception.

Quick Summary:
DEBUG = detailed troubleshooting
INFO = normal progress
WARNING = something unexpected but execution can continue
ERROR = an operation failed
CRITICAL = severe failure that may stop the system
Data Engineering Practical Rule

Think of the levels like this:
DEBUG → "What exactly is happening inside?"
INFO → "What is the pipeline doing?"
WARNING → "Something looks wrong, but we can continue."
ERROR → "This operation failed."
CRITICAL → "The pipeline cannot continue normally."
practice: Step 1: Create a Python file named log_levels.py.

import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) logging.debug("Debug message") logging.info("Info message") logging.warning("Warning message") logging.error("Error message") logging.critical("Critical message")
Step 2: Change the logging level from DEBUG to INFO. Run the program and observe which messages disappear.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
Step 3: Change the level to WARNING and observe the difference.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING)
Step 4: Create a small ETL-style program and use different levels for different events.

import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) logging.info("Reading input data") logging.info("1000 records loaded") logging.warning("20 invalid records found") logging.error("Failed to load invalid records") logging.critical("Destination database unavailable")
Step 5: Practice deciding the correct level for each message: normal pipeline progress, invalid records, failed database operation, detailed debugging information, and complete pipeline failure.
Practice Goal: Be able to choose the correct log level based on the severity and purpose of an event instead of using print() for everything.

qna.q: Q1. What is a log level?
qna.a: A log level indicates the severity or importance of a log message and helps control which messages are recorded.

qna.q: Q2. What are the five standard Python log levels?
qna.a: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL.

qna.q: Q3. Which level is used for detailed troubleshooting?
qna.a: DEBUG.

qna.q: Q4. Which level is normally used for pipeline progress messages?
qna.a: INFO.

qna.q: Q5. What is the difference between WARNING and ERROR?
qna.a: WARNING indicates a potential or unexpected problem where execution can usually continue. ERROR indicates that an operation failed.

qna.q: Q6. When should CRITICAL be used?
qna.a: For severe failures that can prevent the application or pipeline from continuing normally.

qna.q: Q7. If the logging level is INFO, will DEBUG messages normally appear?
qna.a: No. DEBUG is below INFO, so DEBUG messages are normally filtered out.

qna.q: Q8. Does logging.exception() replace try/except?
qna.a: No. It is normally used inside an exception handler to record the exception and traceback.

qna.q: Q9. Why are log levels useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: They help separate normal pipeline progress, warnings, failures, and detailed troubleshooting information, making pipeline monitoring and debugging easier.

qna.q: Q10. Should passwords and API keys be written to logs?
qna.a: No. Sensitive credentials and secrets should not be exposed in log messages.

items.title: Basic `logging` Module
explanation: What is the Python logging Module?

The logging module is Python's built-in module for creating log messages while a program is running. It allows you to record information about what your application is doing, including normal execution, warnings, errors, and failures.
Unlike print(), logging provides standard log levels, configurable output, timestamps, formatting, and the ability to send logs to different destinations such as the console or a file.
import logging logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.warning("Input file contains invalid records") logging.error("Database connection failed")
Why Use the logging Module?
A small Python script may work with print(), but Data Engineering applications and pipelines need a more structured way to record execution details.

print()logging
Simple console outputStructured application logging
No standard severity levelsDEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL
Limited configurationConfigurable level and format
Mainly for user output or quick debuggingUseful for application and pipeline monitoring
Not designed for log destinationsCan write to console, files, and other handlers
Importing the Module
logging is part of Python's standard library, so you normally do not need to install it with pip.
import logging
After importing it, you can use the module's logging functions and configuration methods.
Basic Logging Functions
The simplest way to create logs is to use the functions provided by the logging module.

import logging logging.debug("Debug message") logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.warning("Input data has missing values") logging.error("Unable to load data") logging.critical("Pipeline cannot continue")
Each function corresponds to a different log level.
Using logging.basicConfig()
basicConfig() provides a simple way to configure the root logger for basic programs and scripts.
import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.warning("Missing values detected") logging.error("Database operation failed")
Here, INFO is the minimum level, so INFO and higher-severity messages are normally processed.
Setting the Log Format
You can use format to control what information appears in each log message.
import logging logging.basicConfig( level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" ) logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.warning("Missing values detected")
A typical output may look like:
2026-10-02 10:30:15,123 - INFO - Pipeline started 2026-10-02 10:30:16,456 - WARNING - Missing values detected
Common format fields include %(asctime)s for time, %(levelname)s for the log level, and %(message)s for the actual message.
Logging a Variable
You will often need to include runtime values such as record counts, file names, or table names in logs.
import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) records = 5000 logging.info("Records loaded: %s", records)
The logging module supports arguments after the message template. This is preferable to unnecessarily building the final string before the logging call.
Logging Inside a Function
Logging becomes more useful when each important operation in a pipeline records its progress.

import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) def extract_data(): logging.info("Starting data extraction") records = 1000 logging.info("Extracted %s records", records) return records extract_data()
Logging Exceptions
When an exception occurs, you can log the error inside an except block.
import logging logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) try: number = 10 / 0 except ZeroDivisionError: logging.error("Division by zero occurred")
When you need the exception traceback as well, logging.exception() is useful inside an exception handler.
try: number = 10 / 0 except ZeroDivisionError: logging.exception("Calculation failed")
Important: Logging records information about an error. It does not automatically handle or fix the exception. Exception handling still requires try, except, or another appropriate mechanism.
Logging in a Data Engineering Pipeline

import logging logging.basicConfig( level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" ) def run_pipeline(): logging.info("Pipeline started") try: logging.info("Extracting data") records = 10000 logging.info("Extracted %s records", records) logging.info("Transforming data") logging.warning("25 records contain invalid values") logging.info("Loading data into PostgreSQL") logging.info("Pipeline completed successfully") except Exception: logging.exception("Pipeline failed") run_pipeline()
This gives a basic execution trail showing when the pipeline started, what stages were executed, data-quality warnings, and whether an unexpected failure occurred.
Basic Logging Configuration Options

OptionPurpose
levelSets the minimum log level
formatControls the structure of log messages
filenameWrites logs to a file
filemodeControls how the log file is opened, such as append or overwrite
Writing Logs to a File
For a basic script, you can configure logging to write messages to a file instead of only displaying them on the console.

import logging logging.basicConfig( filename="pipeline.log", level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" ) logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.info("Pipeline completed")
The log messages are written to pipeline.log. This is useful when you need to inspect what happened after a pipeline has finished.
Console vs File Logging
Python Pipeline │ ▼ logging module │ ├── Console │ └── Log File

The logging system can be configured to send messages to different destinations. The simple basicConfig() approach is enough for learning the fundamentals; more advanced applications commonly use loggers and handlers explicitly.
Common Mistakes

• Forgetting to import logging.
  • Using print() for every operational message in a pipeline.
  • Using CRITICAL for ordinary errors.
  • Logging passwords, API keys, database credentials, or other secrets.
  • Assuming logging replaces exception handling.
  • Creating excessive DEBUG logs in production without considering log volume.
Quick Summary

Remember:
import logging → imports the module
logging.info() → records normal information
logging.warning() → records warnings
logging.error() → records errors
logging.exception() → records an exception with traceback inside an exception handler
logging.basicConfig() → provides simple logging configuration
Data Engineering Connection

In Data Engineering, logging is essential for understanding what happened during a pipeline run. A pipeline may extract millions of records, transform them, validate them, and load them into a database. Logs provide a history of these operations so failures and unexpected conditions can be investigated.

Practical Rule: Use INFO for important pipeline progress, WARNING for unexpected but recoverable conditions, ERROR for failed operations, and logging.exception() when you need the traceback of an exception.
practice: Step 1: Create a file named logging_basic.py and import the logging module.
import logging
Step 2: Configure the minimum log level as INFO and create messages at different levels.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) logging.debug("Debug message") logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.warning("Warning message") logging.error("Error message")
Step 3: Add a useful log format containing the timestamp, level, and message.
logging.basicConfig( level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" )
Step 4: Create a small function that logs the number of records processed.
def process_data(): records = 5000 logging.info("Records processed: %s", records) process_data()
Step 5: Practice logging an exception using logging.exception().
try: result = 100 / 0 except ZeroDivisionError: logging.exception("Calculation failed")
Step 6: Build a small ETL simulation with three stages: extract, transform, and load. Add INFO logs for each stage and a WARNING for invalid records.
logging.info("Extracting data") logging.info("Transforming data") logging.warning("10 invalid records found") logging.info("Loading data") logging.info("Pipeline completed")
Practice Goal: Be able to import the logging module, configure basic logging, record messages at different levels, include runtime values, and log exceptions in a small Data Engineering-style script.

qna.q: Q1. What is the Python logging module?
qna.a: It is a built-in Python module used to record application events, progress, warnings, errors, and other diagnostic information.

qna.q: Q2. Do you need to install logging using pip?
qna.a: No. logging is part of Python's standard library.

qna.q: Q3. How do you import the logging module?
qna.a: Use import logging.

qna.q: Q4. What does logging.basicConfig() do?
qna.a: It provides simple configuration for the root logger, such as the minimum log level, message format, and basic file output.

qna.q: Q5. How do you set INFO as the minimum log level?
qna.a: Use logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO).

qna.q: Q6. How can you include a variable in a log message?
qna.a: Pass the value as an additional argument, for example logging.info("Rows loaded: %s", rows).

qna.q: Q7. What is logging.exception() used for?
qna.a: It is commonly used inside an exception handler to log an error message together with the current exception traceback.

qna.q: Q8. Does logging.exception() handle an exception automatically?
qna.a: No. It records the exception information. The exception still needs to be handled appropriately by the program.

qna.q: Q9. How can logging be written to a file?
qna.a: For basic configuration, use the filename argument in logging.basicConfig(), such as filename="pipeline.log".

qna.q: Q10. Why is logging useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It provides an execution history of data pipelines, helping engineers understand pipeline progress, warnings, failures, and processing results.

items.title: Logging to Files
explanation: What Is Logging to a File?

Logging to a file means saving log messages into a file instead of displaying them only in the console. This is useful when you need to review what happened during a program or Data Engineering pipeline run after the program has finished.
import logging logging.basicConfig( filename="pipeline.log", level=logging.INFO ) logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.info("Pipeline completed")
After running the program, a file named pipeline.log can contain the generated log messages.
Why Save Logs to a File?
Console messages disappear when the terminal is closed, while a log file provides a persistent record that can be inspected later.

Console LoggingFile Logging
Useful while running the programUseful for reviewing execution later
Output is visible in terminalOutput is stored on disk
Can disappear after terminal closesCan be retained for troubleshooting
Useful for quick developmentUseful for pipeline execution history
Basic File Logging
The filename argument tells the logging system where to write the log messages.

import logging logging.basicConfig( filename="pipeline.log", level=logging.INFO ) logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.warning("Missing values detected") logging.error("Database operation failed")
The log file is created when the logging system needs to write to it, provided the process has permission to create or write to the specified location.
Adding a Log Format
A useful log file should contain more than just the message. You can include the timestamp, log level, and message.

import logging logging.basicConfig( filename="pipeline.log", level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" ) logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.info("Reading input data") logging.warning("10 invalid records found")
A log file may then contain entries similar to:
2026-10-02 10:30:15,123 - INFO - Pipeline started 2026-10-02 10:30:16,245 - INFO - Reading input data 2026-10-02 10:30:17,512 - WARNING - 10 invalid records found
Using a Relative File Path
If you provide only a filename such as pipeline.log, Python normally creates the file relative to the program's current working directory.
logging.basicConfig( filename="pipeline.log", level=logging.INFO )
Current Working Directory │ ▼ pipeline.log
The exact location therefore depends on where the Python process is running from.
Using a Specific Directory
You can provide a path when you want logs to be stored in a particular directory.
logging.basicConfig( filename="logs/pipeline.log", level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" )

The directory must exist and the process must have permission to write there. For reliable applications, create required directories explicitly or manage the logging path as part of the application configuration.
Append vs Overwrite
By default, file logging uses append-style behavior, so new log messages are added to the existing log file rather than replacing previous content.
The filemode argument can be used to control how the file is opened.
logging.basicConfig( filename="pipeline.log", filemode="a", level=logging.INFO )
a means append. This keeps existing log entries and adds new ones.
logging.basicConfig( filename="pipeline.log", filemode="w", level=logging.INFO )
w means write mode. Existing contents can be overwritten when the logging system opens the file for the new run.
Logging an Exception to a File
File logging becomes particularly useful when a pipeline fails because the error information remains available after the program stops.

import logging logging.basicConfig( filename="pipeline.log", level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" ) try: result = 100 / 0 except ZeroDivisionError: logging.exception("Data calculation failed")
logging.exception() records the error message and traceback when used inside an exception handler.
Data Engineering Example

import logging logging.basicConfig( filename="etl_pipeline.log", level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" ) def run_pipeline(): logging.info("ETL pipeline started") try: logging.info("Extracting data") records = 10000 logging.info("Extracted %s records", records) logging.info("Transforming data") logging.warning("25 invalid records detected") logging.info("Loading data into PostgreSQL") logging.info("ETL pipeline completed successfully") except Exception: logging.exception("ETL pipeline failed") run_pipeline()
Instead of relying on terminal output, the pipeline now leaves an execution record in etl_pipeline.log.
Using pathlib for the Log Path
Since you already learned pathlib, you can use a Path object to build a platform-friendly log path.

from pathlib import Path import logging log_file = Path("logs") / "pipeline.log" logging.basicConfig( filename=log_file, level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" ) logging.info("Pipeline started")
For a real application, make sure the logs directory exists before configuring the file handler or create it using Path.mkdir().
File Logging Does Not Automatically Manage Log Size
A log file can continue growing as more pipeline runs occur. In long-running or frequently executed systems, uncontrolled log growth can become a problem.

Important: For production applications, Python's logging package provides handlers such as rotating file handlers that can manage log files by size or time. You will learn those concepts later when working with production-style pipeline monitoring.
Common Mistakes

• Using a directory that does not exist without creating it first.
  • Not checking whether the process has permission to write to the log location.
  • Using filemode="w" without realizing that previous log contents can be overwritten.
  • Logging passwords, API keys, tokens, or database credentials.
  • Allowing log files to grow indefinitely in long-running systems.
  • Using vague messages such as "Error occurred" instead of describing the operation that failed.
Quick Summary

Remember:
filename → specifies the log file
level → specifies the minimum log level
format → controls the structure of each log entry
filemode="a" → append to existing file
filemode="w" → write mode and can overwrite existing contents
logging.exception() → records exception information and traceback inside an exception handler
Data Engineering Connection

File logging is especially useful for batch jobs and ETL pipelines. If a scheduled pipeline runs at 2 AM and fails when nobody is watching the terminal, the log file can provide information about which stage was running, how many records were processed, and what error occurred.
Scheduled ETL Job │ ▼ Extract → Transform → Load │ │ │ └─────────┴──────────┴──→ etl_pipeline.log │ ▼ Troubleshooting
practice: Step 1: Create a file named file_logging.py and configure logging to write to pipeline.log.

import logging logging.basicConfig( filename="pipeline.log", level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s" ) logging.info("Pipeline started") logging.info("Pipeline completed")
Step 2: Run the program and open pipeline.log. Verify that the log messages were saved in the file.
Step 3: Add different log levels and observe how they appear in the file.
logging.debug("Debug information") logging.info("Data extraction started") logging.warning("Invalid records found") logging.error("Database load failed")
Step 4: Practice logging an exception and check the resulting log file.
try: value = 10 / 0 except ZeroDivisionError: logging.exception("Calculation failed")
Step 5: Create a small ETL simulation and save its execution history to etl_pipeline.log.

logging.info("Extract started") logging.info("10000 records extracted") logging.info("Transform started") logging.warning("25 invalid records found") logging.info("Load started") logging.info("Pipeline completed")
Step 6: Change filemode from "a" to "w", run the program multiple times, and observe the difference.
logging.basicConfig( filename="pipeline.log", filemode="w", level=logging.INFO )
Practice Goal: Be able to configure Python logging to save pipeline execution information to a file, use useful formats and log levels, and record exceptions for later troubleshooting.

qna.q: Q1. How do you configure logging to write to a file?
qna.a: Use the filename argument in logging.basicConfig(), for example logging.basicConfig(filename="pipeline.log", level=logging.INFO).

qna.q: Q2. What does the filename argument specify?
qna.a: It specifies the file where log messages should be written.

qna.q: Q3. What happens when you use a relative filename such as pipeline.log?
qna.a: The file is normally created relative to the process's current working directory.

qna.q: Q4. What does filemode="a" mean?
qna.a: It opens the log file in append mode, allowing new log entries to be added while preserving existing contents.

qna.q: Q5. What does filemode="w" mean?
qna.a: It uses write mode, so existing file contents can be overwritten when the file is opened for a new logging run.

qna.q: Q6. Why should you include timestamps in log files?
qna.a: Timestamps help you determine when individual pipeline operations, warnings, and failures occurred.

qna.q: Q7. Why is file logging useful for Data Engineering?
qna.a: It preserves a record of batch or ETL pipeline execution that can be reviewed later for troubleshooting and operational monitoring.

qna.q: Q8. Can logging.exception() be used outside an exception handler?
qna.a: It is intended to be used when handling an exception so that the current exception traceback can be recorded.

qna.q: Q9. What can happen if a pipeline keeps writing to the same log file indefinitely?
qna.a: The log file can become very large. Production systems commonly use log rotation or other retention strategies to control log size.

qna.q: Q10. Should sensitive credentials be written to log files?
qna.a: No. Passwords, API keys, access tokens, and other sensitive credentials should not be exposed in logs.

items.title: `datetime`
explanation: What is datetime?
datetime is a class from Python's built-in datetime module used to represent both a date and a time.
It is useful when your program needs to work with timestamps such as when a record was created, when a pipeline started, or when a file was processed.
from datetime import datetime now = datetime.now() print(now)
Simple idea: A datetime represents a specific point in time, such as 2026-10-02 10:30:15.
Importing datetime
The datetime class comes from Python's built-in datetime module.
from datetime import datetime
You can also import the entire module.
import datetime now = datetime.datetime.now() print(now)
For everyday Python code, from datetime import datetime is often easier to read.
Getting the Current Date and Time
datetime.now() returns the current local date and time according to the system's clock.
from datetime import datetime now = datetime.now() print(now)
A result may look similar to:
The value contains the year, month, day, hour, minute, second, and microseconds.
Getting Individual Components
You can access individual parts of a datetime object using attributes.
from datetime import datetime now = datetime.now() print(now.year) print(now.month) print(now.day) print(now.hour) print(now.minute) print(now.second) print(now.microsecond)

AttributeMeaning
yearYear
monthMonth
dayDay of the month
hourHour
minuteMinute
secondSecond
microsecondMicrosecond
Creating a Specific Date and Time
You can create a datetime object by providing the year, month, day, and optional time values.
from datetime import datetime created_at = datetime(2026, 10, 2, 10, 30, 0) print(created_at)
The basic order is:
datetime(year, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond)
Current Date vs Current Date and Time
datetime.now() gives both date and time. If you only need the date, use date.today().
from datetime import datetime, date current_datetime = datetime.now() current_date = date.today() print(current_datetime) print(current_date)
Remember: date represents a calendar date, while datetime represents a date together with a time.
Formatting a datetime with strftime()
strftime() converts a datetime object into a formatted string.
from datetime import datetime now = datetime.now() formatted = now.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") print(formatted)
A result may look like:
2026-10-02 10:30:15

CodeMeaning
%Y4-digit year
%m2-digit month
%d2-digit day
%HHour in 24-hour format
%MMinute
%SSecond
Parsing a String with strptime()
strptime() performs the opposite operation: it converts a string into a datetime object using a specified format.
from datetime import datetime text = "2026-10-02 10:30:15" dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") print(dt) print(dt.year)
String "2026-10-02 10:30:15" │ │ strptime() ▼ datetime object
The format passed to strptime() must match the input string's structure.
Comparing datetime Values
Two datetime objects can be compared using normal comparison operators when they are comparable.
from datetime import datetime start = datetime(2026, 10, 1, 10, 0) end = datetime(2026, 10, 2, 10, 0) print(start < end) print(start == end)
This is useful for checking whether a record is newer or older than a particular timestamp.
Subtracting datetime Values
Subtracting two compatible datetime objects produces a timedelta.
from datetime import datetime start = datetime(2026, 10, 1, 10, 0) end = datetime(2026, 10, 1, 15, 30) difference = end - start print(difference)
This is useful for measuring how long a process took. The details of timedelta are covered separately.
Adding a Duration to datetime
You can add a timedelta to a datetime to calculate a future timestamp.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta start = datetime.now() future = start + timedelta(hours=2) print("Start:", start) print("Future:", future)
This is useful for deadlines, retry times, expiration times, and processing windows.
Data Engineering Example — Pipeline Timestamp
Data pipelines often record when processing starts and finishes.

from datetime import datetime pipeline_start = datetime.now() print("Pipeline started at:", pipeline_start) # Data extraction and transformation happen here pipeline_end = datetime.now() print("Pipeline ended at:", pipeline_end)
Pipeline Start │ ▼ Extract │ ▼ Transform │ ▼ Load │ ▼ Pipeline End Start and End timestamps can be used to measure execution time.
Data Engineering Example — Filtering Recent Data
A pipeline may need to process records created after a specific timestamp.
from datetime import datetime last_run = datetime(2026, 10, 1, 18, 0) current_run = datetime.now() print("Process records between:") print(last_run) print(current_run)
These timestamps can later be used as boundaries in database queries for incremental data processing.
Important: Naive vs Time-Zone-Aware datetime
A naive datetime does not contain time-zone information. A time-zone-aware datetime contains time-zone information.
from datetime import datetime, timezone naive = datetime.now() aware = datetime.now(timezone.utc) print(naive) print(aware)

Data Engineering Tip: When data comes from systems in different regions or when timestamps cross time zones, time-zone-aware timestamps are important. Avoid mixing naive and aware datetimes in the same calculation.
Common Mistakes

• Confusing datetime.now() with date.today().
  • Using the wrong format string with strptime().
  • Assuming a formatted string is still a datetime object.
  • Mixing naive and time-zone-aware datetime objects.
  • Ignoring time zones when data comes from systems operating in different regions.
  • Doing manual string manipulation instead of using datetime parsing and formatting functions.
Quick Summary

Remember:
datetime.now() → current local date and time
datetime(...) → create a specific datetime
strftime() → datetime → formatted string
strptime() → string → datetime
datetime2 - datetime1 → timedelta
datetime + timedelta → future datetime
Data Engineering Connection
datetime is frequently used for pipeline timestamps, database records, incremental loads, execution tracking, data freshness checks, API timestamps, and partition-based processing.
Practical Rule: Use datetime when you need to represent an exact date and time. Use timedelta when you need to represent the amount of time between two points or move a timestamp forward or backward.
practice: Step 1: Import datetime and print the current date and time.
from datetime import datetime now = datetime.now() print(now)
Step 2: Print the year, month, day, hour, minute, and second separately.
print("Year:", now.year) print("Month:", now.month) print("Day:", now.day) print("Hour:", now.hour) print("Minute:", now.minute) print("Second:", now.second)
Step 3: Create a specific datetime for October 1, 2026 at 9:30 AM.
dt = datetime(2026, 10, 1, 9, 30, 0) print(dt)
Step 4: Convert the datetime into the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.
formatted = dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") print(formatted)
Step 5: Convert the string "2026-10-02 14:30:00" back into a datetime object using strptime().
text = "2026-10-02 14:30:00" parsed = datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") print(parsed)
Step 6: Create pipeline start and end timestamps and calculate how long the pipeline ran.
from datetime import datetime start = datetime.now() # Simulate pipeline work end = datetime.now() duration = end - start print("Start:", start) print("End:", end) print("Duration:", duration)
Practice Goal: Be able to create and inspect datetime values, format and parse timestamps, compare datetime values, and use them for basic Data Engineering pipeline tracking.

qna.q: Q1. What is datetime?
qna.a: datetime is a Python class used to represent a specific date and time.

qna.q: Q2. From which module is datetime imported?
qna.a: It is imported from Python's built-in datetime module.

qna.q: Q3. What does datetime.now() return?
qna.a: It returns the current local date and time according to the system clock.

qna.q: Q4. What is the difference between date and datetime?
qna.a: date represents a calendar date, while datetime represents a date together with a time.

qna.q: Q5. What does strftime() do?
qna.a: It converts a datetime object into a formatted string.

qna.q: Q6. What does strptime() do?
qna.a: It parses a string according to a specified format and converts it into a datetime object.

qna.q: Q7. What happens when you subtract two datetime objects?
qna.a: The result is a timedelta representing the difference between the two timestamps.

qna.q: Q8. How can datetime be useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It can be used for pipeline timestamps, incremental data processing, execution tracking, data freshness checks, and timestamp-based database queries.

qna.q: Q9. What is a naive datetime?
qna.a: A naive datetime does not contain time-zone information.

qna.q: Q10. Why are time-zone-aware datetimes important?
qna.a: They help represent timestamps correctly when data comes from systems operating in different time zones and help avoid ambiguity in time-based processing.

items.title: `timedelta`
explanation: What is timedelta?
timedelta is a class from Python's datetime module used to represent a duration or difference between dates and times.
You can use it to add or subtract days, hours, minutes, seconds, and other time units from a date or datetime object.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta now = datetime.now() future = now + timedelta(days=7) print(now) print(future)
Simple idea: datetime represents a point in time, while timedelta represents an amount of time.
Importing timedelta
timedelta is available in Python's built-in datetime module.
from datetime import timedelta
You can also import it together with datetime.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
Creating a timedelta
You can create a duration using supported time units such as days, seconds, microseconds, milliseconds, minutes, hours, and weeks.
from datetime import timedelta d1 = timedelta(days=5) d2 = timedelta(hours=10) d3 = timedelta(minutes=30) d4 = timedelta(seconds=45) d5 = timedelta(weeks=2)
For example, timedelta(days=5) represents a duration of five days.
Adding Days to a Date
A common use of timedelta is calculating a future date.
from datetime import date, timedelta today = date.today() next_week = today + timedelta(days=7) print("Today:", today) print("Next week:", next_week)
Today │ │ + timedelta(days=7) ▼ Future Date
Subtracting Days
You can subtract a timedelta from a date or datetime to calculate a previous date.
from datetime import date, timedelta today = date.today() previous_week = today - timedelta(days=7) print(previous_week)
Adding Hours and Minutes
timedelta is not limited to days. It can also represent smaller durations.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta now = datetime.now() one_hour_later = now + timedelta(hours=1) thirty_minutes_later = now + timedelta(minutes=30) print(one_hour_later) print(thirty_minutes_later)
Combining Multiple Time Units
You can specify multiple units when creating a timedelta.
from datetime import timedelta duration = timedelta( days=2, hours=5, minutes=30 ) print(duration)
The values are normalized internally into a standard duration representation.
Finding the Difference Between Two Dates
Subtracting two date or datetime objects produces a timedelta.
from datetime import date start = date(2026, 10, 1) end = date(2026, 10, 10) difference = end - start print(difference) print(difference.days)
Here, the result represents the duration between the two dates.
Using .days
The days attribute gives the number of whole days represented by a timedelta.
from datetime import date start = date(2026, 10, 1) end = date(2026, 10, 10) difference = end - start print(difference.days) # 9
Using .seconds
The seconds attribute represents the remaining seconds after the duration's whole days have been accounted for. It is not necessarily the total number of seconds in the duration.
from datetime import timedelta duration = timedelta(days=2, hours=3, minutes=20) print(duration.days) print(duration.seconds)
Important: If you need the total duration in seconds, use total_seconds() instead of relying only on .seconds.
Using total_seconds()
total_seconds() converts the complete duration into seconds, including its days component.
from datetime import timedelta duration = timedelta(days=1, hours=2) print(duration.total_seconds())
This is useful when measuring processing time or calculating elapsed time.
Comparing Durations
timedelta objects can be compared with each other.
from datetime import timedelta short = timedelta(hours=2) long = timedelta(hours=5) print(short < long) print(short == long)
Using timedelta with datetime
This is particularly useful when working with timestamps.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta created_at = datetime.now() expires_at = created_at + timedelta(hours=24) print("Created:", created_at) print("Expires:", expires_at)
This pattern can be used to calculate deadlines, expiration times, retry times, and processing windows.
Data Engineering Example — Processing Window
Suppose a pipeline needs to process records from the last 24 hours.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta now = datetime.now() start_time = now - timedelta(hours=24) print("Start time:", start_time) print("End time:", now)
24-hour processing window Start Time ───────────────────────► Current Time │ │ └──── timedelta(hours=24) ─────────┘
This type of time window is common in incremental data processing and scheduled pipelines.
Data Engineering Example — Incremental Processing
A pipeline may process only data created after the previous successful run.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta last_run = datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=6) current_run = datetime.now() print("Process records from:", last_run) print("Process records until:", current_run)
The pipeline can use these timestamps as boundaries for querying only the required data instead of processing the entire dataset every time.
Negative timedelta
A timedelta can also represent a negative duration.
from datetime import timedelta duration = timedelta(days=-3) print(duration)
Negative durations are useful when calculating dates or times before a reference point.
Common Mistakes

• Confusing a datetime with a timedelta.
  • Using .seconds when you actually need the total number of seconds.
  • Forgetting that subtracting two dates produces a timedelta.
  • Doing manual date arithmetic when timedelta can handle the duration safely.
  • Ignoring time-zone considerations when working with timestamps from different systems.
Quick Summary

Remember:
timedelta(days=7) → duration of 7 days
date + timedelta → future date
date - timedelta → previous date
date2 - date1 → duration between dates
difference.days → whole days component
difference.total_seconds() → complete duration in seconds
Data Engineering Connection
timedelta becomes useful when working with pipeline schedules, incremental loads, processing windows, retry delays, data freshness checks, and timestamp-based database queries.
Practical Rule: Whenever you need to say "before this time", "after this time", "last 24 hours", "next 7 days", or "difference between these timestamps", think about timedelta.
practice: Step 1: Import date and timedelta, then calculate the date seven days from today.
from datetime import date, timedelta today = date.today() future = today + timedelta(days=7) print("Today:", today) print("Future:", future)
Step 2: Calculate the date seven days before today.
previous = today - timedelta(days=7) print("Previous:", previous)
Step 3: Create two dates and calculate the number of days between them.
from datetime import date start = date(2026, 10, 1) end = date(2026, 10, 15) difference = end - start print("Days:", difference.days)
Step 4: Create a 24-hour processing window using datetime.now() and timedelta.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta end_time = datetime.now() start_time = end_time - timedelta(hours=24) print("Start:", start_time) print("End:", end_time)
Step 5: Calculate a future expiration time that is 30 minutes from now.
expires_at = datetime.now() + timedelta(minutes=30) print("Expires at:", expires_at)
Step 6: Create a duration containing days, hours, and minutes. Print its days, seconds, and total seconds.
duration = timedelta(days=2, hours=3, minutes=30) print("Days:", duration.days) print("Seconds:", duration.seconds) print("Total seconds:", duration.total_seconds())
Practice Goal: Be able to use timedelta to calculate future and past dates, find differences between dates, create processing windows, and measure durations in Data Engineering-style problems.

qna.q: Q1. What is timedelta?
qna.a: timedelta represents a duration or difference between dates and times.

qna.q: Q2. From which module is timedelta imported?
qna.a: It is imported from Python's built-in datetime module.

qna.q: Q3. How do you add seven days to a date?
qna.a: Use date + timedelta(days=7).

qna.q: Q4. What happens when you subtract two date objects?
qna.a: The result is a timedelta representing the difference between the two dates.

qna.q: Q5. What is the difference between datetime and timedelta?
qna.a: datetime represents a specific point in time, while timedelta represents a duration or amount of time.

qna.q: Q6. What does timedelta(hours=24) represent?
qna.a: It represents a duration of 24 hours, which is equivalent to one day.

qna.q: Q7. What does the days attribute of timedelta provide?
qna.a: It provides the whole-days component of the duration.

qna.q: Q8. Why should you use total_seconds() instead of only seconds when measuring a complete duration?
qna.a: Because seconds represents only the seconds component remaining after whole days, while total_seconds() includes the complete duration.

qna.q: Q9. How can timedelta be useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It can be used for incremental processing windows, last-24-hour queries, pipeline deadlines, retry delays, freshness checks, and timestamp calculations.

qna.q: Q10. Can timedelta represent a negative duration?
qna.a: Yes. Negative values such as timedelta(days=-3) can represent a duration before a reference point.

items.title: Date Formatting
explanation: What Is Date Formatting?
Date formatting means converting a Python date or datetime object into a string in the format you need.
For example, Python may represent a datetime as 2026-10-02 14:30:15, but you may want to display it as 02-10-2026 or 02 Oct 2026.
from datetime import datetime now = datetime.now() formatted = now.strftime("%d-%m-%Y") print(formatted)
Remember: strftime() means string format time. It converts a date or datetime object into a formatted string.
Why Is Date Formatting Important?
Date formatting is useful when displaying dates to users, creating reports, generating filenames, writing logs, preparing API responses, and exporting data.

RequirementExample Format
Database-style date2026-10-02
Indian-style display02-10-2026
Readable date02 Oct 2026
Date and time2026-10-02 14:30:15
Filename timestamp20261002_143015
Using strftime()
The basic syntax is:
datetime_object.strftime("format")
Example:
from datetime import datetime dt = datetime(2026, 10, 2, 14, 30, 15) print(dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")) print(dt.strftime("%d-%m-%Y"))
Output:
2026-10-02 02-10-2026
Important Date Format Codes

CodeMeaningExample
%Y4-digit year2026
%y2-digit year26
%mMonth as 01–1210
%dDay as 01–3102
%BFull month nameOctober
%bAbbreviated month nameOct
%AFull weekday nameFriday
%aAbbreviated weekday nameFri
Formatting Time
Date formatting can also include the time portion.

CodeMeaningExample
%HHour, 24-hour format14
%IHour, 12-hour format02
%MMinute30
%SSecond15
%pAM or PMPM
from datetime import datetime dt = datetime(2026, 10, 2, 14, 30, 15) print(dt.strftime("%H:%M:%S")) print(dt.strftime("%I:%M:%S %p"))
Output:
14:30:15 02:30:15 PM
Formatting a Complete Date and Time
You can combine multiple format codes with normal characters.
from datetime import datetime dt = datetime(2026, 10, 2, 14, 30, 15) formatted = dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") print(formatted)
2026-10-02 14:30:15
Readable Date Format
You can use month and weekday names to create human-readable dates.
from datetime import datetime dt = datetime(2026, 10, 2) print(dt.strftime("%d %B %Y")) print(dt.strftime("%A, %d %B %Y"))
Possible output:
02 October 2026 Friday, 02 October 2026
Creating a Filename with a Timestamp
Date formatting is commonly used to create unique and meaningful filenames.
from datetime import datetime timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S") filename = f"pipeline_{timestamp}.log" print(filename)
A filename may look like:
pipeline_20261002_143015.log
This pattern is useful when storing pipeline outputs, reports, exports, or execution logs.
Data Engineering Example — Daily Report
Suppose a pipeline generates a daily report. You can format the processing date for the report name.
from datetime import datetime run_date = datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d") report_name = f"sales_report_{run_date}.csv" print(report_name)
sales_report_2026-10-02.csv
Data Engineering Example — Pipeline Logs
A pipeline can format timestamps when creating readable operational messages.
from datetime import datetime start_time = datetime.now() print("Pipeline started:", start_time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"))
This is especially useful when displaying or exporting pipeline execution information.
Data Engineering Example — Partition Dates
Date values are often used when organizing data by date partitions.
from datetime import datetime dt = datetime(2026, 10, 2) partition_date = dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") print(partition_date)
Raw Timestamp │ ▼ 2026-10-02 14:30:15 │ │ strftime("%Y-%m-%d") ▼ 2026-10-02 │ ▼ Date Partition
Formatting a Date Object
strftime() also works with a date object.
from datetime import date today = date.today() formatted = today.strftime("%d-%m-%Y") print(formatted)
Formatting Does Not Change the Original datetime
strftime() returns a new string. It does not modify the original datetime object.
from datetime import datetime dt = datetime(2026, 10, 2, 14, 30) formatted = dt.strftime("%d-%m-%Y") print(type(dt)) print(type(formatted))
The first value remains a datetime object, while the formatted result is a str.
Formatting vs Parsing
datetime object │ │ strftime() ▼ formatted string formatted string │ │ strptime() ▼ datetime object

FunctionConversion
strftime()datetime/date → string
strptime()string → datetime
Easy way to remember: strftime() = format a time into a string. strptime() = parse a string into a time object.
Common Mistakes

• Using %m when you mean minutes; minutes use %M.
  • Using %H when you need 12-hour time with AM/PM; use %I %p.
  • Forgetting that strftime() returns a string.
  • Using the wrong year code: %Y is four-digit year and %y is two-digit year.
  • Confusing strftime() with strptime().
  • Using a display format as a substitute for proper timestamp handling in databases or APIs.
Quick Summary

Remember:
%Y → 4-digit year
%m → month
%d → day
%H → 24-hour hour
%I → 12-hour hour
%M → minute
%S → second
%p → AM/PM
strftime() → date/datetime to string
Data Engineering Connection
Date formatting is commonly used when generating reports, filenames, partition paths, pipeline logs, API output, and human-readable monitoring information.

Practical Rule: Keep date/time values as proper date or datetime objects while performing calculations. Format them into strings only when you need to display, export, name, or serialize them in a specific format.
practice: Step 1: Create a datetime object for October 2, 2026 at 2:30:15 PM.
from datetime import datetime dt = datetime(2026, 10, 2, 14, 30, 15) print(dt)
Step 2: Format the date as YYYY-MM-DD.
print(dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
Step 3: Format the date as DD-MM-YYYY.
print(dt.strftime("%d-%m-%Y"))
Step 4: Format the complete datetime as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.
print(dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"))
Step 5: Create a readable format containing the weekday and full month name.
print(dt.strftime("%A, %d %B %Y"))
Step 6: Create a timestamp-based filename for a Data Engineering pipeline output.
timestamp = dt.strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S") filename = f"sales_pipeline_{timestamp}.csv" print(filename)
Step 7: Create a date partition value in the format YYYY-MM-DD.
partition_date = dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d") print("Partition:", partition_date)
Practice Goal: Be able to use strftime() confidently to create standard, readable, filename-safe, and Data Engineering-friendly date and timestamp formats.

qna.q: Q1. What is date formatting?
qna.a: Date formatting is converting a date or datetime object into a string representation using a specified format.

qna.q: Q2. Which function is used for date formatting in Python?
qna.a: strftime() is used to convert a date or datetime object into a formatted string.

qna.q: Q3. What does %Y represent?
qna.a: It represents the year using four digits, such as 2026.

qna.q: Q4. What is the difference between %m and %M?
qna.a: %m represents the month, while %M represents the minute.

qna.q: Q5. What is the difference between %H and %I?
qna.a: %H represents the hour in 24-hour format, while %I represents the hour in 12-hour format.

qna.q: Q6. What does %p represent?
qna.a: It represents the AM or PM designation.

qna.q: Q7. What type does strftime() return?
qna.a: It returns a string (str).

qna.q: Q8. What is the difference between strftime() and strptime()?
qna.a: strftime() converts a date/datetime object to a string, while strptime() parses a string into a datetime object.

qna.q: Q9. How can date formatting be useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It can be used for pipeline logs, report names, output filenames, date partitions, API output, and human-readable timestamps.

qna.q: Q10. Should you format a datetime before performing date calculations?
qna.a: Generally no. Keep it as a date or datetime object for calculations and format it into a string when you need a specific display or output representation.

items.title: Date Parsing
explanation: What Is Date Parsing?
Date parsing means converting a string containing a date or timestamp into a Python datetime or date object.

This is important because data commonly arrives from CSV files, APIs, databases, and external systems as text. Once parsed into a datetime object, Python can compare dates, calculate differences, and perform date/time operations.
from datetime import datetime text = "2026-10-02 14:30:15" dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") print(dt) print(type(dt))
Simple idea: Parsing converts string → date/datetime object. Formatting does the opposite: date/datetime object → string.
Why Is Date Parsing Important?
Real-world data rarely arrives in exactly the Python object type you want. A CSV column may contain dates as strings, and an API may return timestamps as text.
External Data │ ▼ "2026-10-02 14:30:15" │ │ strptime() ▼ datetime object │ ├── Compare ├── Calculate duration ├── Filter records └── Build processing windows
Using strptime()
The main method introduced at this level for parsing a known date format is datetime.strptime().
from datetime import datetime text = "2026-10-02" dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d") print(dt)
The first argument is the input string and the second argument describes the format of that string.
datetime.strptime(date_string, format)
Matching the Format
The format string must match the structure of the input string.
from datetime import datetime text = "02-10-2026" dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%d-%m-%Y") print(dt)
Here:
02 → %d 10 → %m 2026 → %Y
If the format does not match the input string, Python raises a ValueError.
Parsing a Date and Time
You can parse both the date and time when the input contains them.
from datetime import datetime text = "2026-10-02 14:30:15" dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") print(dt)
Parsing Different Date Formats
Different data sources may use different date representations. The format string should match the source format.

from datetime import datetime value1 = "2026-10-02" value2 = "02/10/2026" value3 = "02-Oct-2026" print(datetime.strptime(value1, "%Y-%m-%d")) print(datetime.strptime(value2, "%d/%m/%Y")) print(datetime.strptime(value3, "%d-%b-%Y"))
Parsing Month Names
%B is used for a full month name and %b is used for an abbreviated month name.
from datetime import datetime full_month = datetime.strptime("02 October 2026", "%d %B %Y") short_month = datetime.strptime("02 Oct 2026", "%d %b %Y") print(full_month) print(short_month)
Parsing 12-Hour Time
When the input uses AM or PM, use %I for the 12-hour clock and %p for AM/PM.
from datetime import datetime text = "02-10-2026 02:30 PM" dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%d-%m-%Y %I:%M %p") print(dt)
Do not confuse %I with %H. %I is for 12-hour time, while %H is for 24-hour time.
Handling Parsing Errors
If the input does not match the expected format, strptime() can raise ValueError.
from datetime import datetime text = "2026/10/02" try: dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d") print(dt) except ValueError: print("Invalid date format")
Handling the exception is useful when processing external or user-provided data because the input may not always follow the expected format.
Parsing Data from a List
You can parse multiple date strings using a loop or other Python techniques.
from datetime import datetime dates = [ "2026-10-01", "2026-10-02", "2026-10-03" ] parsed_dates = [] for value in dates: parsed_dates.append(datetime.strptime(value, "%Y-%m-%d")) print(parsed_dates)
Data Engineering Example — Parsing CSV Data
CSV files commonly contain dates as strings. After reading the file, you may need to convert the date column into datetime values before performing date-based operations.
from datetime import datetime created_at = "2026-10-02 14:30:15" parsed_created_at = datetime.strptime( created_at, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" ) print(parsed_created_at)
Once parsed, the value can be compared with other timestamps or used to calculate processing windows.
Data Engineering Example — API Timestamp
An API may return a timestamp as text. Before performing datetime operations, parse it into a Python datetime object when appropriate.
from datetime import datetime api_timestamp = "2026-10-02 09:45:20" created_at = datetime.strptime( api_timestamp, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" ) print("Created at:", created_at)
Parsing and Comparing Dates
After parsing, you can compare the resulting datetime objects instead of comparing the original strings.
from datetime import datetime first = datetime.strptime("2026-10-01", "%Y-%m-%d") second = datetime.strptime("2026-10-05", "%Y-%m-%d") if second > first: print("Second date is later")
Parsing and Calculating a Difference
Once strings have been converted to datetime objects, subtracting them produces a timedelta.
from datetime import datetime start = datetime.strptime("2026-10-01", "%Y-%m-%d") end = datetime.strptime("2026-10-10", "%Y-%m-%d") difference = end - start print("Days:", difference.days)
Parsing vs Formatting

OperationFunctionDirection
Parsingstrptime()String → datetime
Formattingstrftime()datetime → String
Parsing: "2026-10-02" ──strptime()──► datetime object Formatting: datetime object ──strftime()──► "2026-10-02"
Parsing Does Not Mean Validation of Every Business Rule

Successful parsing means that the string matches the supplied date format and represents a valid date/time value. It does not automatically verify business rules such as whether a date is allowed for a particular pipeline.
from datetime import datetime value = "2026-10-02" dt = datetime.strptime(value, "%Y-%m-%d") # Parsing succeeded. # Additional business validation may still be required.
Common Mistakes

• Using the wrong format code for the input string.
  • Confusing %m month with %M minute.
  • Using %H for a 12-hour AM/PM value.
  • Forgetting to handle ValueError when external data may contain invalid formats.
  • Comparing date strings in inconsistent formats instead of parsing them.
  • Assuming parsing automatically handles time-zone differences.
Quick Summary

Remember:
strptime() → converts a string into a datetime object
%Y-%m-%d → common date format
%H:%M:%S → 24-hour time
%I:%M %p → 12-hour time with AM/PM
ValueError → commonly raised when the input does not match the expected format
Data Engineering Connection

Date parsing is an important step when ingesting data from CSV files, APIs, logs, databases, and external systems. Converting timestamp strings into proper datetime objects allows pipelines to filter records, compare timestamps, calculate durations, and perform incremental processing.
Practical Rule: When a date or timestamp arrives as text and you need to perform date/time operations on it, parse it into the appropriate Python date or datetime representation first.
practice: Step 1: Parse the string "2026-10-02" into a datetime object.
from datetime import datetime text = "2026-10-02" dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d") print(dt) print(type(dt))
Step 2: Parse "02-10-2026" using the correct format.
text = "02-10-2026" dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%d-%m-%Y") print(dt)
Step 3: Parse a complete timestamp containing date and time.
text = "2026-10-02 14:30:15" dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") print(dt)
Step 4: Parse a 12-hour timestamp containing AM/PM.
text = "02-10-2026 02:30 PM" dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%d-%m-%Y %I:%M %p") print(dt)
Step 5: Add exception handling for an invalid date string.
text = "2026/10/02" try: dt = datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d") print(dt) except ValueError: print("Invalid date format")
Step 6: Parse two timestamps and calculate the number of hours between them.

start = datetime.strptime("2026-10-02 09:00:00", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") end = datetime.strptime("2026-10-02 17:00:00", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") difference = end - start print("Seconds:", difference.total_seconds()) print("Hours:", difference.total_seconds() / 3600)

Practice Goal: Be able to recognize date strings, choose the correct format codes, parse them into datetime objects, handle invalid input, and use the parsed values in Data Engineering-style calculations.

qna.q: Q1. What is date parsing?
qna.a: Date parsing is converting a date or timestamp stored as a string into a Python date or datetime object.

qna.q: Q2. Which function is commonly used to parse a datetime string?
qna.a: datetime.strptime().

qna.q: Q3. What does strptime() return?
qna.a: It returns a datetime object.

qna.q: Q4. Why must the format string match the input string?
qna.a: The format string tells Python how the characters in the input should be interpreted. If the structure does not match, parsing normally raises ValueError.

qna.q: Q5. What is the format for parsing 2026-10-02?
qna.a: Use "%Y-%m-%d".

qna.q: Q6. What is the difference between %m and %M?
qna.a: %m represents the month, while %M represents minutes.

qna.q: Q7. Which format codes are used for a 12-hour time with AM/PM?
qna.a: Use %I for the 12-hour clock and %p for AM/PM.

qna.q: Q8. What exception can occur when parsing fails?
qna.a: ValueError can be raised when the input does not match the expected format or represents an invalid date/time.

qna.q: Q9. Why is date parsing useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: It converts timestamp strings from sources such as CSV files and APIs into datetime objects that can be compared, filtered, and used for time-based calculations.

qna.q: Q10. What is the difference between parsing and formatting?
qna.a: Parsing converts a string into a datetime object using strptime(), while formatting converts a datetime object into a string using strftime().

items.title: Date Calculations
explanation: What Are Date Calculations?

Date calculations mean performing operations with dates and times, such as finding the difference between two dates, adding or subtracting days, calculating deadlines, and determining how long a process took.
Python provides the datetime module and timedelta class for these operations.
from datetime import date, timedelta today = date.today() next_week = today + timedelta(days=7) print("Today:", today) print("Next week:", next_week)
Simple idea: Use datetime or date for points in time, and timedelta for durations or movement between points in time.
Adding Days to a Date
You can add a timedelta to a date to calculate a future date.
from datetime import date, timedelta today = date.today() future_date = today + timedelta(days=10) print("Today:", today) print("Future date:", future_date)
Today │ │ + 10 days ▼ Future Date
Subtracting Days from a Date
You can subtract a timedelta to calculate a date in the past.
from datetime import date, timedelta today = date.today() past_date = today - timedelta(days=10) print("Past date:", past_date)
Adding or Subtracting Weeks
timedelta also supports weeks.

from datetime import date, timedelta today = date.today() next_two_weeks = today + timedelta(weeks=2) previous_week = today - timedelta(weeks=1) print("After two weeks:", next_two_weeks) print("One week before:", previous_week)
Adding Hours and Minutes to datetime
For calculations involving time as well as dates, use a datetime object.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta now = datetime.now() one_hour_later = now + timedelta(hours=1) thirty_minutes_earlier = now - timedelta(minutes=30) print("Now:", now) print("One hour later:", one_hour_later) print("30 minutes earlier:", thirty_minutes_earlier)
Finding the Difference Between Two Dates
Subtracting one date from another produces a timedelta.
from datetime import date start = date(2026, 10, 1) end = date(2026, 10, 15) difference = end - start print("Difference:", difference) print("Days:", difference.days)
The result represents the amount of time between the two dates.
Finding the Difference Between Two datetimes
The same principle works with timestamps containing both date and time.

from datetime import datetime start = datetime(2026, 10, 2, 9, 0, 0) end = datetime(2026, 10, 2, 17, 30, 0) difference = end - start print("Duration:", difference) print("Seconds:", difference.total_seconds())
Here, the difference represents 8 hours and 30 minutes.
Calculating Hours from a Duration
total_seconds() can be used when you need to convert a complete duration into hours.
from datetime import timedelta duration = timedelta(hours=8, minutes=30) hours = duration.total_seconds() / 3600 print("Hours:", hours)
Calculating Minutes from a Duration
from datetime import timedelta duration = timedelta(hours=2, minutes=30) minutes = duration.total_seconds() / 60 print("Minutes:", minutes)
Comparing Dates
Date and datetime objects can be compared using operators such as <, >, <=, >=, and ==.
from datetime import date start = date(2026, 10, 1) end = date(2026, 10, 10) print(start < end) print(start > end) print(start == end)
This is useful when checking whether a record is before or after a processing cutoff.
Checking Whether a Date Is Inside a Range
You can combine comparisons to determine whether a date falls between two dates.
