from datetime import date start = date(2026, 10, 1) end = date(2026, 10, 31) record_date = date(2026, 10, 15) if start <= record_date <= end: print("Date is inside the range")
Data Engineering use: This pattern is useful for filtering records that belong to a particular processing period.
Calculating a Pipeline Duration
A common Data Engineering requirement is measuring how long a pipeline took to run.

from datetime import datetime start_time = datetime.now() # Pipeline processing happens here end_time = datetime.now() duration = end_time - start_time print("Start:", start_time) print("End:", end_time) print("Duration:", duration)
Pipeline Start │ ▼ Processing │ ▼ Pipeline End │ ▼ End - Start │ ▼ Duration
Data Engineering Example — Last 24 Hours
A pipeline may need to process only records from the previous 24 hours.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta end_time = datetime.now() start_time = end_time - timedelta(hours=24) print("Process from:", start_time) print("Process until:", end_time)
These timestamps can be used as boundaries for an incremental database query or API request.
Data Engineering Example — Last 7 Days
from datetime import datetime, timedelta end_time = datetime.now() start_time = end_time - timedelta(days=7) print("Start:", start_time) print("End:", end_time)
This creates a rolling seven-day processing window.
Calculating a Future Deadline
You can calculate a deadline by adding a duration to the current timestamp.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta created_at = datetime.now() deadline = created_at + timedelta(hours=4) print("Created:", created_at) print("Deadline:", deadline)
Checking Whether a Deadline Has Passed
Compare the current time with the deadline to determine whether an operation is overdue.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta created_at = datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=5) deadline = created_at + timedelta(hours=4) if datetime.now() > deadline: print("Deadline has passed") else: print("Still within deadline")
Negative Differences
If the first date is later than the second date, subtraction produces a negative timedelta.
from datetime import date first = date(2026, 10, 15) second = date(2026, 10, 10) difference = second - first print(difference) print(difference.days)
Negative durations can be useful when determining how far something is ahead of or behind a reference date.
Important: Date Arithmetic Is Not the Same as Month Arithmetic
timedelta supports fixed durations such as days and weeks, but it does not provide a direct months=1 argument because calendar months do not all have the same number of days.
# This is valid timedelta(days=30) # This is not valid timedelta(months=1)
If you need calendar-aware operations such as "one month later", use an appropriate calendar/date library or handle the calendar rule explicitly.
Common Mistakes

• Trying to use timedelta(months=1).
  • Using .seconds when the complete duration is needed; use total_seconds().
  • Mixing incompatible naive and time-zone-aware datetime objects.
  • Comparing date strings in inconsistent formats instead of converting them to date/datetime objects.
  • Forgetting that subtracting two dates produces a timedelta, not an integer.
Quick Summary

Remember:
date + timedelta → future date
date - timedelta → previous date
date2 - date1 → timedelta difference
difference.days → whole-day component
difference.total_seconds() → complete duration in seconds
datetime + timedelta → future timestamp
Data Engineering Connection

Date calculations are frequently used in incremental ETL jobs, pipeline execution tracking, data freshness checks, rolling processing windows, SLA/deadline checks, and timestamp-based database queries.

Practical Rule: Keep dates and timestamps as Python date/datetime objects while calculating. Use timedelta for fixed durations, and format the final result into a string only when you need to display or export it.
practice: Step 1: Calculate the date 30 days from today.
from datetime import date, timedelta today = date.today() future = today + timedelta(days=30) print("Today:", today) print("After 30 days:", future)
Step 2: Calculate the date 30 days before today.
past = today - timedelta(days=30) print("30 days before:", past)
Step 3: Calculate the number of days between two dates.
start = date(2026, 10, 1) end = date(2026, 10, 20) difference = end - start print("Days:", difference.days)
Step 4: Create a 24-hour processing window from the current time.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta end_time = datetime.now() start_time = end_time - timedelta(hours=24) print("Start:", start_time) print("End:", end_time)
Step 5: Simulate a pipeline and calculate its execution duration.

from datetime import datetime start_time = datetime.now() # Simulate some processing here end_time = datetime.now() duration = end_time - start_time print("Pipeline duration:", duration) print("Duration in seconds:", duration.total_seconds())
Step 6: Create a deadline four hours after a job starts and check whether the deadline has passed.
from datetime import datetime, timedelta start_time = datetime.now() deadline = start_time + timedelta(hours=4) if datetime.now() > deadline: print("Deadline passed") else: print("Within deadline")
Practice Goal: Be able to add and subtract time, calculate date differences, create processing windows, measure pipeline duration, and check deadlines using Python date calculations.

qna.q: Q1. How do you add days to a date?
qna.a: Add a timedelta to the date, for example today + timedelta(days=7).

qna.q: Q2. What is returned when two dates are subtracted?
qna.a: A timedelta object representing the difference between the dates.

qna.q: Q3. How do you calculate the number of days between two dates?
qna.a: Subtract the dates and access the days attribute of the resulting timedelta.

qna.q: Q4. How do you calculate the complete duration in seconds?
qna.a: Use difference.total_seconds().

qna.q: Q5. How can you calculate the last 24 hours?
qna.a: Use the current datetime as the end time and subtract timedelta(hours=24) to obtain the start time.

qna.q: Q6. Can timedelta directly represent one month?
qna.a: No. timedelta does not support a months argument because calendar months have different lengths.

qna.q: Q7. How can you measure how long a pipeline took?
qna.a: Record the start and end timestamps and subtract them: end_time - start_time.

qna.q: Q8. How can you check whether a deadline has passed?
qna.a: Compare the current datetime with the deadline using an operator such as >.

qna.q: Q9. Why are date calculations useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: They are useful for incremental processing windows, pipeline duration, data freshness checks, deadlines, rolling time periods, and timestamp-based filtering.

qna.q: Q10. Should date values be converted to strings before performing calculations?
qna.a: Generally no. Keep them as date or datetime objects for calculations and format them as strings when needed for display or output.

items.title: Time Zones Basics
explanation: What Is a Time Zone?
A time zone is a region that uses a particular local time relative to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). The same moment can have different clock times in different parts of the world.
One moment in time │ ├── India → IST (UTC+05:30) ├── London → UTC / GMT └── New York → Eastern Time Same moment → Different local clock times
For Data Engineering, understanding time zones is important because data can come from applications, databases, APIs, and servers operating in different locations.
What Is UTC?
UTC stands for Coordinated Universal Time. It is the primary reference used for comparing times across different regions.
UTC itself is not a local time zone such as India Standard Time. Instead, it provides a common reference point from which time-zone offsets are expressed.
Simple idea: If a time zone is UTC+05:30, its local clock is five hours and thirty minutes ahead of UTC.
India Standard Time (IST)
India uses India Standard Time (IST), which is UTC+05:30.
UTC → 10:00 IST → 15:30
India uses the same standard time throughout the country and does not currently switch between standard time and daylight saving time.
UTC Offset
A UTC offset tells you how far a local time is ahead of or behind UTC.

OffsetMeaning
UTCSame clock time as UTC
UTC+05:305 hours 30 minutes ahead of UTC
UTC-05:005 hours behind UTC
Offsets can include hours and minutes, which is why India's offset is +05:30 rather than a whole number of hours.
Naive vs Time-Zone-Aware datetime
A naive datetime does not contain time-zone information. An aware datetime contains enough time-zone or offset information to identify its relationship to a time zone.
from datetime import datetime, timezone naive = datetime.now() aware = datetime.now(timezone.utc) print(naive) print(aware)
Important: A naive datetime such as 2026-10-02 10:00:00 does not tell Python whether that time is in India, London, New York, or another location.
Creating a UTC datetime
Python provides timezone.utc for creating an aware datetime representing UTC.
from datetime import datetime, timezone utc_now = datetime.now(timezone.utc) print(utc_now)
This produces an aware UTC timestamp with UTC offset information.
Using timezone and timedelta
Python's datetime.timezone can represent a fixed UTC offset.
from datetime import datetime, timezone, timedelta ist = timezone(timedelta(hours=5, minutes=30)) now_ist = datetime.now(ist) print(now_ist)
This is useful for learning fixed offsets. However, for real-world locations and applications with changing time-zone rules, named IANA time zones are generally more appropriate.
Named Time Zones with zoneinfo
Modern Python provides the built-in zoneinfo module for working with IANA time-zone names.
from datetime import datetime from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo india_time = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Asia/Kolkata")) print(india_time)
Asia/Kolkata is an IANA time-zone identifier for India's time zone.
Data Engineering Tip: Named zones such as Asia/Kolkata are preferable to manually assuming an offset when the actual geographic time zone matters.
Converting Between Time Zones
An aware datetime can be converted to another time zone using astimezone().

from datetime import datetime from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo india_time = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Asia/Kolkata")) new_york_time = india_time.astimezone(ZoneInfo("America/New_York")) print("India:", india_time) print("New York:", new_york_time)
The important point is that the instant in time remains the same; only its local representation changes.
Time Zone Conversion Concept
UTC / Instant │ ├──► Asia/Kolkata │ Local representation │ ├──► America/New_York │ Local representation │ └──► Europe/London Local representation
Think of the UTC instant as the common reference. Different time zones provide different local clock representations of that same instant.
Attaching vs Converting a Time Zone
There is an important difference between creating a timezone-aware datetime with the correct local time and converting an already-aware datetime to another zone.
For example, astimezone() converts an aware datetime while preserving the same instant. Simply replacing the tzinfo field should not be treated as a general-purpose time-zone conversion.
Practical rule: Use astimezone() when you want to convert an aware timestamp from one time zone to another.
Why Time Zones Matter in Data Engineering
Imagine an application in India sends data to a cloud server operating on UTC. A timestamp such as 2026-10-02 10:00:00 can be interpreted incorrectly if its time zone is not known.
Application Asia/Kolkata │ │ timestamp ▼ Data Pipeline UTC processing │ ▼ Data Warehouse │ ▼ Reports / Analytics
If different systems use different time zones without a clear convention, records can appear to arrive on the wrong date or in the wrong processing window.
Common Data Engineering Problems

ProblemPossible Result
Mixing local time and UTCIncorrect timestamps
Dropping timezone informationAmbiguous times
Comparing naive and aware datetimesErrors or incorrect logic
Ignoring source timezoneIncorrect date filtering
Using a fixed offset where a named zone is neededIncorrect local-time conversions in zones with changing rules
UTC as a Common Pipeline Convention
Many distributed systems use UTC as a common representation for timestamps because it avoids repeatedly interpreting timestamps according to the location of individual servers.
from datetime import datetime, timezone created_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc) print(created_at)

Whether a particular organization stores timestamps in UTC or another standard should be determined by its system design and requirements. The important point is to use a clear, consistent convention.
Time Zones and Date Calculations
Time-zone-aware datetime values can be used with timedelta, but you should understand whether your calculation represents a fixed duration or a calendar-based local-time rule.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo india_time = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Asia/Kolkata")) future = india_time + timedelta(hours=24) print("Current:", india_time) print("After 24 hours:", future)
For basic Data Engineering work, the key concept is to keep timestamp semantics clear: know whether you are dealing with an instant, a local wall-clock time, or a duration.
Common Mistakes

• Assuming a naive datetime automatically represents UTC.
  • Mixing naive and aware datetime objects.
  • Hard-coding a UTC offset when a named time zone is required.
  • Using replace(tzinfo=...) as a substitute for time-zone conversion.
  • Ignoring the source time zone when ingesting timestamps from APIs or databases.
  • Storing or comparing timestamps without deciding what time-zone convention the pipeline follows.
Quick Summary

Remember:
UTC → common global time reference
UTC offset → difference from UTC
Naive datetime → no timezone information
Aware datetime → contains timezone/offset information
timezone.utc → UTC timezone object
zoneinfo.ZoneInfo() → named IANA time zone
astimezone() → convert an aware datetime to another time zone
Data Engineering Connection

Time zones become important when data is collected from applications, servers, APIs, databases, and users in different geographic locations. Correct timestamp handling prevents incorrect incremental loads, date partitions, reports, and pipeline scheduling logic.

Practical Rule: Always know what time zone a timestamp represents. For distributed Data Engineering systems, use a clear timestamp convention, commonly UTC, and convert to a local time zone only when required for presentation or business logic.
practice: Step 1: Create a naive datetime and a UTC-aware datetime. Inspect both values.
from datetime import datetime, timezone naive = datetime.now() aware = datetime.now(timezone.utc) print("Naive:", naive) print("Aware:", aware)
Step 2: Create the current time in India's IANA time zone using ZoneInfo.
from datetime import datetime from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo india_time = datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Asia/Kolkata")) print("India:", india_time)
Step 3: Convert the same aware timestamp from India time to UTC.
utc_time = india_time.astimezone(ZoneInfo("UTC")) print("UTC:", utc_time)
Step 4: Convert the same timestamp to another named time zone and compare the displayed clock times.
new_york_time = india_time.astimezone(ZoneInfo("America/New_York")) print("New York:", new_york_time)
Step 5: Create a UTC timestamp for a simulated pipeline event and convert it to India time for display.

from datetime import datetime, timezone from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo pipeline_time = datetime.now(timezone.utc) india_display = pipeline_time.astimezone(ZoneInfo("Asia/Kolkata")) print("Stored/Reference UTC:", pipeline_time) print("India display time:", india_display)
Step 6: Write down why a timestamp such as 2026-10-02 10:00:00 is incomplete when no timezone information is provided.
Practice Goal: Understand UTC, UTC offsets, naive vs aware datetimes, named time zones, and basic time-zone conversion so you can safely handle timestamps in Data Engineering pipelines.

qna.q: Q1. What is a time zone?
qna.a: A time zone is a regional time standard that represents local time relative to a common reference such as UTC.

qna.q: Q2. What is UTC?
qna.a: UTC, or Coordinated Universal Time, is the primary reference used for comparing times across different regions.

qna.q: Q3. What is India's UTC offset?
qna.a: India Standard Time is UTC+05:30.

qna.q: Q4. What is a naive datetime?
qna.a: A naive datetime does not contain time-zone information.

qna.q: Q5. What is an aware datetime?
qna.a: An aware datetime contains time-zone or offset information that allows it to be interpreted relative to a time zone.

qna.q: Q6. How do you create a UTC-aware datetime?
qna.a: Use datetime.now(timezone.utc).

qna.q: Q7. What is ZoneInfo used for?
qna.a: ZoneInfo provides named IANA time zones such as Asia/Kolkata and America/New_York.

qna.q: Q8. What does astimezone() do?
qna.a: It converts an aware datetime to another time zone while representing the same instant in the target zone.

qna.q: Q9. Why are time zones important in Data Engineering?
qna.a: Data can come from systems operating in different regions. Correct time-zone handling prevents incorrect filtering, partitions, incremental loads, reports, and pipeline processing windows.

qna.q: Q10. Why should you avoid mixing naive and aware datetimes?
qna.a: They have different timestamp semantics, and Python does not allow certain comparisons or operations between naive and aware datetimes.

items.title: Environment Variables
explanation: What Are Environment Variables?
Environment variables are values stored outside your Python source code that provide configuration information to a program while it is running.
They are commonly used for database credentials, API keys, application settings, file paths, environment names, and other values that may change between development, testing, and production.

Python Application
↓
Environment Variables
├── DATABASE_HOST
├── DATABASE_USER
├── DATABASE_PASSWORD
├── API_KEY
└── APP_ENV
↓
Application Configuration
Definition: An environment variable is a named value provided by the operating system or execution environment that a program can read while it runs.
Why Use Environment Variables?
Hardcoding configuration directly into Python code makes the application harder to configure and can expose sensitive information.

database_host = "localhost"
database_user = "admin"
database_password = "mysecretpassword"
The password above is stored directly in the source code. This is a bad practice, especially when the code is pushed to GitHub.
Instead, keep configuration outside the source code:

import os

database_host = os.getenv("DATABASE_HOST")
database_user = os.getenv("DATABASE_USER")
database_password = os.getenv("DATABASE_PASSWORD")
Reading Environment Variables with os.environ
Python provides the os.environ mapping for accessing environment variables.

import os

print(os.environ["PATH"])
If the requested variable does not exist, accessing it with os.environ["NAME"] raises a KeyError.

import os

database_host = os.environ["DATABASE_HOST"]
print(database_host)
Important: os.environ["NAME"] expects the variable to exist. Use os.getenv() when you want a safer lookup with an optional default.
Using os.getenv()
os.getenv() reads an environment variable and returns its value.

import os

database_host = os.getenv("DATABASE_HOST")
print(database_host)
If the variable does not exist, os.getenv() returns None.

import os

api_key = os.getenv("API_KEY")

if api_key is None:
print("API key is not configured")
Using Default Values
You can provide a default value as the second argument to os.getenv().

import os

app_env = os.getenv("APP_ENV", "development")
print(app_env)
If APP_ENV exists, its value is returned. Otherwise, development is returned.
DATABASE_PORT = os.getenv("DATABASE_PORT", "5432")
Setting Environment Variables in Python
Python can also set environment variables for the current process using os.environ.

import os

os.environ["APP_ENV"] = "development"

print(os.getenv("APP_ENV"))
This changes the environment variable for the current Python process and processes started from it. It should not be confused with permanently configuring the operating system.
Setting Environment Variables in Windows CMD
On Windows CMD, you can temporarily set an environment variable for the current CMD session.

set DATABASE_HOST=localhost
set DATABASE_USER=admin
Then Python can read those values:

import os

print(os.getenv("DATABASE_HOST"))
print(os.getenv("DATABASE_USER"))
Environment Variables and Sensitive Information
Environment variables are commonly used to keep secrets such as passwords, API keys, and tokens outside the source code.

import os

api_key = os.getenv("API_KEY")
database_password = os.getenv("DATABASE_PASSWORD")
This helps prevent accidentally committing credentials directly into a Git repository.
Security Rule: Never commit real passwords, API keys, database credentials, access tokens, or other secrets directly into your source code or Git repository.
.env Files
A .env file is commonly used during local development to store environment-style configuration.

DATABASE_HOST=localhost
DATABASE_USER=admin
DATABASE_PASSWORD=mysecret
DATABASE_PORT=5432
APP_ENV=development
Python does not automatically load a .env file. A commonly used package called python-dotenv can load these values into the process environment.
Using python-dotenv
Install the package using pip:
pip install python-dotenv
Then load the .env file:

from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os

load_dotenv()

database_host = os.getenv("DATABASE_HOST")
database_user = os.getenv("DATABASE_USER")

print(database_host)
print(database_user)
The load_dotenv() function reads the .env file and loads its values so that Python can access them through os.getenv().
Protecting the .env File with .gitignore
If your .env file contains secrets, it should normally not be committed to Git.

# .gitignore
.env
A safer approach is to provide a template containing only variable names and example values.

# .env.example
DATABASE_HOST=localhost
DATABASE_USER=your_username
DATABASE_PASSWORD=your_password
DATABASE_PORT=5432

Important: .env is a development configuration file, not a security system. Anyone who has access to the actual secret can use it, so production systems should use an appropriate secret-management solution.
Environment-Based Configuration
The same Python application may run in different environments such as development, testing, and production.
APP_ENV=development

import os

environment = os.getenv("APP_ENV", "development")

if environment == "development":
print("Development configuration")
elif environment == "production":
print("Production configuration")
The Python code can remain the same while the configuration changes through environment variables.
Data Engineering Example
Imagine a data pipeline that connects to PostgreSQL. The connection information should not be hardcoded in the pipeline code.

import os

DB_HOST = os.getenv("DB_HOST")
DB_PORT = os.getenv("DB_PORT", "5432")
DB_NAME = os.getenv("DB_NAME")
DB_USER = os.getenv("DB_USER")
DB_PASSWORD = os.getenv("DB_PASSWORD")

print(DB_HOST)
print(DB_PORT)
print(DB_NAME)
print(DB_USER)
The same pipeline can then run against different databases by changing the environment configuration instead of changing the Python source code.

Python ETL Pipeline
↓
Read Configuration
↓
Environment Variables
↓
Database Connection
↓
Extract → Transform → Load
Environment Variables in Data Engineering

VariableExample Purpose
DB_HOSTDatabase server address
DB_PORTDatabase port
DB_NAMEDatabase name
DB_USERDatabase username
DB_PASSWORDDatabase password
API_KEYAPI authentication key
APP_ENVDevelopment/testing/production environment
Common Mistakes

• Hardcoding passwords or API keys inside Python files.
  • Committing a real .env file containing secrets to Git.
  • Using os.environ["NAME"] without understanding that a missing variable raises KeyError.
  • Assuming Python automatically reads .env files.
  • Printing passwords, API keys, or tokens into logs.
  • Using different variable names between the configuration and Python code.
Quick Summary

ConceptMeaning
Environment VariableExternal configuration value available to a running process
os.environMapping used to access environment variables
os.getenv()Reads an environment variable safely and can provide a default
.envCommon local-development file for environment-style configuration
python-dotenvPackage commonly used to load values from a .env file
.gitignoreCan prevent the local .env file from being committed

Data Engineering Takeaway: Environment variables separate application code from environment-specific configuration. You will encounter this concept again when working with databases, APIs, Docker, Airflow, cloud services, CI/CD, and production data pipelines.
practice: Step 1: Create a Python file named env_demo.py.

import os

print(os.getenv("USERNAME"))
Step 2: Read a variable using os.environ.

import os

print(os.environ["USERNAME"])
Step 3: Create your own environment variable in Python and read it using os.getenv().

import os

os.environ["APP_ENV"] = "development"

print(os.getenv("APP_ENV"))
Step 4: Practice using a default value when the variable does not exist.

import os

port = os.getenv("APP_PORT", "5432")
print(port)
Step 5: Install python-dotenv and create a local .env file.
pip install python-dotenv

# .env
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_USER=admin
DB_NAME=analytics
Step 6: Load the .env values from Python.

from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os

load_dotenv()

print(os.getenv("DB_HOST"))
print(os.getenv("DB_USER"))
print(os.getenv("DB_NAME"))
Step 7: Create a .gitignore file and add .env so the local configuration file is not committed.

# .gitignore
.env
Step 8: Create a small Data Engineering-style configuration program that reads database host, port, database name, username, and password from environment variables.

import os

db_config = {
"host": os.getenv("DB_HOST"),
"port": os.getenv("DB_PORT", "5432"),
"database": os.getenv("DB_NAME"),
"user": os.getenv("DB_USER"),
"password": os.getenv("DB_PASSWORD")
}

print(db_config["host"])
print(db_config["port"])
print(db_config["database"])
print(db_config["user"])

Practice Goal: By the end of this practice, you should be able to keep configuration outside your Python code and read environment variables using os.getenv(). Do not print real passwords or API keys while practicing.

qna.q: Q1. What is an environment variable?
qna.a: An environment variable is a named value provided to a running program by its execution environment. It is commonly used for configuration such as database settings, API keys, and environment names.

qna.q: Q2. Why should database passwords not be hardcoded in Python?
qna.a: Hardcoding passwords can expose credentials in source code, Git history, logs, or shared repositories. Configuration and secrets should be kept outside the source code.

qna.q: Q3. What is the difference between os.environ and os.getenv()?
qna.a: os.environ["NAME"] accesses an environment variable and raises KeyError if it does not exist. os.getenv("NAME") returns None when it is missing, or a supplied default value if one is provided.

qna.q: Q4. How do you provide a default value with os.getenv()?
qna.a: Pass the default value as the second argument, for example os.getenv("DB_PORT", "5432").

qna.q: Q5. Does Python automatically read a .env file?
qna.a: No. A .env file is not automatically loaded by Python. A package such as python-dotenv can be used to load its values during local development.

qna.q: Q6. What is python-dotenv?
qna.a: python-dotenv is a Python package commonly used to load configuration values from a .env file into the process environment.

qna.q: Q7. Why is .gitignore important when using .env?
qna.a: A .gitignore entry such as .env helps prevent the local .env file from being accidentally committed to Git when it contains sensitive configuration.

qna.q: Q8. How are environment variables useful in Data Engineering?
qna.a: They allow the same pipeline code to use different database connections, API credentials, storage locations, and environment-specific settings without changing the source code.

qna.q: Q9. Can Python set an environment variable?
qna.a: Yes. You can assign a value through os.environ["NAME"] = "value". This affects the current process environment and can also affect processes started from it.

qna.q: Q10. Should passwords be printed while debugging environment variables?
qna.a: No. Avoid printing passwords, API keys, access tokens, and other secrets. Log only the non-sensitive information needed for troubleshooting.
